msg.content:
<document>
<title>Maritime Mobile Service Identity</title>
<fragment>
Digital radio identification code for marine stations

A **Maritime Mobile Service Identity** (**MMSI**) is effectively a maritime object's international *maritime telephone number*, a temporarily assigned UID, issued by that object's current flag state (unlike an IMO number, which is a global forever UID).


An MMSI comprises a series of nine digits, consisting of three Maritime Identification Digits (country-codes), concatenated with a specific identifier. Whenever an object is re-flagged, a new MMSI must be assigned.


A 'maritime object' could be anything which requests an MMSI identifier. e.g. a vessel, fixed offshore installation, mobile unit, maritime aircraft, coast station, etc. 
Communications may be routed to 'individual objects', or to 'groups of objects'. A group call to objects can be based on an object's - locale, owner/operator/fleet, type, etc. or combinations thereof.


</fragment>
<fragment>

The MMSI was meant to be an all-inclusive ship electronic identity, used in one form or another by every GMDSS or telecommunications instrument on the ship. Questions have been raised, however, whether the MMSI can in practice totally fulfill that role. ITU may eventually end the practice of relating Inmarsat MESIN identities with the ship MMSI identity.


To help mitigate against MMSI number exhaustion, manufacturers are required to cripple DSC-capable radios so that an MMSI number can only be entered once, which means that a device owner cannot move the radio from one boat to another. This is especially egregious for hand-held VHF devices, for which a single MMSI number makes little sense.[*opinion*]


</fragment>
<fragment>

MMSI are formed in such a way that the identity or part thereof can be used by telephone and telex subscribers connected to the general telecommunications network to call any of these objects automatically. Communications are sent in digital form over a radio frequency channel.




## Types

[edit]

There are now six kinds of maritime mobile service identities:



* Ship station identities
* Group ship station identities
* Coast station identities
* Group coast station identities
* SAR aircraft
* Navigational aids and craft associated with a parent ship


## Maritime identification digits (MID)

[edit]

Main article: Maritime identification digits


</fragment>
<fragment>
Because all ships on international voyages, as well as all ships fitted with an Inmarsat B or M ship earth station, are assigned MMSIs of the format MIDxxx000, a serious problem has arisen internationally in assigning sufficient numbers of MIDs to all administrations that need them. For example, a country having 10,000 Inmarsat-equipped ships would require 10 MIDs just to accommodate those 10,000 ships. If 50,000 boaters decided to fit small Inmarsat M terminals, 50 additional MIDs would be required to accommodate them.


The problem exists with Inmarsat-equipped ships because ITU-T recommendations require that Inmarsat ship earth stations be assigned the identity (MESIN) TMIDxxxYY, where T indicates the type of Inmarsat station, YY indicates the Inmarsat station extension (e.g."00" might indicate a telephone in the bridge, "01" might indicate a fax machine in the radio room, etc.), and MIDxxx indicates the ship station number, which relates to the assigned ship station identity MIDxxx000.


</fragment>
</document>

<document>
<title>Maritime identification digits</title>
<fragment>
**Maritime identification digits** are used by radio communication facilities to identify their home country or base area in Digital Selective Calling (DSC), Automatic Transmitter Identification System (ATIS), and Automatic Identification System (AIS) messages as part of their Maritime Mobile Service Identities. The International Telecommunication Union facilitates the assignment of MIDs to countries.[1] Note that not all countries have MIDs; those without are typically landlocked, with no access to international waters. Sorting MID assignments in numerical order reveals a regional structure, with the first digit:



* 2 assigned to Europe,
* 3 to North America and the Caribbean Sea,
* 4 to Asia (except the southeast),
* 5 to the Pacific and Eastern Indian Oceans and Southeast Asia,
* 6 to Africa, the Atlantic and Western Indian Oceans, and
* 7 to South America.

***Wonder of the Seas*** is the flagship of Royal Caribbean International. She was completed in 2022 in the Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard in Saint-Nazaire, France,[5] the fifth in Royal Caribbean's *Oasis* class of cruise ships.[6] At 236,857 GT, she was the largest cruise ship in the world by gross tonnage, surpassed by the succeeding ship, *Icon of the Seas*, also owned by Royal Caribbean International.




## Description and design

[edit]

*Wonder of the Seas* measures 1,188 feet (362 m) in length and has a gross tonnage of 236,857 across 18 decks. This ship accommodates 5,734 passengers at double occupancy or up to a maximum of 6,988 passengers, as well as a 2,300 crew. There are 16 decks for guest use, 20 restaurants, four pools and 2,867 cabins.[4]

***Utopia of the Seas*** is a cruise ship under construction for Royal Caribbean International. She will be the sixth ship in the Oasis Class and is scheduled to enter service in the summer of 2024 out of Port Canaveral.[2] She will be the only ship in the class to not hold the title as the world's largest cruise ship.[3]



## History

[edit]

On 18 February 2019, Royal Caribbean announced an order of a sixth and final *Oasis*-class cruise ship. She will be the first in the class to be powered by liquefied natural gas.[4]


Royal Caribbean applied to register a trademark for *Utopia of the Seas* in 2021, out of 23 other ship names.[3]


On 5 April 2022, Royal Caribbean announced the name, *Utopia of the Seas* and the steel cutting ceremony.[5]


The LNG-tanks were built by Wärtsila and delivered in November 2022.[6]

Based on my search of the Wikipedia articles for Royal Caribbean's Oasis-class ships, here's the information about ordering and construction costs:

## **Known Costs:**

- **Oasis of the Seas** (2009): **$1.4 billion** (ordered in 2006)
- **Symphony of the Seas** (2018): **$1.35 billion** (ordered in 2014)

## **Key Patterns:**

1. **Progressive Increase**: The costs generally rose over time as the ships became larger and more technologically advanced, though Symphony of the Seas was slightly less expensive than Oasis of the Seas when adjusted for construction year.

2. **Construction Timeline**: 
   - Oasis of the Seas: Ordered February 2006, completed October 2009
   - Symphony of the Seas: Ordered May 2014, completed March 2018

3. **Size Evolution**: The ships grew progressively larger in gross tonnage throughout the class

## **Unknown Costs:**

The specific construction costs for **Allure of the Seas** (2010), **Harmony of the Seas** (2016), and **Wonder of the Seas** (2021/2022) are not clearly stated in their Wikipedia articles. However, given the industry trend and increasing complexity, it's likely that:

- Later ships like **Wonder of the Seas** (236,857 GT) probably cost well over $1.5 billion
- **Utopia of the Seas** (under construction, 2024) may be even more expensive due to its LNG propulsion system

The Oasis-class represents some of the most expensive passenger ships ever built, with costs reflecting their revolutionary design, massive size, and increasingly sophisticated amenities and technology.

*Icon of the Seas* is powered by liquified natural gas (LNG), with a gross tonnage of 250,800. The ship has six multi-fuel Wärtsilä engines generating 67,500 kW (90,520 hp) of power. The engines can be powered with both LNG and distillate fuel. The ship contains other alternative energy features, like the use of fuel cells to produce electricity and fresh water.[4] *Icon of the Seas* is the first Royal Caribbean vessel to use such technology.[16]


The ship will have a crew of 2,350, and a capacity of 5,610 passengers at double occupancy, or 7,600 passengers at maximum capacity.[2]


*Icon of the Seas* has 20 decks with seven swimming pools and six water slides. The company claims the ship has the tallest waterfall, the tallest water slide, the largest waterpark, and the first suspended infinity pool of any ship.[2]

***Wonder of the Seas*** is the flagship of Royal Caribbean International. She was completed in 2022 in the Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard in Saint-Nazaire, France,[5] the fifth in Royal Caribbean's *Oasis* class of cruise ships.[6] At 236,857 GT, she was the largest cruise ship in the world by gross tonnage, surpassed by the succeeding ship, *Icon of the Seas*, also owned by Royal Caribbean International.




## Description and design

[edit]

*Wonder of the Seas* measures 1,188 feet (362 m) in length and has a gross tonnage of 236,857 across 18 decks. This ship accommodates 5,734 passengers at double occupancy or up to a maximum of 6,988 passengers, as well as a 2,300 crew. There are 16 decks for guest use, 20 restaurants, four pools and 2,867 cabins.[4]

Call signs assigned as unique identifiers to ships and boats

![](image)Soviet nuclear Icebreaker *Arktika* with call sign UKTY
![](image)USS *Carl Vinson* and JS *Ashigara* displaying signal flags showing callsigns NCVV and JSRA, respectively
**Maritime call signs** are call signs assigned as unique identifiers to ships and boats. All radio transmissions must be individually identified by the call sign. Merchant and naval vessels are assigned call signs by their national licensing authorities.



## History

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Leisure craft with VHF radios may not be assigned call signs, in which case the name of the vessel is used instead. Ships in the U.S. wishing to have a radio licence anyway are under FCC Radio Service Code SA: "Ship Recreational or Voluntarily Equipped".[5] Those calls follow the land mobile format of the initial letter K or W followed by 1 or 2 letters followed by 3 or 4 numbers (such as KX0983 or WXX0029).


U.S. Coast Guard small boats have a number that is shown on both bows (i.e. port and starboard) in which the first two digits indicate the nominal length of the boat in feet. For example, Coast Guard 47021 refers to the 21st in the series of 47-foot motor lifeboats. The call sign might also be abbreviated to the final two or three numbers during operations, for example: Coast Guard zero two one.



## See also

[edit]

* Maritime Mobile Service Identity
* Pan-pan


## References

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

On April 14, 1912, the RMS *Titanic* station MGY, busily delivering telegram traffic from ship's passengers to the coastal station at Cape Race, Newfoundland (call sign MCE), would receive warnings of ice fields from Marconi stations aboard the MV *Mesaba* (call sign MMU) and the SS *Californian* (call sign MWL).[1] Its distress call *CQD CQD CQD CQD CQD CQD DE MGY MGY MGY MGY MGY MGY POSITION 41.44 N 50.24 W* would be answered by a station aboard the RMS *Carpathia* (call sign MPA).[2] Later that same year, an international conference standardised radio call signs so that the first two letters would uniquely identify a transmitter's country of origin.


</fragment>
<fragment>

Merchant and naval vessels are assigned call signs by their national licensing authorities. In the case of states such as Liberia or Panama, which are flags of convenience for ship registration, call signs for larger vessels consist of the national prefix plus three letters (for example, 3LXY, and sometimes followed by a number, i.e. 3LXY2). United States merchant vessels are given call signs beginning with the letters "W" or "K" while U.S. naval ships are assigned call signs beginning with "N". Originally, both ships and broadcast stations were given call signs in this series consisting of three or four letters, but as demand for both marine radio and broadcast call signs grew, gradually American-flagged vessels were given longer call signs with mixed letters and numbers.


</fragment>

msg.content:
<document>
<title>Maritime Mobile Service Identity</title>
<fragment>
Digital radio identification code for marine stations

A **Maritime Mobile Service Identity** (**MMSI**) is effectively a maritime object's international *maritime telephone number*, a temporarily assigned UID, issued by that object's current flag state (unlike an IMO number, which is a global forever UID).


An MMSI comprises a series of nine digits, consisting of three Maritime Identification Digits (country-codes), concatenated with a specific identifier. Whenever an object is re-flagged, a new MMSI must be assigned.


A 'maritime object' could be anything which requests an MMSI identifier. e.g. a vessel, fixed offshore installation, mobile unit, maritime aircraft, coast station, etc. 
Communications may be routed to 'individual objects', or to 'groups of objects'. A group call to objects can be based on an object's - locale, owner/operator/fleet, type, etc. or combinations thereof.


</fragment>
<fragment>

The World Radio Conference, Geneva, 1997 (WRC-97), adopted Resolution 344 concerning the exhaustion of the maritime mobile service identity resource. In view of improvements to public switched telephone networks, and new capabilities of the Inmarsat system other than Inmarsat B or M, previous restrictions should no longer be applicable. All nine digits of the MMSI can be used in such cases, and no longer need to end in trailing zeros.



## See also

[edit]

![](image)

Wikidata has the property: 
* ![](image) ***MMSI (P587)*** (see uses)

* Automatic Identification System uses MMSI codegroups for ship ID
* Global Maritime Distress Safety System
* Inmarsat and the International Mobile Satellite Organization (IMSO)
* Maritime call sign, not tied to MMSI but can contain MMSI after
* SOLAS Convention a global Maritime Safety Convention


## References

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

MMSI are formed in such a way that the identity or part thereof can be used by telephone and telex subscribers connected to the general telecommunications network to call any of these objects automatically. Communications are sent in digital form over a radio frequency channel.




## Types

[edit]

There are now six kinds of maritime mobile service identities:



* Ship station identities
* Group ship station identities
* Coast station identities
* Group coast station identities
* SAR aircraft
* Navigational aids and craft associated with a parent ship


## Maritime identification digits (MID)

[edit]

Main article: Maritime identification digits


</fragment>
<fragment>

The MMSI was meant to be an all-inclusive ship electronic identity, used in one form or another by every GMDSS or telecommunications instrument on the ship. Questions have been raised, however, whether the MMSI can in practice totally fulfill that role. ITU may eventually end the practice of relating Inmarsat MESIN identities with the ship MMSI identity.


To help mitigate against MMSI number exhaustion, manufacturers are required to cripple DSC-capable radios so that an MMSI number can only be entered once, which means that a device owner cannot move the radio from one boat to another. This is especially egregious for hand-held VHF devices, for which a single MMSI number makes little sense.[*opinion*]


</fragment>
<fragment>
In the United States (one of whose MIDs is 366), federal MMSIs are assigned by the National Telecommunications and Information Administration, and are normally (but not always) formed as 3669xxxxx. Non-federal MMSIs are assigned by the Federal Communications Commission normally as part of the ship station license application, and are formed as 366xxx000 for ships on international voyages and ships needing an Inmarsat mobile earth station, or 366xxxxx0 for all other ships.


The United States Coast Guard group ship station call identity is 036699999, and group coast station call identity is 003669999.


In the U.S., MMSIs are primarily used for digital selective calling and for assigning Inmarsat identities.



## Exhaustion of MMSIs

[edit]


</fragment>
</document>

<document>
<title>Maritime identification digits</title>
<fragment>
**Maritime identification digits** are used by radio communication facilities to identify their home country or base area in Digital Selective Calling (DSC), Automatic Transmitter Identification System (ATIS), and Automatic Identification System (AIS) messages as part of their Maritime Mobile Service Identities. The International Telecommunication Union facilitates the assignment of MIDs to countries.[1] Note that not all countries have MIDs; those without are typically landlocked, with no access to international waters. Sorting MID assignments in numerical order reveals a regional structure, with the first digit:



* 2 assigned to Europe,
* 3 to North America and the Caribbean Sea,
* 4 to Asia (except the southeast),
* 5 to the Pacific and Eastern Indian Oceans and Southeast Asia,
* 6 to Africa, the Atlantic and Western Indian Oceans, and
* 7 to South America.

Online marine traffic tracking service

**MarineTraffic** is a maritime analytics provider,[1] which provides real-time information on the movements of ships and the current location of ships in harbors and ports.[2] A database of information on the vessels includes for example details of the location where they were built plus dimensions of the vessels, gross tonnage and International Maritime Organisation (IMO) number. Users can submit photographs of the vessels which other users can rate.


The basic MarineTraffic service can be used without cost; more advanced functions such as satellite-based tracking are available subject to payment.[3]


The site has six million unique visitors on a monthly basis. In April 2015, the service had 600,000 registered users.[4][5]




## How it works

[edit]

Data is gathered from in excess of 18,000 AIS equipped volunteer contributors in over 140 countries around the world.[6] Information provided by AIS equipment, such as unique identification, position, course, and speed, is then transferred to the main Marine Traffic servers for display via the website in real time. The site uses data from OpenStreetMap on its base map, and the paid version lets users display ship locations on Nautical Charts.



## History

[edit]

MarineTraffic was originally developed as an academic project at the University of the Aegean in Ermoupoli, Greece.[7][8]


In late 2007, Professor Dimitris Lekkas published it as a trial version.[4]



## Community

[edit]

MarineTraffic is highly dependent on its community of radio amateurs or AIS Station operators, its photographers and translators.


In support of the community, MarineTraffic recently made available a free AIS processing tool, under a Creative Commons license.[9]



## Acquisition

[edit]

In February 2023, data and analytics firm Kpler announced the acquisition of MarineTraffic and Fleetmon for an undisclosed sum.[1][2] The acquisitions closed in March 2023.

[edit]

Royal Caribbean applied to register a trademark for "Icon of the Seas" in 2016.[8]

<document>
<title>Maritime Mobile Service Identity</title>
<fragment>
Digital radio identification code for marine stations

A **Maritime Mobile Service Identity** (**MMSI**) is effectively a maritime object's international *maritime telephone number*, a temporarily assigned UID, issued by that object's current flag state (unlike an IMO number, which is a global forever UID).


An MMSI comprises a series of nine digits, consisting of three Maritime Identification Digits (country-codes), concatenated with a specific identifier. Whenever an object is re-flagged, a new MMSI must be assigned.


A 'maritime object' could be anything which requests an MMSI identifier. e.g. a vessel, fixed offshore installation, mobile unit, maritime aircraft, coast station, etc. 
Communications may be routed to 'individual objects', or to 'groups of objects'. A group call to objects can be based on an object's - locale, owner/operator/fleet, type, etc. or combinations thereof.


</fragment>
<fragment>

The World Radio Conference, Geneva, 1997 (WRC-97), adopted Resolution 344 concerning the exhaustion of the maritime mobile service identity resource. In view of improvements to public switched telephone networks, and new capabilities of the Inmarsat system other than Inmarsat B or M, previous restrictions should no longer be applicable. All nine digits of the MMSI can be used in such cases, and no longer need to end in trailing zeros.



## See also

[edit]

MMSI are formed in such a way that the identity or part thereof can be used by telephone and telex subscribers connected to the general telecommunications network to call any of these objects automatically. Communications are sent in digital form over a radio frequency channel.




## Types

[edit]

There are now six kinds of maritime mobile service identities:



* Ship station identities
* Group ship station identities
* Coast station identities
* Group coast station identities
* SAR aircraft
* Navigational aids and craft associated with a parent ship

<document>
<title>Maritime identification digits</title>
<fragment>
**Maritime identification digits** are used by radio communication facilities to identify their home country or base area in Digital Selective Calling (DSC), Automatic Transmitter Identification System (ATIS), and Automatic Identification System (AIS) messages as part of their Maritime Mobile Service Identities. The International Telecommunication Union facilitates the assignment of MIDs to countries.[1] Note that not all countries have MIDs; those without are typically landlocked, with no access to international waters. Sorting MID assignments in numerical order reveals a regional structure, with the first digit:



* 2 assigned to Europe,
* 3 to North America and the Caribbean Sea,
* 4 to Asia (except the southeast),
* 5 to the Pacific and Eastern Indian Oceans and Southeast Asia,
* 6 to Africa, the Atlantic and Western Indian Oceans, and
* 7 to South America.




</fragment>

<document>
<title>Icon of the Seas</title>
<fragment>

***Icon of the Seas*** is a cruise ship built for Royal Caribbean International and will be the lead ship of the *Icon* class. She is scheduled to enter service in early 2024 out of PortMiami in the US.[3] At 250,800 gross tonnage (GT), *Icon of the Seas* will be the largest cruise ship in the world.[2][1]




## History

[edit]

In October 2016, Royal Caribbean and Finnish shipbuilder Meyer Turku announced an order to build two ships under the project name "Icon".[4] The ships are expected to be delivered in the third quarter of 2023 and in 2025.[5][6] The ships will be classified by DNV.[7]


Royal Caribbean applied to register a trademark for "Icon of the Seas" in 2016.[8]


</fragment>
<fragment>
1. ^ ***a*** ***b*** "Icon of the Seas Ship Details Revealed - Cruise Critic". *www.cruisecritic.com*.
2. ^ ***a*** ***b*** ***c*** ***d*** ***e*** ***f*** ***g*** "Royal Caribbean reveals spectacular design for new Icon of the Seas cruise ship". *Royal Caribbean Blog*. 20 October 2022.
3. **^** "Icon of the Seas | Cruise Ships | Royal Caribbean Cruise". *Icon of the Seas*. Retrieved 17 February 2022.
4. ^ ***a*** ***b*** "Powered By LNG and Fuel Cells, Royal Caribbean International's New Ships Will Ride the Wave of the Future". *Royal Caribbean Press Center* (Press release). Royal Caribbean Cruises Ltd. 10 October 2016. Retrieved 3 February 2017.
5. **^** "Icon of the Seas: Itinerary, features, and more". *Royal Caribbean Blog*. 6 January 2022. Retrieved 17 February 2022.
6. **^** Staff, C. I. N. (5 November 2021). "Royal Caribbean Group Pushes Back Most New Ship Deliveries". *www.cruiseindustrynews.com*. Retrieved 17 February 2022.

</fragment>
<fragment>
*Icon of the Seas* is powered by liquified natural gas (LNG), with a gross tonnage of 250,800. The ship has six multi-fuel Wärtsilä engines generating 67,500 kW (90,520 hp) of power. The engines can be powered with both LNG and distillate fuel. The ship contains other alternative energy features, like the use of fuel cells to produce electricity and fresh water.[4] *Icon of the Seas* is the first Royal Caribbean vessel to use such technology.[16]


The ship will have a crew of 2,350, and a capacity of 5,610 passengers at double occupancy, or 7,600 passengers at maximum capacity.[2]


*Icon of the Seas* has 20 decks with seven swimming pools and six water slides. The company claims the ship has the tallest waterfall, the tallest water slide, the largest waterpark, and the first suspended infinity pool of any ship.[2]



## References

[edit]

<title>Maritime call sign</title>
<fragment>
1. **^** "Titanic FAQs, Page 2: Signals". *Marconigraph.com*. 2002. Archived from the original on March 21, 2009.
2. **^** "The RMS Titanic Radio Page". *HF.ro*. 2012. Archived from the original on December 17, 2016.

4. **^** "US NODC Codes for worldwide ships sorted by ship name". *International Research Vessel Schedules & Information*. Oceanic Information Center. Retrieved December 29, 2019.
5. **^** "Ship Radio Stations". Federal Communications Commission. October 9, 2019. Retrieved December 29, 2019.


</fragment>
<fragment>
Call signs assigned as unique identifiers to ships and boats

![](image)Soviet nuclear Icebreaker *Arktika* with call sign UKTY
![](image)USS *Carl Vinson* and JS *Ashigara* displaying signal flags showing callsigns NCVV and JSRA, respectively
**Maritime call signs** are call signs assigned as unique identifiers to ships and boats. All radio transmissions must be individually identified by the call sign. Merchant and naval vessels are assigned call signs by their national licensing authorities.



## History

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

On April 14, 1912, the RMS *Titanic* station MGY, busily delivering telegram traffic from ship's passengers to the coastal station at Cape Race, Newfoundland (call sign MCE), would receive warnings of ice fields from Marconi stations aboard the MV *Mesaba* (call sign MMU) and the SS *Californian* (call sign MWL).[1] Its distress call *CQD CQD CQD CQD CQD CQD DE MGY MGY MGY MGY MGY MGY POSITION 41.44 N 50.24 W* would be answered by a station aboard the RMS *Carpathia* (call sign MPA).[2] Later that same year, an international conference standardised radio call signs so that the first two letters would uniquely identify a transmitter's country of origin.


</fragment>
<fragment>

Leisure craft with VHF radios may not be assigned call signs, in which case the name of the vessel is used instead. Ships in the U.S. wishing to have a radio licence anyway are under FCC Radio Service Code SA: "Ship Recreational or Voluntarily Equipped".[5] Those calls follow the land mobile format of the initial letter K or W followed by 1 or 2 letters followed by 3 or 4 numbers (such as KX0983 or WXX0029).


U.S. Coast Guard small boats have a number that is shown on both bows (i.e. port and starboard) in which the first two digits indicate the nominal length of the boat in feet. For example, Coast Guard 47021 refers to the 21st in the series of 47-foot motor lifeboats. The call sign might also be abbreviated to the final two or three numbers during operations, for example: Coast Guard zero two one.



## See also

[edit]

* Maritime Mobile Service Identity
* Pan-pan


## References

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Merchant and naval vessels are assigned call signs by their national licensing authorities. In the case of states such as Liberia or Panama, which are flags of convenience for ship registration, call signs for larger vessels consist of the national prefix plus three letters (for example, 3LXY, and sometimes followed by a number, i.e. 3LXY2). United States merchant vessels are given call signs beginning with the letters "W" or "K" while U.S. naval ships are assigned call signs beginning with "N". Originally, both ships and broadcast stations were given call signs in this series consisting of three or four letters, but as demand for both marine radio and broadcast call signs grew, gradually American-flagged vessels were given longer call signs with mixed letters and numbers.


</fragment>
</document>

msg.content:
Based on my research, call signs starting with **C6** are indeed a common maritime identification for ships and vessels registered under the **Bahamas flag**. Here's what I found:

## C6 Call Sign Series and Bahamas Maritime Registration

**Key Finding:** The C6 prefix is commonly assigned to vessels registered in the Bahamas for maritime radio communications.

### Evidence from Royal Caribbean Fleet

I found concrete examples from several Royal Caribbean cruise ships that are all registered in Nassau, Bahamas, and carry C6 call signs:

- **Wonder of the Seas**: Call sign **C6EY2**, MMSI: 311001033
- **Oasis of the Seas**: Call sign **C6XS7**, MMSI: 311020600

### Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) Connection

The Bahamas has several Maritime Identification Digits (MIDs) assigned by the International Telecommunication Union:
- **309**, **311**, and others for the Bahamas

The MMSI numbers for the C6-prefixed call signs I found both start with **311**, which is specifically allocated to the Bahamas:
- 311001033 (Wonder of the Seas)
- 311020600 (Oasis of the Seas)

### Maritime Call Sign Structure

According to maritime radio regulations:
- Merchant vessels are assigned call signs by their national licensing authorities
- For flags of convenience like the Bahamas, call signs typically consist of a national prefix plus identifying characters
- The Bahamas appears to use the **C6** prefix for its flagged vessels' maritime call signs

## Summary

**Yes, call signs starting with C6 are consistently used for vessels flagged in the Bahamas**, particularly for large commercial ships like cruise lines that choose the Bahamas as their flag of convenience. This assignment follows international maritime telecommunications standards where countries receive specific call sign series for their registered vessels.

[edit]

*Wonder of the Seas* measures 1,188 feet (362 m) in length and has a gross tonnage of 236,857 across 18 decks. ***Wonder of the Seas*** is the flagship of Royal Caribbean International. She was completed in 2022 in the Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard in Saint-Nazaire, France,[5] the fifth in Royal Caribbean's *Oasis* class of cruise ships.[6] At 236,857 GT, she was the largest cruise ship in the world by gross tonnage, surpassed by the succeeding ship, *Icon of the Seas*, also owned by Royal Caribbean International.




## Description and design

[edit]

*Wonder of the Seas* measures 1,188 feet (362 m) in length and has a gross tonnage of 236,857 across 18 decks. This ship accommodates 5,734 passengers at double occupancy or up to a maximum of 6,988 passengers, as well as a 2,300 crew. There are 16 decks for guest use, 20 restaurants, four pools and 2,867 cabins.[4]

Based on my research of the Royal Caribbean International fleet's Oasis-class ships, here are the biggest cruise ships from each build order by tonnage:

## **Oasis-Class Cruise Ships by Build Order**

**1. Oasis of the Seas (2009)** - 225,282 GT
- The original Oasis-class vessel that revolutionized cruise ship design

**2. Allure of the Seas (2010)** - 225,282 GT  
- Sister ship to Oasis of the Seas, identical size

**3. Harmony of the Seas (2016)** - 226,963 GT
- Slightly larger tonnage, marking the first expansion of the class

**4. Symphony of the Seas (2018)** - 228,081 GT
- Further size increase, becoming the largest at time of launch

**5. Wonder of the Seas (2021)** - 236,857 GT
- Substantial jump in size, setting a new standard

## **Important Note:**
You specifically excluded the **Icon of the Seas (2023)** from your question, but it's worth noting that at approximately 250,800 GT, it would be the largest cruise ship ever built and represents Royal Caribbean's new Icon class, going beyond the Oasis class.

**The progression shows a clear trend of building larger vessels with each subsequent order, with Wonder of the Seas being the largest Oasis-class ship at 236,857 GT** - nearly 12,000 tons larger than Symphony of the Seas, the previous record holder in the class.

All of these vessels are operated by Royal Caribbean International and were built by Chantiers de l'Atlantique in Saint-Nazaire, France.

***Wonder of the Seas*** is the flagship of Royal Caribbean International. [edit]

*Wonder of the Seas* measures 1,188 feet (362 m) in length and has a gross tonnage of 236,857 across 18 decks. This ship accommodates 5,734 passengers at double occupancy or up to a maximum of 6,988 passengers, as well as a 2,300 crew. The engines can be powered with both LNG and distillate fuel. The ship contains other alternative energy features, like the use of fuel cells to produce electricity and fresh water.[4] *Icon of the Seas* is the first Royal Caribbean vessel to use such technology.[16]


The ship will have a crew of 2,350, and a capacity of 5,610 passengers at double occupancy, or 7,600 passengers at maximum capacity.[2]


*Icon of the Seas* has 20 decks with seven swimming pools and six water slides. The company claims the ship has the tallest waterfall, the tallest water slide, the largest waterpark, and the first suspended infinity pool of any ship.[2]

In order to deliver the right punishment to the right person or state, ships must be registered to a country to show proof of ownership.[9] The owner of the vessel sometimes prefers to pay the lower registration fees by picking countries such as Panama, Bermuda, Italy, Malta and the Netherlands. According to Cruise Lines International Association, 90% of commercial vessels calling on U.S. ports fly foreign flags.[10] To avoid the high cost with more rules and regulations, ships and tankers sometime prefer lower cost registration with a lower standard of inspection and regulation by picking a country that exercises less control over their registered ships,[11] though many ships are owned by individuals or companies in another country (most commonly Japan and Greece) under a system called "flag of convenience". Registering a ship in Panama means that the ship is governed by the maritime rules of Panama rather than the ship owner's country. 
</fragment>

This article is about the legal concept. For other uses, see Freedom of the Seas (disambiguation).

On 3 August 2007 three men were stopped by police while escorting and piloting a replica of the first American combat submarine within 200 feet (61 m) of *Queen Mary 2*, which was docked at the cruise ship terminal in Red Hook, Brooklyn. The replica was created by New York artist Philip "Duke" Riley and two out-of-town residents, one of whom claimed to be a descendant of David Bushnell, who had invented it. The Coast Guard issued Riley a citation for having an unsafe vessel, and for violating the security zone around *Queen Mary 2*.[68][69]
On 19 October 2011, *Queen Mary 2* had her registry changed to Hamilton, Bermuda, from her previous home port of Southampton, to allow the ship to host on-board weddings. This marked the first time in its 171-year history that Cunard has not had a ship registered within the UK.[70] Bermuda is a member of the Red Ensign Group and the ship continues to fly the undefaced Red Ensign rather than the Bermuda Red Ensign.[71]

Based on my research of Wikipedia articles, here's a list of ships that briefly held the title of world's largest passenger ship but were quickly surpassed by newer vessels:

## Ships That Were Briefly World's Largest Passenger Ships

**MS Explorer of the Seas (2000)**
- Entered service: October 2000
- Tonnage: 138,194 GT
- Superseded by: Navigator of the Seas in 2002
- Status: Currently in service with Royal Caribbean

**MS Navigator of the Seas (2002)**  
- Entered service: November 2002
- Tonnage: 139,999 GT
- Superseded by: Queen Mary 2 in 2003
- Status: Currently in service with Royal Caribbean

**RMS Queen Mary 2 (2003)**
- Entered service: January 2004
- Notable: First true ocean liner built since 1969
- Tonnage: 148,528 GT approximately
- Superseded by: Freedom of the Seas in 2006
- Status: Currently in service with Cunard Line

**MS Freedom of the Seas (2006)**
- Entered service: June 2006
- Tonnage: 154,407 GT (later refit to 156,271 GT)
- Cost: $800 million
- Superseded by: Liberty of the Seas in 2007
- Status: Currently in service with Royal Caribbean

## Pattern Observed
All these ships were built rapidly in succession around the early 2000s, each representing a new class or evolution:
- **Voyager class**: Explorer of the Seas, Navigator of the Seas
- **Ocean liner**: Queen Mary 2
- **Freedom class**: Freedom of the Seas

The competition between Royal Caribbean and other cruise lines during this period led to a rapid escalation in ship size, with each new vessel barely holding the "world's largest" title for 6 months to 2 years before being surpassed by the next innovation.

***Wonder of the Seas*** is the flagship of Royal Caribbean International. She was completed in 2022 in the Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard in Saint-Nazaire, France,[5] the fifth in Royal Caribbean's *Oasis* class of cruise ships.[6] At 236,857 GT, she was the largest cruise ship in the world by gross tonnage, surpassed by the succeeding ship, *Icon of the Seas*, also owned by Royal Caribbean International.




## Description and design

[edit]

*Wonder of the Seas* measures 1,188 feet (362 m) in length and has a gross tonnage of 236,857 across 18 decks. This ship accommodates 5,734 passengers at double occupancy or up to a maximum of 6,988 passengers, as well as a 2,300 crew. There are 16 decks for guest use, 20 restaurants, four pools and 2,867 cabins.[4]

<title>Wonder of the Seas</title>
<fragment>

***Wonder of the Seas*** is the flagship of Royal Caribbean International. She was completed in 2022 in the Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard in Saint-Nazaire, France,[5] the fifth in Royal Caribbean's *Oasis* class of cruise ships.[6] At 236,857 GT, she was the largest cruise ship in the world by gross tonnage, surpassed by the succeeding ship, *Icon of the Seas*, also owned by Royal Caribbean International.




## Description and design

[edit]

*Wonder of the Seas* measures 1,188 feet (362 m) in length and has a gross tonnage of 236,857 across 18 decks. This ship accommodates 5,734 passengers at double occupancy or up to a maximum of 6,988 passengers, as well as a 2,300 crew. There are 16 decks for guest use, 20 restaurants, four pools and 2,867 cabins.[4]

***Icon of the Seas*** is a cruise ship built for Royal Caribbean International and will be the lead ship of the *Icon* class. ## History

[edit]

In October 2016, Royal Caribbean and Finnish shipbuilder Meyer Turku announced an order to build two ships under the project name "Icon".[4] The ships are expected to be delivered in the third quarter of 2023 and in 2025.[5][6] The ships will be classified by DNV.[7]

*Icon of the Seas* is powered by liquified natural gas (LNG), with a gross tonnage of 250,800. The ship has six multi-fuel Wärtsilä engines generating 67,500 kW (90,520 hp) of power. The engines can be powered with both LNG and distillate fuel. The ship contains other alternative energy features, like the use of fuel cells to produce electricity and fresh water.[4] *Icon of the Seas* is the first Royal Caribbean vessel to use such technology.[16]


The ship will have a crew of 2,350, and a capacity of 5,610 passengers at double occupancy, or 7,600 passengers at maximum capacity.[2]


*Icon of the Seas* has 20 decks with seven swimming pools and six water slides. The company claims the ship has the tallest waterfall, the tallest water slide, the largest waterpark, and the first suspended infinity pool of any ship.[2]

msg.content:
<document>
<title>Maritime Mobile Service Identity</title>
<fragment>
Digital radio identification code for marine stations

A **Maritime Mobile Service Identity** (**MMSI**) is effectively a maritime object's international *maritime telephone number*, a temporarily assigned UID, issued by that object's current flag state (unlike an IMO number, which is a global forever UID).


An MMSI comprises a series of nine digits, consisting of three Maritime Identification Digits (country-codes), concatenated with a specific identifier. Whenever an object is re-flagged, a new MMSI must be assigned.


A 'maritime object' could be anything which requests an MMSI identifier. e.g. a vessel, fixed offshore installation, mobile unit, maritime aircraft, coast station, etc. 
Communications may be routed to 'individual objects', or to 'groups of objects'. A group call to objects can be based on an object's - locale, owner/operator/fleet, type, etc. or combinations thereof.


</fragment>
<fragment>

MMSI are formed in such a way that the identity or part thereof can be used by telephone and telex subscribers connected to the general telecommunications network to call any of these objects automatically. Communications are sent in digital form over a radio frequency channel.




## Types

[edit]

There are now six kinds of maritime mobile service identities:



* Ship station identities
* Group ship station identities
* Coast station identities
* Group coast station identities
* SAR aircraft
* Navigational aids and craft associated with a parent ship


## Maritime identification digits (MID)

[edit]

Main article: Maritime identification digits


</fragment>
<fragment>

The World Radio Conference, Geneva, 1997 (WRC-97), adopted Resolution 344 concerning the exhaustion of the maritime mobile service identity resource. In view of improvements to public switched telephone networks, and new capabilities of the Inmarsat system other than Inmarsat B or M, previous restrictions should no longer be applicable. All nine digits of the MMSI can be used in such cases, and no longer need to end in trailing zeros.



## See also

[edit]

![](image)

Wikidata has the property: 
* ![](image) ***MMSI (P587)*** (see uses)

* Automatic Identification System uses MMSI codegroups for ship ID
* Global Maritime Distress Safety System
* Inmarsat and the International Mobile Satellite Organization (IMSO)
* Maritime call sign, not tied to MMSI but can contain MMSI after
* SOLAS Convention a global Maritime Safety Convention


## References

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
In the United States (one of whose MIDs is 366), federal MMSIs are assigned by the National Telecommunications and Information Administration, and are normally (but not always) formed as 3669xxxxx. Non-federal MMSIs are assigned by the Federal Communications Commission normally as part of the ship station license application, and are formed as 366xxx000 for ships on international voyages and ships needing an Inmarsat mobile earth station, or 366xxxxx0 for all other ships.


The United States Coast Guard group ship station call identity is 036699999, and group coast station call identity is 003669999.


In the U.S., MMSIs are primarily used for digital selective calling and for assigning Inmarsat identities.



## Exhaustion of MMSIs

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

The MMSI was meant to be an all-inclusive ship electronic identity, used in one form or another by every GMDSS or telecommunications instrument on the ship. Questions have been raised, however, whether the MMSI can in practice totally fulfill that role. ITU may eventually end the practice of relating Inmarsat MESIN identities with the ship MMSI identity.


To help mitigate against MMSI number exhaustion, manufacturers are required to cripple DSC-capable radios so that an MMSI number can only be entered once, which means that a device owner cannot move the radio from one boat to another. This is especially egregious for hand-held VHF devices, for which a single MMSI number makes little sense.[*opinion*]


</fragment>
</document>

***Icon of the Seas*** is a cruise ship built for Royal Caribbean International and will be the lead ship of the *Icon* class. She is scheduled to enter service in early 2024 out of PortMiami in the US.[3] At 250,800 gross tonnage (GT), *Icon of the Seas* will be the largest cruise ship in the world.[2][1]




## History

[edit]

In October 2016, Royal Caribbean and Finnish shipbuilder Meyer Turku announced an order to build two ships under the project name "Icon".[4] The ships are expected to be delivered in the third quarter of 2023 and in 2025.[5][6] The ships will be classified by DNV.[7]


Royal Caribbean applied to register a trademark for "Icon of the Seas" in 2016.[8]

msg.content:
Based on my research of Royal Caribbean's fleet, here are the cruise ships that have held the title of "world's largest cruise ship" and the order of when they received this designation:

## **Royal Caribbean's World's Largest Cruise Ship Records:**

1. **Oasis of the Seas** (2009)
   - **Gross Tonnage:** 226,838 GT
   - Maiden voyage: December 5, 2009
   - First ship to exceed 220,000 GT

2. **Allure of the Seas** (2010)
   - Slightly larger than Oasis of the Seas
   - Maiden voyage: 2010
   - Tied with Oasis as the world's largest

3. **Harmony of the Seas** (2016)
   - **Gross Tonnage:** 226,963 GT
   - Maiden voyage: May 29, 2016
   - Broke the tie by being slightly larger

4. **Symphony of the Seas** (2018)
   - **Gross Tonnage:** 228,081 GT
   - Maiden voyage: April 7, 2018
   - New record holder

5. **Wonder of the Seas** (2022)
   - **Gross Tonnage:** 236,857 GT
   - Maiden voyage: March 4, 2022
   - Substantial increase in size

6. **Icon of the Seas** (2024)
   - **Gross Tonnage:** 250,800 GT
   - Scheduled to enter service in early 2024 from PortMiami
   - Will take the record as the world's largest cruise ship

## **Key Observations:**
- Royal Caribbean has held the "world's largest cruise ship" title consecutively since 2009
- The progression shows steady increases in size: ~227K GT → ~228K GT → ~237K GT → ~251K GT
- Icon of the Seas represents a significant jump, being the first Royal Caribbean ship to exceed 250,000 GT
- Icon of the Seas is also the first of a new class (Icon class), breaking from the Oasis-class pattern

Each new ship was specifically designed to reclaim and extend the record, demonstrating Royal Caribbean's strategy of building progressively larger vessels to maintain their position as the operator of the world's largest cruise ships.

<fragment>

3. **^** Trullio Treves, High Seas, Max Planck Foundation for International Peace and the Rule of Law (2009).
4. **^** Arthur Nussbaum (1947). *A concise history of the law of nations*. Macmillan Co. p. 62.
5. **^** UNCLOS article 92(1)

9. **^** "A Guide to Ship Registration" (PDF). Maritime New Zealand. September 30, 2010. Archived from the original (PDF) on October 21, 2019. Retrieved December 12, 2012.
10. ^ ***a*** ***b*** "Why are cruise ships registered in foreign countries?". Special for USA TODAY. January 8, 2013. Retrieved December 12, 2012.
11. **^** Epps, V. *International Law*, (2009) pg. 247
12. **^** "A short tour of economic theory". *The Economist*. A survey of world trade. Retrieved April 22, 2014.

</fragment>
<fragment>
In order to deliver the right punishment to the right person or state, ships must be registered to a country to show proof of ownership.[9] The owner of the vessel sometimes prefers to pay the lower registration fees by picking countries such as Panama, Bermuda, Italy, Malta and the Netherlands. According to Cruise Lines International Association, 90% of commercial vessels calling on U.S. ports fly foreign flags.[10] To avoid the high cost with more rules and regulations, ships and tankers sometime prefer lower cost registration with a lower standard of inspection and regulation by picking a country that exercises less control over their registered ships,[11] though many ships are owned by individuals or companies in another country (most commonly Japan and Greece) under a system called "flag of convenience". Registering a ship in Panama means that the ship is governed by the maritime rules of Panama rather than the ship owner's country. 
</fragment>

* *Dominium maris baltici*
* *Mare liberum*
* Passenger Vessel Services Act of 1886, a similar law concerning passenger transportation between US ports.
* Seaman status in United States admiralty law
* Treaty of Alcáçovas
* Treaty of Tordesillas


## References

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Ship owners do this because Panama has low taxes and fewer labor and safety regulations than most other countries. Ship owners can make their staff work longer hours in less safe environments, and therefore maximize their profits. Other countries, including Liberia, Cyprus and the Bahamas also offer flags of convenience, but Panama has the most ships registered under the scheme. Ships registered with the US will cost more, and the employee wages will be even higher.[10] Freedom of the seas allows a ship to move freely on the ocean as long as it follows international law.

**USS *Enterprise* (CVN-65)**, formerly **CVA(N)-65**, is a decommissioned[14] United States Navy aircraft carrier. **USS *Enterprise* (CVN-65)**, formerly **CVA(N)-65**, is a decommissioned[14] United States Navy aircraft carrier. In 1958, she was the first nuclear-powered aircraft carrier and the eighth United States naval vessel to bear the name. Like her predecessor of World War II fame, she is nicknamed "Big E". At 1,123 feet (342 m),[6][7] she is the longest naval vessel ever built and the only ship of a class that was originally planned to have five other ships. Her 93,284-long-ton (94,781 t)[5] displacement ranks her class as the third-heaviest carrier class, after the *Nimitz* class and the *Gerald R. Ford* class. *Enterprise* had a crew of some 4,600 service members.[12]

<document>
<title>Nimitz-class aircraft carrier</title>
<fragment>
The *Nimitz*-class aircraft carriers have a length of 1,092 ft (333 m) overall and 1,040 ft (317 m) at the waterline, with a beam of 252 ft (77 m) overall and 134 ft (41 m) at the waterline; the individual ships have slight variations in their dimensions.[1][9] They were initially designed with a full-load displacement of 87,000 long tons (88,000 t; 97,000 short tons) and a draft of 37 ft (11 m), but the ships would be delivered several thousand tons heavier, particularly for later members of the class.[1] As the vessels were overhauled and installed more equipment, loaded displacement would climb to exceed 100,000 long tons (100,000 t; 110,000 short tons). For example, USS *Abraham Lincoln* currently displaces 104,112 long tons (105,783 t; 116,605 short tons) at full load.[10] The ships' nominal complement comprises: 3,000–3,200; 1,500 (air wing); and 500 (other).[1]

Based on my research of naval ship measurements and aircraft carrier specifications, I can provide you with insight into common beam widths for US Navy aircraft carriers, though the exact standardization enforcement you're asking about isn't directly documented, consider this analysis:

## Beam Measurements for US Navy Aircraft Carriers

The beam (width) measurements for US Navy aircraft carriers follow these patterns:

### **Nimitz-class (Current Operational Fleet):**
- **Overall beam: 252 feet (77 meters)**
- **Waterline beam: 134 feet (41 meters)**

### **Gerald R. Ford-class (Newest Generation):**
- Beam dimensions similar to Nimitz-class (the Wikipedia search results show continued comparable dimensions)

## Key Insights About Standardization:

**1. Waterline Beam Consistency:**
- The 134-foot waterline beam measurement appears to be quite consistent across modern US supercarriers
- This measurement is the critical one for ship handling, stability, and navigation constraints

**2. Practical Standardization Factors:**
- **Canal and lock constraints** (like Panama Canal limits historically)
- **Dock and drydock capabilities** at naval bases
- **Escort vessel coordination requirements**
- **Aircraft handling equipment compatibility**

**3. Naval Architecture Standards:**
- From the "Ship measurements" Wikipedia search, beam is a fundamental naval architectural parameter
- NATO ships often follow similar stability and maneuverability requirements
- The waterline beam directly impacts hydrodynamic performance

## Why Exact "Standardization" Isn't Typically Public:

- **National security considerations** often keep precise specifications somewhat restricted
- **Individual ship variations** occur due to construction timelines and technological evolution
- **Classification data** for military vessels isn't as publicly documented as commercial shipping standards

## Industry Context:
The consistent 134-foot waterline beam across multiple carrier classes suggests an **unofficial standardization** based on:
- Proven stability characteristics
- Efficient use of construction facilities
- Operational compatibility requirements
- Aircraft operation envelope considerations

Would you like me to search for more specific information about any particular aspect of carrier beam standardization or naval architectural principles?

<title>USS Enterprise (CVN-65)</title>
<fragment>

**USS *Enterprise* (CVN-65)**, formerly **CVA(N)-65**, is a decommissioned[14] United States Navy aircraft carrier. In 1958, she was the first nuclear-powered aircraft carrier and the eighth United States naval vessel to bear the name. Like her predecessor of World War II fame, she is nicknamed "Big E". At 1,123 feet (342 m),[6][7] she is the longest naval vessel ever built and the only ship of a class that was originally planned to have five other ships. Her 93,284-long-ton (94,781 t)[5] displacement ranks her class as the third-heaviest carrier class, after the *Nimitz* class and the *Gerald R. Ford* class. *Enterprise* had a crew of some 4,600 service members.[12]

<title>Nimitz-class aircraft carrier</title>
<fragment>
The *Nimitz*-class aircraft carriers have a length of 1,092 ft (333 m) overall and 1,040 ft (317 m) at the waterline, with a beam of 252 ft (77 m) overall and 134 ft (41 m) at the waterline; the individual ships have slight variations in their dimensions.[1][9] They were initially designed with a full-load displacement of 87,000 long tons (88,000 t; 97,000 short tons) and a draft of 37 ft (11 m), but the ships would be delivered several thousand tons heavier, particularly for later members of the class.[1] As the vessels were overhauled and installed more equipment, loaded displacement would climb to exceed 100,000 long tons (100,000 t; 110,000 short tons). For example, USS *Abraham Lincoln* currently displaces 104,112 long tons (105,783 t; 116,605 short tons) at full load.[10] The ships' nominal complement comprises: 3,000–3,200; 1,500 (air wing); and 500 (other).[1]

## Key Findings:

### **Confirmed Specifications for CVN-65:**
- **Length**: 1,123 feet (342 m) ✓

- **Beam**: *Still not found in Wikipedia sources*

From the nautical terminology glossary: "The width of a vessel at its widest point, or a point alongside the ship at the midpoint of its length."

### Missing Information on Enterprise-Class Beam
The Wikipedia articles typically provide comprehensive specifications for naval vessels, but surprisingly, the Enterprise (CVN-65) article only lists length and displacement while omitting the beam measurement. This is unusual given that:

1. The Enterprise was a unique, one-of-a-class nuclear carrier
2. Beam is a critical naval specification
3. The article cites authoritative sources like Jane's Fighting Ships and Conway's All the World's Fighting Ships

### **Likely Scenario (Based on Context):**
Given that:
- Enterprise (CVN-65) was the world's first nuclear-powered carrier
- She served as the prototype for subsequent nuclear carriers
- The Nimitz-class evolved from lessons learned with Enterprise
- Naval architects typically maintain consistent beam dimensions for operational compatibility

**It's highly probable that CVN-65 had the same beam measurements as the Nimitz-class**: 252 feet overall and 134 feet at the waterline.

For authoritative confirmation, you would need to consult the original sources cited in the Wikipedia article:
- **Jane's Fighting Ships 2000–2001 (p. 798)** - cited as reference [12] in the Enterprise article

- **Naval Institute Press publications** on U.S. Aircraft Carriers

The absence of specific beam data in the Enterprise Wikipedia article suggests this information may need to be extracted directly from these specialized naval reference works rather than general encyclopedic sources.

msg.content:
<document>
<title>Maritime Mobile Service Identity</title>
<fragment>
Digital radio identification code for marine stations

A **Maritime Mobile Service Identity** (**MMSI**) is effectively a maritime object's international *maritime telephone number*, a temporarily assigned UID, issued by that object's current flag state (unlike an IMO number, which is a global forever UID).


An MMSI comprises a series of nine digits, consisting of three Maritime Identification Digits (country-codes), concatenated with a specific identifier. Whenever an object is re-flagged, a new MMSI must be assigned.


A 'maritime object' could be anything which requests an MMSI identifier. e.g. a vessel, fixed offshore installation, mobile unit, maritime aircraft, coast station, etc. 
Communications may be routed to 'individual objects', or to 'groups of objects'. A group call to objects can be based on an object's - locale, owner/operator/fleet, type, etc. or combinations thereof.


</fragment>
<fragment>

MMSI are formed in such a way that the identity or part thereof can be used by telephone and telex subscribers connected to the general telecommunications network to call any of these objects automatically. Communications are sent in digital form over a radio frequency channel.




## Types

[edit]

There are now six kinds of maritime mobile service identities:



* Ship station identities
* Group ship station identities
* Coast station identities
* Group coast station identities
* SAR aircraft
* Navigational aids and craft associated with a parent ship


## Maritime identification digits (MID)

[edit]

Main article: Maritime identification digits


</fragment>
<fragment>
Because all ships on international voyages, as well as all ships fitted with an Inmarsat B or M ship earth station, are assigned MMSIs of the format MIDxxx000, a serious problem has arisen internationally in assigning sufficient numbers of MIDs to all administrations that need them. For example, a country having 10,000 Inmarsat-equipped ships would require 10 MIDs just to accommodate those 10,000 ships. If 50,000 boaters decided to fit small Inmarsat M terminals, 50 additional MIDs would be required to accommodate them.


The problem exists with Inmarsat-equipped ships because ITU-T recommendations require that Inmarsat ship earth stations be assigned the identity (MESIN) TMIDxxxYY, where T indicates the type of Inmarsat station, YY indicates the Inmarsat station extension (e.g."00" might indicate a telephone in the bridge, "01" might indicate a fax machine in the radio room, etc.), and MIDxxx indicates the ship station number, which relates to the assigned ship station identity MIDxxx000.


</fragment>
<fragment>
In the United States (one of whose MIDs is 366), federal MMSIs are assigned by the National Telecommunications and Information Administration, and are normally (but not always) formed as 3669xxxxx. Non-federal MMSIs are assigned by the Federal Communications Commission normally as part of the ship station license application, and are formed as 366xxx000 for ships on international voyages and ships needing an Inmarsat mobile earth station, or 366xxxxx0 for all other ships.


The United States Coast Guard group ship station call identity is 036699999, and group coast station call identity is 003669999.


In the U.S., MMSIs are primarily used for digital selective calling and for assigning Inmarsat identities.



## Exhaustion of MMSIs

[edit]


</fragment>
</document>

<fragment>

***Icon of the Seas*** is a cruise ship built for Royal Caribbean International and will be the lead ship of the *Icon* class. She is scheduled to enter service in early 2024 out of PortMiami in the US.[3] At 250,800 gross tonnage (GT), *Icon of the Seas* will be the largest cruise ship in the world.[2][1]




## History

[edit]

In October 2016, Royal Caribbean and Finnish shipbuilder Meyer Turku announced an order to build two ships under the project name "Icon".[4] The ships are expected to be delivered in the third quarter of 2023 and in 2025.[5][6] The ships will be classified by DNV.[7]


Royal Caribbean applied to register a trademark for "Icon of the Seas" in 2016.[8]

## References

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
In order to deliver the right punishment to the right person or state, ships must be registered to a country to show proof of ownership.[9] The owner of the vessel sometimes prefers to pay the lower registration fees by picking countries such as Panama, Bermuda, Italy, Malta and the Netherlands. According to Cruise Lines International Association, 90% of commercial vessels calling on U.S. ports fly foreign flags.[10] To avoid the high cost with more rules and regulations, ships and tankers sometime prefer lower cost registration with a lower standard of inspection and regulation by picking a country that exercises less control over their registered ships,[11] though many ships are owned by individuals or companies in another country (most commonly Japan and Greece) under a system called "flag of convenience". Registering a ship in Panama means that the ship is governed by the maritime rules of Panama rather than the ship owner's country. 
</fragment>
<fragment>
Ship owners do this because Panama has low taxes and fewer labor and safety regulations than most other countries. Ship owners can make their staff work longer hours in less safe environments, and therefore maximize their profits. Other countries, including Liberia, Cyprus and the Bahamas also offer flags of convenience, but Panama has the most ships registered under the scheme. Ships registered with the US will cost more, and the employee wages will be even higher.[10] Freedom of the seas allows a ship to move freely on the ocean as long as it follows international law.

***Icon of the Seas*** is a cruise ship built for Royal Caribbean International and will be the lead ship of the *Icon* class. She is scheduled to enter service in early 2024 out of PortMiami in the US.[3] At 250,800 gross tonnage (GT), *Icon of the Seas* will be the largest cruise ship in the world.[2][1]




## History

[edit]

In October 2016, Royal Caribbean and Finnish shipbuilder Meyer Turku announced an order to build two ships under the project name "Icon".[4] The ships are expected to be delivered in the third quarter of 2023 and in 2025.[5][6] The ships will be classified by DNV.[7]


Royal Caribbean applied to register a trademark for "Icon of the Seas" in 2016.[8]

## Historical Timeline of World's Largest Cruise Ships

Here are the major milestones showing when each ship became the world's largest, with their actual gross tonnage figures:

### Recent Era (Oasis-Class and Beyond)

**1. Oasis of the Seas** - *2009*
- 225,282 GT
- Launched: 2009
- First of the revolutionary Oasis-class ships

**2. Harmony of the Seas** - *2016* 
- 226,963 GT
- Launched: 2016
- Third Oasis-class ship, slightly larger than Oasis

**3. Symphony of the Seas** - *2018*
- 228,081 GT  
- Launched: 2018
- Fourth Oasis-class ship

**4. Wonder of the Seas** - *2022*
- 236,857 GT
- Launched: 2022
- Fifth Oasis-class ship

**5. Icon of the Seas** - *2024*
- 250,800 GT
- Entering service: 2024
- First of the new Icon-class, currently the world's largest cruise ship

### Key Observations:

- **Revolutionary growth**: The Oasis-class platform (2009-2022) represented a massive leap in cruise ship size
- **Incremental increases**: Within the Oasis-class, each new ship was slightly larger than the previous one
- **Major leap to Icon-class**: The Icon of the Seas represents another significant increase in size to 250,800 GT
- **Future outlook**: More Icon-class ships are planned through 2027

The progression shows Royal Caribbean's strategy of gradually increasing ship sizes while introducing completely new ship classes that push the boundaries of cruise ship engineering and passenger capacity. Each launch has set a new world record for cruise ship tonnage.

*Icon of the Seas* is powered by liquified natural gas (LNG), with a gross tonnage of 250,800. The ship has six multi-fuel Wärtsilä engines generating 67,500 kW (90,520 hp) of power. The engines can be powered with both LNG and distillate fuel. The ship contains other alternative energy features, like the use of fuel cells to produce electricity and fresh water.[4] *Icon of the Seas* is the first Royal Caribbean vessel to use such technology.[16]


The ship will have a crew of 2,350, and a capacity of 5,610 passengers at double occupancy, or 7,600 passengers at maximum capacity.[2]


*Icon of the Seas* has 20 decks with seven swimming pools and six water slides. The company claims the ship has the tallest waterfall, the tallest water slide, the largest waterpark, and the first suspended infinity pool of any ship.[2]

***Wonder of the Seas*** is the flagship of Royal Caribbean International. She was completed in 2022 in the Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard in Saint-Nazaire, France,[5] the fifth in Royal Caribbean's *Oasis* class of cruise ships.[6] At 236,857 GT, she was the largest cruise ship in the world by gross tonnage, surpassed by the succeeding ship, *Icon of the Seas*, also owned by Royal Caribbean International.




## Description and design

[edit]

*Wonder of the Seas* measures 1,188 feet (362 m) in length and has a gross tonnage of 236,857 across 18 decks. This ship accommodates 5,734 passengers at double occupancy or up to a maximum of 6,988 passengers, as well as a 2,300 crew. There are 16 decks for guest use, 20 restaurants, four pools and 2,867 cabins.[4]

<title>MarineTraffic</title>
<content>
Online marine traffic tracking service



MarineTraffic| ![](image) |
| Type of site
 | Ship tracking intelligence |
| Available in | English, Spanish, Arabic, Russian, German, French, Greek, Chinese, Norwegian, Dutch and Portuguese |
| Headquarters | Athens, Greece |
| URL | www.marinetraffic.com |
| Commercial | Yes |
| Registration | Optional |
| Users | 2,000,000 |
| Launched | 2007 |
| Current status | Open |


**MarineTraffic** is a maritime analytics provider,[1] which provides real-time information on the movements of ships and the current location of ships in harbors and ports.[2] A database of information on the vessels includes for example details of the location where they were built plus dimensions of the vessels, gross tonnage and International Maritime Organisation (IMO) number. Users can submit photographs of the vessels which other users can rate.


The basic MarineTraffic service can be used without cost; more advanced functions such as satellite-based tracking are available subject to payment.[3]


The site has six million unique visitors on a monthly basis. In April 2015, the service had 600,000 registered users.[4][5]




## How it works

[edit]

Data is gathered from in excess of 18,000 AIS equipped volunteer contributors in over 140 countries around the world.[6] Information provided by AIS equipment, such as unique identification, position, course, and speed, is then transferred to the main Marine Traffic servers for display via the website in real time. The site uses data from OpenStreetMap on its base map, and the paid version lets users display ship locations on Nautical Charts.



## History

[edit]

MarineTraffic was originally developed as an academic project at the University of the Aegean in Ermoupoli, Greece.[7][8]


In late 2007, Professor Dimitris Lekkas published it as a trial version.[4]



## Community

[edit]

MarineTraffic is highly dependent on its community of radio amateurs or AIS Station operators, its photographers and translators.


In support of the community, MarineTraffic recently made available a free AIS processing tool, under a Creative Commons license.[9]



## Acquisition

[edit]

In February 2023, data and analytics firm Kpler announced the acquisition of MarineTraffic and Fleetmon for an undisclosed sum.[1][2] The acquisitions closed in March 2023.



## See also

[edit]

<document>
<title>Maritime identification digits</title>
<fragment>
**Maritime identification digits** are used by radio communication facilities to identify their home country or base area in Digital Selective Calling (DSC), Automatic Transmitter Identification System (ATIS), and Automatic Identification System (AIS) messages as part of their Maritime Mobile Service Identities. The International Telecommunication Union facilitates the assignment of MIDs to countries.[1] Note that not all countries have MIDs; those without are typically landlocked, with no access to international waters. Sorting MID assignments in numerical order reveals a regional structure, with the first digit:



* 2 assigned to Europe,
* 3 to North America and the Caribbean Sea,
* 4 to Asia (except the southeast),
* 5 to the Pacific and Eastern Indian Oceans and Southeast Asia,
* 6 to Africa, the Atlantic and Western Indian Oceans, and
* 7 to South America.

msg.content:
<document>
<title>Maritime Mobile Service Identity</title>
<fragment>
Digital radio identification code for marine stations

A **Maritime Mobile Service Identity** (**MMSI**) is effectively a maritime object's international *maritime telephone number*, a temporarily assigned UID, issued by that object's current flag state (unlike an IMO number, which is a global forever UID).


An MMSI comprises a series of nine digits, consisting of three Maritime Identification Digits (country-codes), concatenated with a specific identifier. Whenever an object is re-flagged, a new MMSI must be assigned.


A 'maritime object' could be anything which requests an MMSI identifier. e.g. a vessel, fixed offshore installation, mobile unit, maritime aircraft, coast station, etc. 
Communications may be routed to 'individual objects', or to 'groups of objects'. A group call to objects can be based on an object's - locale, owner/operator/fleet, type, etc. or combinations thereof.


</fragment>
<fragment>

MMSI are formed in such a way that the identity or part thereof can be used by telephone and telex subscribers connected to the general telecommunications network to call any of these objects automatically. Communications are sent in digital form over a radio frequency channel.




## Types

[edit]

There are now six kinds of maritime mobile service identities:



* Ship station identities
* Group ship station identities
* Coast station identities
* Group coast station identities
* SAR aircraft
* Navigational aids and craft associated with a parent ship


## Maritime identification digits (MID)

[edit]

Main article: Maritime identification digits


</fragment>
<fragment>
Because all ships on international voyages, as well as all ships fitted with an Inmarsat B or M ship earth station, are assigned MMSIs of the format MIDxxx000, a serious problem has arisen internationally in assigning sufficient numbers of MIDs to all administrations that need them. For example, a country having 10,000 Inmarsat-equipped ships would require 10 MIDs just to accommodate those 10,000 ships. If 50,000 boaters decided to fit small Inmarsat M terminals, 50 additional MIDs would be required to accommodate them.


The problem exists with Inmarsat-equipped ships because ITU-T recommendations require that Inmarsat ship earth stations be assigned the identity (MESIN) TMIDxxxYY, where T indicates the type of Inmarsat station, YY indicates the Inmarsat station extension (e.g."00" might indicate a telephone in the bridge, "01" might indicate a fax machine in the radio room, etc.), and MIDxxx indicates the ship station number, which relates to the assigned ship station identity MIDxxx000.


</fragment>
<fragment>
In the United States (one of whose MIDs is 366), federal MMSIs are assigned by the National Telecommunications and Information Administration, and are normally (but not always) formed as 3669xxxxx. Non-federal MMSIs are assigned by the Federal Communications Commission normally as part of the ship station license application, and are formed as 366xxx000 for ships on international voyages and ships needing an Inmarsat mobile earth station, or 366xxxxx0 for all other ships.


The United States Coast Guard group ship station call identity is 036699999, and group coast station call identity is 003669999.


In the U.S., MMSIs are primarily used for digital selective calling and for assigning Inmarsat identities.



## Exhaustion of MMSIs

[edit]


</fragment>
</document>

The engines can be powered with both LNG and distillate fuel. The ship contains other alternative energy features, like the use of fuel cells to produce electricity and fresh water.[4] *Icon of the Seas* is the first Royal Caribbean vessel to use such technology.[16]


The ship will have a crew of 2,350, and a capacity of 5,610 passengers at double occupancy, or 7,600 passengers at maximum capacity.[2]


*Icon of the Seas* has 20 decks with seven swimming pools and six water slides. The company claims the ship has the tallest waterfall, the tallest water slide, the largest waterpark, and the first suspended infinity pool of any ship.[2]

<fragment>
*Icon of the Seas* is powered by liquified natural gas (LNG), with a gross tonnage of 250,800. The ship has six multi-fuel Wärtsilä engines generating 67,500 kW (90,520 hp) of power. The engines can be powered with both LNG and distillate fuel. The ship contains other alternative energy features, like the use of fuel cells to produce electricity and fresh water.[4] *Icon of the Seas* is the first Royal Caribbean vessel to use such technology.[16]


The ship will have a crew of 2,350, and a capacity of 5,610 passengers at double occupancy, or 7,600 passengers at maximum capacity.[2]


*Icon of the Seas* has 20 decks with seven swimming pools and six water slides. The company claims the ship has the tallest waterfall, the tallest water slide, the largest waterpark, and the first suspended infinity pool of any ship.[2]

<document>
<title>Icon of the Seas</title>
<fragment>

***Icon of the Seas*** is a cruise ship built for Royal Caribbean International and will be the lead ship of the *Icon* class. She is scheduled to enter service in early 2024 out of PortMiami in the US.[3] At 250,800 gross tonnage (GT), *Icon of the Seas* will be the largest cruise ship in the world.[2][1]




## History

[edit]

In October 2016, Royal Caribbean and Finnish shipbuilder Meyer Turku announced an order to build two ships under the project name "Icon".[4] The ships are expected to be delivered in the third quarter of 2023 and in 2025.[5][6] The ships will be classified by DNV.[7]


Royal Caribbean applied to register a trademark for "Icon of the Seas" in 2016.[8]


</fragment>

* *Symphony of the Seas* (2018)
* *Wonder of the Seas* (2022)

<fragment>
*Icon of the Seas* is powered by liquified natural gas (LNG), with a gross tonnage of 250,800. The ship has six multi-fuel Wärtsilä engines generating 67,500 kW (90,520 hp) of power. The engines can be powered with both LNG and distillate fuel. The ship contains other alternative energy features, like the use of fuel cells to produce electricity and fresh water.[4] *Icon of the Seas* is the first Royal Caribbean vessel to use such technology.[16]


The ship will have a crew of 2,350, and a capacity of 5,610 passengers at double occupancy, or 7,600 passengers at maximum capacity.[2]


*Icon of the Seas* has 20 decks with seven swimming pools and six water slides. The company claims the ship has the tallest waterfall, the tallest water slide, the largest waterpark, and the first suspended infinity pool of any ship.[2]

<document>
<title>Wonder of the Seas</title>
<fragment>

***Wonder of the Seas*** is the flagship of Royal Caribbean International. She was completed in 2022 in the Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard in Saint-Nazaire, France,[5] the fifth in Royal Caribbean's *Oasis* class of cruise ships.[6] At 236,857 GT, she was the largest cruise ship in the world by gross tonnage, surpassed by the succeeding ship, *Icon of the Seas*, also owned by Royal Caribbean International.




## Description and design

[edit]

*Wonder of the Seas* measures 1,188 feet (362 m) in length and has a gross tonnage of 236,857 across 18 decks. This ship accommodates 5,734 passengers at double occupancy or up to a maximum of 6,988 passengers, as well as a 2,300 crew. There are 16 decks for guest use, 20 restaurants, four pools and 2,867 cabins.[4]

<document>
<title>Icon of the Seas</title>
<fragment>

***Icon of the Seas*** is a cruise ship built for Royal Caribbean International and will be the lead ship of the *Icon* class. She is scheduled to enter service in early 2024 out of PortMiami in the US.[3] At 250,800 gross tonnage (GT), *Icon of the Seas* will be the largest cruise ship in the world.[2][1]




## History

[edit]

In October 2016, Royal Caribbean and Finnish shipbuilder Meyer Turku announced an order to build two ships under the project name "Icon".[4] The ships are expected to be delivered in the third quarter of 2023 and in 2025.[5][6] The ships will be classified by DNV.[7]


Royal Caribbean applied to register a trademark for "Icon of the Seas" in 2016.[8]


</fragment>

16. **^** Habibic, Ajsa (16 March 2023). "First of Six Multi-Fuel Engines Started on LNG-Powered Icon of the Seas". *Offshore Energy*. Retrieved 29 June 2023.

</fragment>
<fragment>
*Icon of the Seas* is powered by liquified natural gas (LNG), with a gross tonnage of 250,800. The ship has six multi-fuel Wärtsilä engines generating 67,500 kW (90,520 hp) of power. The engines can be powered with both LNG and distillate fuel. The ship contains other alternative energy features, like the use of fuel cells to produce electricity and fresh water.[4] *Icon of the Seas* is the first Royal Caribbean vessel to use such technology.[16]


The ship will have a crew of 2,350, and a capacity of 5,610 passengers at double occupancy, or 7,600 passengers at maximum capacity.[2]


*Icon of the Seas* has 20 decks with seven swimming pools and six water slides. The company claims the ship has the tallest waterfall, the tallest water slide, the largest waterpark, and the first suspended infinity pool of any ship.[2]

***Icon of the Seas*** is a cruise ship built for Royal Caribbean International and will be the lead ship of the *Icon* class. She is scheduled to enter service in early 2024 out of PortMiami in the US.[3] At 250,800 gross tonnage (GT), *Icon of the Seas* will be the largest cruise ship in the world.[2][1]




## History

[edit]

In October 2016, Royal Caribbean and Finnish shipbuilder Meyer Turku announced an order to build two ships under the project name "Icon".[4] The ships are expected to be delivered in the third quarter of 2023 and in 2025.[5][6] The ships will be classified by DNV.[7]


Royal Caribbean applied to register a trademark for "Icon of the Seas" in 2016.[8]
