### Cruise traffic

[edit]

Carnival, Disney, Norwegian and Royal Caribbean International are some of the cruise lines which dock at one of the six cruise terminals. Princess Cruises will begin to homeport a ship at Port Canaveral in 2024, along with Celebrity Cruises[34] The port hosted 109,175 multi-day cruise passengers in October 2008. There was a high of 307,005 passengers in April 2009. This fell to a seasonal low of 221,557 in October. ***Utopia of the Seas*** is a cruise ship under construction for Royal Caribbean International. She will be the sixth ship in the Oasis Class and is scheduled to enter service in the summer of 2024 out of Port Canaveral.[2] She will be the only ship in the class to not hold the title as the world's largest cruise ship.[3]



## History

[edit]

On 18 February 2019, Royal Caribbean announced an order of a sixth and final *Oasis*-class cruise ship. She will be the first in the class to be powered by liquefied natural gas.[4]


Royal Caribbean applied to register a trademark for *Utopia of the Seas* in 2021, out of 23 other ship names.[3]


On 5 April 2022, Royal Caribbean announced the name, *Utopia of the Seas* and the steel cutting ceremony.[5]


The LNG-tanks were built by Wärtsila and delivered in November 2022.[6]

## Current Largest Cruise Ship (as of 2024)

**Icon of the Seas** is currently the world's largest cruise ship with a gross tonnage of **250,800 GT**. Here's the comparison:

## Key Features of Icon of the Seas

- **Operator:** Royal Caribbean International
- **Class:** First ship in the new Icon class
- **Power:** Powered by liquefied natural gas (LNG) with fuel cells
- **Capacity:** 5,610 passengers (double occupancy) or up to 7,600 maximum
- **Crew:** 2,350

- **Propulsion:** Six multi-fuel Wärtsilä engines generating 67,500 kW

Icon of the Seas represents a significant advance in cruise ship technology, being the first Royal Caribbean vessel to use LNG fuel with fuel cells for electricity and fresh water production. <fragment>

The regulation provides that every ship owner and management company shall have a unique identification number. Other amendments require these numbers to be added to the relevant certificates and documents in the International Safety Management Code (ISM) and the International Ship and Port Facility Security Code (ISPS).[1] Like the IMO ship identification number, the company identification number is a seven-digit number with the prefix IMO. For example, for the ship *Atlantic Star* (IMO 8024026), IMO 5304986 referred to the former ship manager Pullmantur Cruises Ship Management Ltd and IMO 5364264 to her former owner, Pullmantur Cruises Empress Ltd.[16]



## Assignment

[edit]

S&P Global is the manager of the scheme and, as such, identifies and assigns IMO numbers without charge.[1] The organization was previously known as Lloyd's Register-Fairplay, IHS Fairplay and IHS Maritime.

msg.content:
<document>
<title>Maritime Mobile Service Identity</title>
<fragment>
Digital radio identification code for marine stations

A **Maritime Mobile Service Identity** (**MMSI**) is effectively a maritime object's international *maritime telephone number*, a temporarily assigned UID, issued by that object's current flag state (unlike an IMO number, which is a global forever UID).


An MMSI comprises a series of nine digits, consisting of three Maritime Identification Digits (country-codes), concatenated with a specific identifier. Whenever an object is re-flagged, a new MMSI must be assigned.


A 'maritime object' could be anything which requests an MMSI identifier. e.g. a vessel, fixed offshore installation, mobile unit, maritime aircraft, coast station, etc. 
Communications may be routed to 'individual objects', or to 'groups of objects'. A group call to objects can be based on an object's - locale, owner/operator/fleet, type, etc. or combinations thereof.


</fragment>
<fragment>
Because all ships on international voyages, as well as all ships fitted with an Inmarsat B or M ship earth station, are assigned MMSIs of the format MIDxxx000, a serious problem has arisen internationally in assigning sufficient numbers of MIDs to all administrations that need them. For example, a country having 10,000 Inmarsat-equipped ships would require 10 MIDs just to accommodate those 10,000 ships. If 50,000 boaters decided to fit small Inmarsat M terminals, 50 additional MIDs would be required to accommodate them.


The problem exists with Inmarsat-equipped ships because ITU-T recommendations require that Inmarsat ship earth stations be assigned the identity (MESIN) TMIDxxxYY, where T indicates the type of Inmarsat station, YY indicates the Inmarsat station extension (e.g."00" might indicate a telephone in the bridge, "01" might indicate a fax machine in the radio room, etc.), and MIDxxx indicates the ship station number, which relates to the assigned ship station identity MIDxxx000.


</fragment>
<fragment>

MMSI are formed in such a way that the identity or part thereof can be used by telephone and telex subscribers connected to the general telecommunications network to call any of these objects automatically. Communications are sent in digital form over a radio frequency channel.




## Types

[edit]

There are now six kinds of maritime mobile service identities:



* Ship station identities
* Group ship station identities
* Coast station identities
* Group coast station identities
* SAR aircraft
* Navigational aids and craft associated with a parent ship


## Maritime identification digits (MID)

[edit]

Main article: Maritime identification digits


</fragment>
<fragment>

The MMSI was meant to be an all-inclusive ship electronic identity, used in one form or another by every GMDSS or telecommunications instrument on the ship. Questions have been raised, however, whether the MMSI can in practice totally fulfill that role. ITU may eventually end the practice of relating Inmarsat MESIN identities with the ship MMSI identity.


To help mitigate against MMSI number exhaustion, manufacturers are required to cripple DSC-capable radios so that an MMSI number can only be entered once, which means that a device owner cannot move the radio from one boat to another. This is especially egregious for hand-held VHF devices, for which a single MMSI number makes little sense.[*opinion*]


</fragment>
</document>

<document>
<title>Maritime identification digits</title>
<fragment>
**Maritime identification digits** are used by radio communication facilities to identify their home country or base area in Digital Selective Calling (DSC), Automatic Transmitter Identification System (ATIS), and Automatic Identification System (AIS) messages as part of their Maritime Mobile Service Identities. The International Telecommunication Union facilitates the assignment of MIDs to countries.[1] Note that not all countries have MIDs; those without are typically landlocked, with no access to international waters. Sorting MID assignments in numerical order reveals a regional structure, with the first digit:



* 2 assigned to Europe,
* 3 to North America and the Caribbean Sea,
* 4 to Asia (except the southeast),
* 5 to the Pacific and Eastern Indian Oceans and Southeast Asia,
* 6 to Africa, the Atlantic and Western Indian Oceans, and
* 7 to South America.

<document>
<title>Icon of the Seas</title>
<fragment>

***Icon of the Seas*** is a cruise ship built for Royal Caribbean International and will be the lead ship of the *Icon* class. She is scheduled to enter service in early 2024 out of PortMiami in the US.[3] At 250,800 gross tonnage (GT), *Icon of the Seas* will be the largest cruise ship in the world.[2][1]




## History

[edit]

In October 2016, Royal Caribbean and Finnish shipbuilder Meyer Turku announced an order to build two ships under the project name "Icon".[4] The ships are expected to be delivered in the third quarter of 2023 and in 2025.[5][6] The ships will be classified by DNV.[7]


Royal Caribbean applied to register a trademark for "Icon of the Seas" in 2016.[8]

*Icon of the Seas* is powered by liquified natural gas (LNG), with a gross tonnage of 250,800. The ship has six multi-fuel Wärtsilä engines generating 67,500 kW (90,520 hp) of power. The engines can be powered with both LNG and distillate fuel. The ship contains other alternative energy features, like the use of fuel cells to produce electricity and fresh water.[4] *Icon of the Seas* is the first Royal Caribbean vessel to use such technology.[16]


The ship will have a crew of 2,350, and a capacity of 5,610 passengers at double occupancy, or 7,600 passengers at maximum capacity.[2]


*Icon of the Seas* has 20 decks with seven swimming pools and six water slides. The company claims the ship has the tallest waterfall, the tallest water slide, the largest waterpark, and the first suspended infinity pool of any ship.[2]

***Icon of the Seas*** is a cruise ship built for Royal Caribbean International and will be the lead ship of the *Icon* class. She is scheduled to enter service in early 2024 out of PortMiami in the US.[3] At 250,800 gross tonnage (GT), *Icon of the Seas* will be the largest cruise ship in the world.[2][1]




## History

[edit]

In October 2016, Royal Caribbean and Finnish shipbuilder Meyer Turku announced an order to build two ships under the project name "Icon".[4] The ships are expected to be delivered in the third quarter of 2023 and in 2025.[5][6] The ships will be classified by DNV.[7]


Royal Caribbean applied to register a trademark for "Icon of the Seas" in 2016.[8]

<document>
<title>Maritime Mobile Service Identity</title>
<fragment>
Digital radio identification code for marine stations

A **Maritime Mobile Service Identity** (**MMSI**) is effectively a maritime object's international *maritime telephone number*, a temporarily assigned UID, issued by that object's current flag state (unlike an IMO number, which is a global forever UID).


An MMSI comprises a series of nine digits, consisting of three Maritime Identification Digits (country-codes), concatenated with a specific identifier. Whenever an object is re-flagged, a new MMSI must be assigned.


A 'maritime object' could be anything which requests an MMSI identifier. e.g. a vessel, fixed offshore installation, mobile unit, maritime aircraft, coast station, etc. 
Communications may be routed to 'individual objects', or to 'groups of objects'. A group call to objects can be based on an object's - locale, owner/operator/fleet, type, etc. or combinations thereof.


</fragment>
<fragment>

MMSI are formed in such a way that the identity or part thereof can be used by telephone and telex subscribers connected to the general telecommunications network to call any of these objects automatically. Communications are sent in digital form over a radio frequency channel.




## Types

[edit]

There are now six kinds of maritime mobile service identities:



* Ship station identities
* Group ship station identities
* Coast station identities
* Group coast station identities
* SAR aircraft
* Navigational aids and craft associated with a parent ship


## Maritime identification digits (MID)

[edit]

Main article: Maritime identification digits


</fragment>
<fragment>
In the United States (one of whose MIDs is 366), federal MMSIs are assigned by the National Telecommunications and Information Administration, and are normally (but not always) formed as 3669xxxxx. Non-federal MMSIs are assigned by the Federal Communications Commission normally as part of the ship station license application, and are formed as 366xxx000 for ships on international voyages and ships needing an Inmarsat mobile earth station, or 366xxxxx0 for all other ships.


The United States Coast Guard group ship station call identity is 036699999, and group coast station call identity is 003669999.


In the U.S., MMSIs are primarily used for digital selective calling and for assigning Inmarsat identities.



## Exhaustion of MMSIs

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

The World Radio Conference, Geneva, 1997 (WRC-97), adopted Resolution 344 concerning the exhaustion of the maritime mobile service identity resource. In view of improvements to public switched telephone networks, and new capabilities of the Inmarsat system other than Inmarsat B or M, previous restrictions should no longer be applicable. All nine digits of the MMSI can be used in such cases, and no longer need to end in trailing zeros.



## See also

[edit]

![](image)

Wikidata has the property: 
* ![](image) ***MMSI (P587)*** (see uses)

* Automatic Identification System uses MMSI codegroups for ship ID
* Global Maritime Distress Safety System
* Inmarsat and the International Mobile Satellite Organization (IMSO)
* Maritime call sign, not tied to MMSI but can contain MMSI after
* SOLAS Convention a global Maritime Safety Convention


## References

[edit]


</fragment>
</document>

<document>
<title>Maritime identification digits</title>
<fragment>
**Maritime identification digits** are used by radio communication facilities to identify their home country or base area in Digital Selective Calling (DSC), Automatic Transmitter Identification System (ATIS), and Automatic Identification System (AIS) messages as part of their Maritime Mobile Service Identities. The International Telecommunication Union facilitates the assignment of MIDs to countries.[1] Note that not all countries have MIDs; those without are typically landlocked, with no access to international waters. Sorting MID assignments in numerical order reveals a regional structure, with the first digit:



* 2 assigned to Europe,
* 3 to North America and the Caribbean Sea,
* 4 to Asia (except the southeast),
* 5 to the Pacific and Eastern Indian Oceans and Southeast Asia,
* 6 to Africa, the Atlantic and Western Indian Oceans, and
* 7 to South America.

<document>
<title>Maritime call sign</title>
<fragment>
Call signs assigned as unique identifiers to ships and boats

![](image)Soviet nuclear Icebreaker *Arktika* with call sign UKTY
![](image)USS *Carl Vinson* and JS *Ashigara* displaying signal flags showing callsigns NCVV and JSRA, respectively
**Maritime call signs** are call signs assigned as unique identifiers to ships and boats. All radio transmissions must be individually identified by the call sign. Merchant and naval vessels are assigned call signs by their national licensing authorities.



## History

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
1. **^** "Titanic FAQs, Page 2: Signals". *Marconigraph.com*. 2002. Archived from the original on March 21, 2009.
2. **^** "The RMS Titanic Radio Page". *HF.ro*. 2012. Archived from the original on December 17, 2016.
3. **^** Fenwick, William (July 1928). "Broadcast Station Calls With a Past". *Radio Broadcast*. Doubleday, Doran & Company, Inc.: 150.
4. **^** "US NODC Codes for worldwide ships sorted by ship name". *International Research Vessel Schedules & Information*. Oceanic Information Center. Retrieved December 29, 2019.
5. **^** "Ship Radio Stations". Federal Communications Commission. October 9, 2019. Retrieved December 29, 2019.


</fragment>
<fragment>

On April 14, 1912, the RMS *Titanic* station MGY, busily delivering telegram traffic from ship's passengers to the coastal station at Cape Race, Newfoundland (call sign MCE), would receive warnings of ice fields from Marconi stations aboard the MV *Mesaba* (call sign MMU) and the SS *Californian* (call sign MWL).[1] Its distress call *CQD CQD CQD CQD CQD CQD DE MGY MGY MGY MGY MGY MGY POSITION 41.44 N 50.24 W* would be answered by a station aboard the RMS *Carpathia* (call sign MPA).[2] Later that same year, an international conference standardised radio call signs so that the first two letters would uniquely identify a transmitter's country of origin.


</fragment>
<fragment>

Merchant and naval vessels are assigned call signs by their national licensing authorities. In the case of states such as Liberia or Panama, which are flags of convenience for ship registration, call signs for larger vessels consist of the national prefix plus three letters (for example, 3LXY, and sometimes followed by a number, i.e. 3LXY2). United States merchant vessels are given call signs beginning with the letters "W" or "K" while U.S. naval ships are assigned call signs beginning with "N". Originally, both ships and broadcast stations were given call signs in this series consisting of three or four letters, but as demand for both marine radio and broadcast call signs grew, gradually American-flagged vessels were given longer call signs with mixed letters and numbers.


</fragment>
<fragment>

Leisure craft with VHF radios may not be assigned call signs, in which case the name of the vessel is used instead. Ships in the U.S. wishing to have a radio licence anyway are under FCC Radio Service Code SA: "Ship Recreational or Voluntarily Equipped".[5] Those calls follow the land mobile format of the initial letter K or W followed by 1 or 2 letters followed by 3 or 4 numbers (such as KX0983 or WXX0029).


U.S. Coast Guard small boats have a number that is shown on both bows (i.e. port and starboard) in which the first two digits indicate the nominal length of the boat in feet. For example, Coast Guard 47021 refers to the 21st in the series of 47-foot motor lifeboats. The call sign might also be abbreviated to the final two or three numbers during operations, for example: Coast Guard zero two one.



## See also

[edit]

* Maritime Mobile Service Identity
* Pan-pan


## References

[edit]


</fragment>
</document>

<title>Automatic identification system</title>
<fragment>
* IMO ship identification number: a seven-digit number that remains unchanged upon transfer of the ship's registration to another country
* Radio call sign: international radio call sign, up to 7 characters, assigned to the vessel by its country of registry
* Name: 20 characters to represent the name of the vessel
* Type of ship/cargo
* Dimensions of ship, to nearest meter
* Location of positioning system's (e.g., GPS) antenna on board the vessel: in meters aft of bow and meters port or starboard
* Type of positioning system: such as GPS, DGPS or LORAN-C.
* Draught of ship: 0.1–25.5 meters
* Destination: max. 20 characters
* Estimated time of arrival (ETA) at destination: UTC month/date hour:minute
* Optional: high precision time request, a vessel can request other vessels provide a high precision UTC time- and date-stamp


### Detailed description: Class B units

[edit]


</fragment>

* Vessel Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI): a unique nine digit identification number.
* Navigation status: e.g., "at anchor", "under way using engine(s)", "not under command", etc.

* True heading: 0 to 359° (for example from a gyro compass)

Online marine traffic tracking service



MarineTraffic| ![](image) |

| Launched | 2007 |

**MarineTraffic** is a maritime analytics provider,[1] which provides real-time information on the movements of ships and the current location of ships in harbors and ports.[2] A database of information on the vessels includes for example details of the location where they were built plus dimensions of the vessels, gross tonnage and International Maritime Organisation (IMO) number. Users can submit photographs of the vessels which other users can rate.


The basic MarineTraffic service can be used without cost; more advanced functions such as satellite-based tracking are available subject to payment.[3]


The site has six million unique visitors on a monthly basis. In April 2015, the service had 600,000 registered users.[4][5]




## How it works

[edit]

Data is gathered from in excess of 18,000 AIS equipped volunteer contributors in over 140 countries around the world.[6] Information provided by AIS equipment, such as unique identification, position, course, and speed, is then transferred to the main Marine Traffic servers for display via the website in real time. The site uses data from OpenStreetMap on its base map, and the paid version lets users display ship locations on Nautical Charts.



## History

[edit]

MarineTraffic was originally developed as an academic project at the University of the Aegean in Ermoupoli, Greece.[7][8]


In late 2007, Professor Dimitris Lekkas published it as a trial version.[4]



## Community

[edit]

MarineTraffic is highly dependent on its community of radio amateurs or AIS Station operators, its photographers and translators.


In support of the community, MarineTraffic recently made available a free AIS processing tool, under a Creative Commons license.[9]



## Acquisition

[edit]

In February 2023, data and analytics firm Kpler announced the acquisition of MarineTraffic and Fleetmon for an undisclosed sum.[1][2] The acquisitions closed in March 2023.

[edit]

<document>
<title>MarineTraffic</title>
<content>
Online marine traffic tracking service



MarineTraffic| ![](image) |
| Type of site
 | Ship tracking intelligence |
| Available in | English, Spanish, Arabic, Russian, German, French, Greek, Chinese, Norwegian, Dutch and Portuguese |
| Headquarters | Athens, Greece |
| URL | www.marinetraffic.com |
| Commercial | Yes |
| Registration | Optional |
| Users | 2,000,000 |
| Launched | 2007 |
| Current status | Open |


**MarineTraffic** is a maritime analytics provider,[1] which provides real-time information on the movements of ships and the current location of ships in harbors and ports.[2] A database of information on the vessels includes for example details of the location where they were built plus dimensions of the vessels, gross tonnage and International Maritime Organisation (IMO) number. Users can submit photographs of the vessels which other users can rate.


The basic MarineTraffic service can be used without cost; more advanced functions such as satellite-based tracking are available subject to payment.[3]


The site has six million unique visitors on a monthly basis. In April 2015, the service had 600,000 registered users.[4][5]




## How it works

[edit]

Data is gathered from in excess of 18,000 AIS equipped volunteer contributors in over 140 countries around the world.[6] Information provided by AIS equipment, such as unique identification, position, course, and speed, is then transferred to the main Marine Traffic servers for display via the website in real time. The site uses data from OpenStreetMap on its base map, and the paid version lets users display ship locations on Nautical Charts.



## History

[edit]

MarineTraffic was originally developed as an academic project at the University of the Aegean in Ermoupoli, Greece.[7][8]


In late 2007, Professor Dimitris Lekkas published it as a trial version.[4]



## Community

[edit]

MarineTraffic is highly dependent on its community of radio amateurs or AIS Station operators, its photographers and translators.


In support of the community, MarineTraffic recently made available a free AIS processing tool, under a Creative Commons license.[9]



## Acquisition

[edit]

In February 2023, data and analytics firm Kpler announced the acquisition of MarineTraffic and Fleetmon for an undisclosed sum.[1][2] The acquisitions closed in March 2023.

[edit]

Marine vessels and structures are classified according to the soundness of their structure and design for the purpose of the vessel. The classification rules are designed to ensure an acceptable degree of stability, safety, environmental impact, etc.

### Functions aboard the vessel

[edit]

The most basic function of a VMS is to determine the vessel's location at a given time, and periodically transmit this information, to a monitoring station ashore. Based on my research, here's a comprehensive guide to the best publicly accessible maritime databases and vessel tracking websites for your shipping fleet research:

## **Major AIS Vessel Tracking Services**

### **1. MarineTraffic**
**URL:** www.marinetraffic.com
**Free Tier:** Robust basic service with advanced paid features

**What it provides:**
- **MMSI numbers** and **IMO numbers**
- **Radio call signs** 
- Real-time vessel positions via AIS
- Vessel dimensions, tonnage, and technical specifications
- Flag state information
- Vessel photographs and historical tracking data
- 6 million monthly unique visitors with strong community features

**Access:** Basic tracking is free; satellite tracking and advanced analytics are paid

### **2. VesselFinder**
**URL:** www.vesselfinder.com
**Free Tier:** Comprehensive free vessel tracking

**What it provides:**
- MMSI, IMO numbers, and call signs
- Real-time and historical vessel positions
- Detailed vessel specifications and dimensions
- Fleet management tools (paid tier)

### **3. FleetMon**
**URL:** www.fleetmon.com
**Free Tier:** Good basic vessel information

**What it provides:**
- MMSI and IMO numbers
- Call signs and flag state data
- Vessel tracking and specifications
- More specialized for maritime professionals

## **Official Maritime Databases**

### **4. EQUASIS (European Quality Shipping Information System)**
**URL:** www.equasis.org
**Cost:** Free (but requires registration)

**What it provides:**
- Official **IMO numbers** and ship identification
- **Classification society information** (LR, DNV, ABS, BV, etc.)
- Flag state and port state control records
- Ship inspection history
- Company ownership details
- Comprehensive vessel particulars

### **5. IMO Ship Identification Database**
**Access:** Through official maritime administration websites
**What it provides:**
- **Official IMO numbers** (permanent vessel identifiers)
- Basic ship registration information

## **Technical Data Available Through AIS**

According to AIS specifications, vessels automatically broadcast:

### **Every 2-6 seconds:**
- **Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI)** - unique 9-digit identification
- Position (latitude/longitude)
- Speed and course over ground
- Navigation status
- True heading

### **Every 6 minutes:**
- **IMO ship identification number** - permanent 7-digit number
- **Radio call sign** - up to 7 characters
- Vessel name
- Ship/cargo type
- **Dimensions** (length, beam) to nearest meter
- Draught
- Destination and ETA

## **Classification Society Information**

For detailed technical specifications and classification data, check:

### **6. Major Classification Societies (Free public registries):**
- **Lloyd's Register** (LR) - www.lr.org
- **DNV** (formerly DNV GL) - www.dnv.com  
- **American Bureau of Shipping** (ABS) - www.eagle.org
- **Bureau Veritas** (BV) - www.bureauveritas.com
- **RINA** - www.rina.org
- **ClassNK** - www.classnk.or.jp

**What they provide:**
- Technical specifications and plans
- Classification status and certificates
- Survey histories
- Construction details

## **Additional Valuable Resources**

### **7. Vessel Monitoring System (VMS) Data**
- Primarily for fishing vessels
- Provides location tracking data
- Used by fisheries management authorities

### **8. Maritime Administration Registries**
- U.S. Coast Guard Vessel Documentation
- UK Maritime and Coastguard Agency
- Other national maritime registries

## **Recommended Research Strategy**

1. **Start with MarineTraffic** for basic vessel identification and tracking
2. **Cross-reference with EQUASIS** for official classification and regulatory information  
3. **Check VesselFinder** for additional technical details and historical data
4. **Visit classification society websites** for detailed technical specifications
5. **Use official registries** for flag state and registration verification

## **Key Information You'll Find**

✅ **MMSI Numbers** - Available on all AIS tracking sites
✅ **IMO Numbers** - Available on AIS sites and EQUASIS (most reliable source)
✅ **Radio Call Signs** - Automatically broadcast via AIS
✅ **Flag State** - Available on AIS platforms and EQUASIS
✅ **Vessel Dimensions** - Detailed specs on AIS and classification sites
✅ **Classification Society** - Best sources are EQUASIS and society websites
✅ **Technical Specifications** - Most comprehensive from classification societies

## **Limitations**

- Some detailed ownership and financial information may require subscription services
- Military and government vessels may have limited public data
- Very recent sales or flag changes may have reporting delays
- Satellite AIS coverage varies by region

This combination of freely available AIS tracking services, official maritime databases, and classification society registries should provide comprehensive coverage of all the vessel information you need for your fleet research.

<document>
<title>IMO number</title>
<fragment>
11. **^** "RESOLUTION A.1117(30) - IMO SHIP IDENTIFICATION NUMBER SCHEME" (PDF). International Maritime Organization. 18 December 2017. Retrieved 21 May 2022.
12. **^** "The IMO Number Explained" (PDF). The Pew Charitable Trusts. May 2017. Retrieved 21 May 2022.
13. **^** "United Nations Treaty Collection: Glossary". treaties.un.org. Retrieved 21 May 2022.
14. **^** "INTERNATIONAL CONVENTION FOR THE SAFETY OF LIFE AT SEA 2004" (PDF). Arctic Portal. Retrieved 21 May 2022. Every ship shall be provided with an identification number which conforms to the IMO ship identification number scheme adopted by the Organization.
15. **^** "IMO International Convention Calendar". Class NK. 25 December 2012. Archived from the original on 3 March 2014. Retrieved 20 March 2013.
16. **^** "*Atlantic Star* (8024026)". *Equasis*. Ministry of Ecology, Sustainable Development and Energy. Retrieved 20 March 2013.

</fragment>
<fragment>

For new vessels, the IMO ship number is assigned to a hull during construction, generally upon keel laying. Many vessels which fall outside the mandatory requirements of SOLAS have numbers allocated by Lloyd's Register or IHS Markit in the same numerical series, including fishing vessels[17] and commercial yachts.[18]



## Structure

[edit]

An IMO number is made of the three letters "IMO" followed by a seven-digit number. This consists of a six-digit sequential unique number followed by a check digit. The integrity of an IMO number can be verified using its check digit. This is done by multiplying each of the first six digits by a factor of *2* to *7* corresponding to their position from right to left. The rightmost digit of this sum is the check digit. For example, for IMO 907472**9**: (9×*7*) + (0×*6*) + (7×*5*) + (4×*4*) + (7×*3*) + (2×*2*) = 13**9**.[19][20]



## See also

[edit]

* ![icon](image)Transport portal


</fragment>
<fragment>
17. **^** "Unique Vessel Identifier (UVI) - Global Record". Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations. Retrieved 20 March 2013.
18. **^** "Setting Industry Standards". IHS Fairplay. Archived from the original on 3 March 2013. Retrieved 20 March 2013.
19. **^** Vuori, Teppo (21 August 2013). "How to compute check characters for Coden and IMO Number". *Teppovuori.fi*. Retrieved 20 September 2013.
20. **^** "Error messages table". *LRIT DB User Manual*. European Maritime Safety Agency. Retrieved 20 March 2013.

## External links

[edit]

![](image)

Wikimedia Commons has media related to Ships by IMO number.

* IMO Identification Numbers for Ships, Companies & Registered Owners by IHS Markit
* IMO NUMBER SEARCH

</fragment>
<fragment>
International ship identification number

![](image)"IMO 8814275" on *Eendracht*
![](image)Stern of *Evangelia* displaying "IMO 9176187"
The **IMO number** of the International Maritime Organization is a generic term covering two distinct meanings. The IMO ship identification number is a unique ship identifier; the IMO company and registered owner identification number is used to identify uniquely each company and/or registered owner managing ships of at least 100 gross tons (gt). The schemes are managed in parallel, but IMO company/owner numbers may also be obtained by managers of vessels *not* having IMO ship numbers. IMO numbers were introduced to improve maritime safety and reduce fraud and pollution, under the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS).[1][2]


</fragment>

**MarineTraffic** is a maritime analytics provider,[1] which provides real-time information on the movements of ships and the current location of ships in harbors and ports.[2] A database of information on the vessels includes for example details of the location where they were built plus dimensions of the vessels, gross tonnage and International Maritime Organisation (IMO) number. Users can submit photographs of the vessels which other users can rate.


The basic MarineTraffic service can be used without cost; more advanced functions such as satellite-based tracking are available subject to payment.[3]


The site has six million unique visitors on a monthly basis. In April 2015, the service had 600,000 registered users.[4][5]




## How it works

[edit]

Data is gathered from in excess of 18,000 AIS equipped volunteer contributors in over 140 countries around the world.[6] Information provided by AIS equipment, such as unique identification, position, course, and speed, is then transferred to the main Marine Traffic servers for display via the website in real time. The site uses data from OpenStreetMap on its base map, and the paid version lets users display ship locations on Nautical Charts.



## History

[edit]

MarineTraffic was originally developed as an academic project at the University of the Aegean in Ermoupoli, Greece.[7][8]


In late 2007, Professor Dimitris Lekkas published it as a trial version.[4]



## Community

[edit]

MarineTraffic is highly dependent on its community of radio amateurs or AIS Station operators, its photographers and translators.


In support of the community, MarineTraffic recently made available a free AIS processing tool, under a Creative Commons license.[9]



## Acquisition

[edit]

In February 2023, data and analytics firm Kpler announced the acquisition of MarineTraffic and Fleetmon for an undisclosed sum.[1][2] The acquisitions closed in March 2023.

<document>
<title>Maritime call sign</title>
<fragment>

Merchant and naval vessels are assigned call signs by their national licensing authorities. In the case of states such as Liberia or Panama, which are flags of convenience for ship registration, call signs for larger vessels consist of the national prefix plus three letters (for example, 3LXY, and sometimes followed by a number, i.e. 3LXY2). United States merchant vessels are given call signs beginning with the letters "W" or "K" while U.S. naval ships are assigned call signs beginning with "N". Originally, both ships and broadcast stations were given call signs in this series consisting of three or four letters, but as demand for both marine radio and broadcast call signs grew, gradually American-flagged vessels were given longer call signs with mixed letters and numbers.


</fragment>
<fragment>
Call signs assigned as unique identifiers to ships and boats

![](image)Soviet nuclear Icebreaker *Arktika* with call sign UKTY
![](image)USS *Carl Vinson* and JS *Ashigara* displaying signal flags showing callsigns NCVV and JSRA, respectively
**Maritime call signs** are call signs assigned as unique identifiers to ships and boats. All radio transmissions must be individually identified by the call sign. Merchant and naval vessels are assigned call signs by their national licensing authorities.



## History

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Leisure craft with VHF radios may not be assigned call signs, in which case the name of the vessel is used instead. Ships in the U.S. wishing to have a radio licence anyway are under FCC Radio Service Code SA: "Ship Recreational or Voluntarily Equipped".[5] Those calls follow the land mobile format of the initial letter K or W followed by 1 or 2 letters followed by 3 or 4 numbers (such as KX0983 or WXX0029).


U.S. Coast Guard small boats have a number that is shown on both bows (i.e. port and starboard) in which the first two digits indicate the nominal length of the boat in feet. For example, Coast Guard 47021 refers to the 21st in the series of 47-foot motor lifeboats. The call sign might also be abbreviated to the final two or three numbers during operations, for example: Coast Guard zero two one.



## See also

[edit]

* Maritime Mobile Service Identity
* Pan-pan


## References

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
1. **^** "Titanic FAQs, Page 2: Signals". *Marconigraph.com*. 2002. Archived from the original on March 21, 2009.
2. **^** "The RMS Titanic Radio Page". *HF.ro*. 2012. Archived from the original on December 17, 2016.
3. **^** Fenwick, William (July 1928). "Broadcast Station Calls With a Past". *Radio Broadcast*. Doubleday, Doran & Company, Inc.: 150.
4. **^** "US NODC Codes for worldwide ships sorted by ship name". *International Research Vessel Schedules & Information*. Oceanic Information Center. Retrieved December 29, 2019.
5. **^** "Ship Radio Stations". Federal Communications Commission. October 9, 2019. Retrieved December 29, 2019.


</fragment>
<fragment>

As broadcast stations became commonplace in the 1920s, some original three- and four-letter call signs were reassigned as the corresponding ships were removed from U.S. registry. The WSB call sign had been held by two ships (the SS *Francis H. Leggett*, shipwrecked off Oregon's coast on September 18, 1914, and later the *Firwood*, a ship destroyed by fire near Peru on December 18, 1919[3]) before being assigned to *The Atlanta Journal* for use by its Atlanta, Georgia, broadcast radio station in 1922. Similarly, WEZU, the international radio call sign of the ship SS *Lash Atlantico*, was assigned in 1997 to a broadcast station.[4] Additional call signs would be reassigned to coastal stations or moved from marine radio to terrestrial broadcast radio when ships were sold for registration to foreign nations, as the new owners would obtain new, local call signs for any existing shipboard radio stations.


</fragment>
</document>

[edit]

*Wonder of the Seas* measures 1,188 feet (362 m) in length and has a gross tonnage of 236,857 across 18 decks. This ship accommodates 5,734 passengers at double occupancy or up to a maximum of 6,988 passengers, as well as a 2,300 crew. As demand for both marine radio and broadcast call signs grew, gradually American-flagged vessels with radiotelephony only were given longer call signs with mixed letters and numbers. 


Leisure craft with VHF radios may not be assigned call signs, in which case the name of the vessel is used instead. Ships in the US still wishing to have a radio license are under FCC class SA: "Ship recreational or voluntarily equipped." Those calls follow the land mobile format of the initial letter K or W followed by 1 or 2 letters followed by 3 or 4 numbers (such as KX0983 or WXX0029). U.S. Coast Guard small boats have a number that is shown on both bows (i.e. port and starboard) in which the first two digits indicate the nominal length of the boat in feet. For example, Coast Guard 47021 refers to the 21st in the series of 47-foot motor lifeboats. The call sign might be abbreviated to the final two or three numbers during operations, for example: *Coast Guard zero two one*.

<title>Maritime Mobile Service Identity</title>
<fragment>

The World Radio Conference, Geneva, 1997 (WRC-97), adopted Resolution 344 concerning the exhaustion of the maritime mobile service identity resource. In view of improvements to public switched telephone networks, and new capabilities of the Inmarsat system other than Inmarsat B or M, previous restrictions should no longer be applicable. All nine digits of the MMSI can be used in such cases, and no longer need to end in trailing zeros.

## References

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
* 0 Ship group, coast station, or group of coast stations
* 1 For use by SAR aircraft (111MIDaxx)[note 1][2]
* 2-7 MMSI's used by individual ships, beginning with an MID:
	+ 2 Europe (e.g., Italy has MID 247; Denmark has MIDs 219 *and* 220)
	+ 3 North and Central America and Caribbean (e.g., Canada, 316; Greenland, 331; Panama, 351 through 357, plus 370 through 373; United States, 303(Alaska), 338(domestic), plus 366 through 369)
	+ 4 Asia (not the southeast) (e.g., PRC, 412, 413, and 414; Maldives, 455; Japan, 431)
	+ 5 Oceania (Australia, 503; New Zealand, 512), and Southeast Asia (Philippines, 548; Indonesia, 525)
	+ 6 Africa (Eritrea, 625)
	+ 7 South America (Peru, 760)
* 8 Handheld VHF transceiver with DSC and GNSS[3]
* 9 Devices using a free-form number identity:[2]
	+ Search and Rescue Transponders (970yyzzzz)[note 2][4][note 3][5]
	+ Man overboard DSC and/or AIS devices (972yyzzzz)[note 2]
	+ 406 MHz EPIRBs fitted with an AIS transmitter (974yyzzzz)[note 2]

</fragment>
<fragment>
In the United States (one of whose MIDs is 366), federal MMSIs are assigned by the National Telecommunications and Information Administration, and are normally (but not always) formed as 3669xxxxx. Non-federal MMSIs are assigned by the Federal Communications Commission normally as part of the ship station license application, and are formed as 366xxx000 for ships on international voyages and ships needing an Inmarsat mobile earth station, or 366xxxxx0 for all other ships.


The United States Coast Guard group ship station call identity is 036699999, and group coast station call identity is 003669999.


In the U.S., MMSIs are primarily used for digital selective calling and for assigning Inmarsat identities.



## Exhaustion of MMSIs

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Digital radio identification code for marine stations

A **Maritime Mobile Service Identity** (**MMSI**) is effectively a maritime object's international *maritime telephone number*, a temporarily assigned UID, issued by that object's current flag state (unlike an IMO number, which is a global forever UID).


An MMSI comprises a series of nine digits, consisting of three Maritime Identification Digits (country-codes), concatenated with a specific identifier. Whenever an object is re-flagged, a new MMSI must be assigned.


A 'maritime object' could be anything which requests an MMSI identifier. e.g. a vessel, fixed offshore installation, mobile unit, maritime aircraft, coast station, etc. 
Communications may be routed to 'individual objects', or to 'groups of objects'. A group call to objects can be based on an object's - locale, owner/operator/fleet, type, etc. or combinations thereof.


</fragment>
</document>

|  |

***Utopia of the Seas*** is a cruise ship under construction for Royal Caribbean International. She will be the sixth ship in the Oasis Class and is scheduled to enter service in the summer of 2024 out of Port Canaveral.[2] She will be the only ship in the class to not hold the title as the world's largest cruise ship.[3]



## History

[edit]

On 18 February 2019, Royal Caribbean announced an order of a sixth and final *Oasis*-class cruise ship. She will be the first in the class to be powered by liquefied natural gas.[4]


Royal Caribbean applied to register a trademark for *Utopia of the Seas* in 2021, out of 23 other ship names.[3]


On 5 April 2022, Royal Caribbean announced the name, *Utopia of the Seas* and the steel cutting ceremony.[5]


The LNG-tanks were built by Wärtsila and delivered in November 2022.[6]

***Harmony of the Seas*** is an *Oasis*-class cruise ship built by STX France at the Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard in Saint-Nazaire, France,[15] for Royal Caribbean International. With a gross tonnage of 226,963 GT,[2] she is the third largest passenger ship in the world, larger than her older sisters *Oasis of the Seas* and *Allure of the Seas*, but surpassed by her newer sisters *Symphony of the Seas* and *Wonder of the Seas*. In length, however, *Harmony of the Seas* is the longest cruise ship in the world.[17]

<document>
<title>Maritime call sign</title>
<fragment>
Call signs assigned as unique identifiers to ships and boats

![](image)Soviet nuclear Icebreaker *Arktika* with call sign UKTY
![](image)USS *Carl Vinson* and JS *Ashigara* displaying signal flags showing callsigns NCVV and JSRA, respectively
**Maritime call signs** are call signs assigned as unique identifiers to ships and boats. All radio transmissions must be individually identified by the call sign. Merchant and naval vessels are assigned call signs by their national licensing authorities.



## History

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
1. **^** "Titanic FAQs, Page 2: Signals". *Marconigraph.com*. 2002. Archived from the original on March 21, 2009.
2. **^** "The RMS Titanic Radio Page". *HF.ro*. 2012. Archived from the original on December 17, 2016.
3. **^** Fenwick, William (July 1928). "Broadcast Station Calls With a Past". *Radio Broadcast*. Doubleday, Doran & Company, Inc.: 150.
4. **^** "US NODC Codes for worldwide ships sorted by ship name". *International Research Vessel Schedules & Information*. Oceanic Information Center. Retrieved December 29, 2019.
5. **^** "Ship Radio Stations". Federal Communications Commission. October 9, 2019. Retrieved December 29, 2019.


</fragment>
<fragment>

Merchant and naval vessels are assigned call signs by their national licensing authorities. In the case of states such as Liberia or Panama, which are flags of convenience for ship registration, call signs for larger vessels consist of the national prefix plus three letters (for example, 3LXY, and sometimes followed by a number, i.e. 3LXY2). United States merchant vessels are given call signs beginning with the letters "W" or "K" while U.S. naval ships are assigned call signs beginning with "N". Originally, both ships and broadcast stations were given call signs in this series consisting of three or four letters, but as demand for both marine radio and broadcast call signs grew, gradually American-flagged vessels were given longer call signs with mixed letters and numbers.


</fragment>
<fragment>

Leisure craft with VHF radios may not be assigned call signs, in which case the name of the vessel is used instead. Ships in the U.S. wishing to have a radio licence anyway are under FCC Radio Service Code SA: "Ship Recreational or Voluntarily Equipped".[5] Those calls follow the land mobile format of the initial letter K or W followed by 1 or 2 letters followed by 3 or 4 numbers (such as KX0983 or WXX0029).


U.S. Coast Guard small boats have a number that is shown on both bows (i.e. port and starboard) in which the first two digits indicate the nominal length of the boat in feet. For example, Coast Guard 47021 refers to the 21st in the series of 47-foot motor lifeboats. The call sign might also be abbreviated to the final two or three numbers during operations, for example: Coast Guard zero two one.



## See also

[edit]

* Maritime Mobile Service Identity
* Pan-pan


## References

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

As broadcast stations became commonplace in the 1920s, some original three- and four-letter call signs were reassigned as the corresponding ships were removed from U.S. registry. The WSB call sign had been held by two ships (the SS *Francis H. Leggett*, shipwrecked off Oregon's coast on September 18, 1914, and later the *Firwood*, a ship destroyed by fire near Peru on December 18, 1919[3]) before being assigned to *The Atlanta Journal* for use by its Atlanta, Georgia, broadcast radio station in 1922. Similarly, WEZU, the international radio call sign of the ship SS *Lash Atlantico*, was assigned in 1997 to a broadcast station.[4] Additional call signs would be reassigned to coastal stations or moved from marine radio to terrestrial broadcast radio when ships were sold for registration to foreign nations, as the new owners would obtain new, local call signs for any existing shipboard radio stations.


</fragment>
</document>

Proposed cruise ship



*Utopia of the Seas*
|  |

***Utopia of the Seas*** is a cruise ship under construction for Royal Caribbean International. She will be the sixth ship in the Oasis Class and is scheduled to enter service in the summer of 2024 out of Port Canaveral.[2] She will be the only ship in the class to not hold the title as the world's largest cruise ship.[3]



## History

[edit]

On 18 February 2019, Royal Caribbean announced an order of a sixth and final *Oasis*-class cruise ship. She will be the first in the class to be powered by liquefied natural gas.[4]


Royal Caribbean applied to register a trademark for *Utopia of the Seas* in 2021, out of 23 other ship names.[3]


On 5 April 2022, Royal Caribbean announced the name, *Utopia of the Seas* and the steel cutting ceremony.[5]


The LNG-tanks were built by Wärtsila and delivered in November 2022.[6]

<title>Icon of the Seas</title>
<fragment>

***Icon of the Seas*** is a cruise ship built for Royal Caribbean International and will be the lead ship of the *Icon* class. She is scheduled to enter service in early 2024 out of PortMiami in the US.[3] At 250,800 gross tonnage (GT), *Icon of the Seas* will be the largest cruise ship in the world.[2][1]




## History

[edit]

In October 2016, Royal Caribbean and Finnish shipbuilder Meyer Turku announced an order to build two ships under the project name "Icon".[4] The ships are expected to be delivered in the third quarter of 2023 and in 2025.[5][6] The ships will be classified by DNV.[7]


Royal Caribbean applied to register a trademark for "Icon of the Seas" in 2016.[8]

<title>Timeline of largest passenger ships</title>
<fragment>

![](image)RMS Queen Elizabeth's size record stood for the longest time at over 54 years
This is a timeline of the world's largest passenger ships based upon internal volume, initially measured by gross register tonnage and later by gross tonnage. This timeline reflects the largest extant passenger ship in the world at any given time. If a given ship was superseded by another, scrapped, or lost at sea, it is then succeeded. Some records for tonnage outlived the ships that set them - notably the SS *Great Eastern*, and RMS *Queen Elizabeth*. The term "largest passenger ship" has gradually fallen out of use since the mid-1990s. Since that time the title of "largest cruise ship" has largely been given to those confined to cruising rather than transatlantic ocean travel.[1]

Marine vessels and structures are classified according to the soundness of their structure and design for the purpose of the vessel. The classification rules are designed to ensure an acceptable degree of stability, safety, environmental impact, etc.


In particular, classification societies may be authorised to inspect ships, oil rigs, submarines, and other marine structures and issue certificates on behalf of the flag state.


As well as providing classification and certification services, the larger societies also conduct research at their own research facilities in order to improve the effectiveness of their rules and to investigate the safety of new innovations in shipbuilding.

A **ship classification society** or **ship classification organisation** is a non-governmental organization that establishes and maintains technical standards for the construction and operation of ships and offshore structures. Classification societies certify that the construction of a vessel comply with relevant standards and carry out regular surveys in service to ensure continuing compliance with the standards. Currently, more than 50 organizations describe their activities as including marine classification, twelve of which are members of the International Association of Classification Societies.[1]

[edit]

In order to accommodate *Mardi Gras* as her new homeport, Port Canaveral developed and constructed Terminal 3, a new two-story, 188,000-square-foot cruise terminal that cost US$163 million to build, becoming the largest project in the port's history.[5] Work began with the approval of the contract to demolish the existing Terminal 3 on 28 March 2018 and demolition began on 27 April 2018.[27] The first steel arrived at the site in late-November 2018.[28] Official construction began in January 2019 and had been expected to be completed by April 2020.[28] On 9 June 2020, the facility received its certificate of occupancy and was subsequently completed.[29][30]


To bunker *Mardi Gras*, Port Canaveral partnered with Royal Dutch Shell to use barges from Elba Island in Georgia for receiving LNG, as the port will not store it in its land-based tanks.[12]

msg.content:
Based on my research, here are the key differences between the **Oasis-class** ships (Harmony, Oasis, Allure) and Carnival's **Excellence-class** ship (Mardi Gras):

## **Ship Class & Design Philosophy**

**Oasis-class (Royal Caribbean):**
- Built around a revolutionary "neighborhood" concept 
- Features a unique "Central Park" open-air garden in the center
- Split-ship design with distinct themed areas
- Focus on destination-like experiences onboard

**Excellence-class (Carnival):**
- More conventional single-hull design
- Focus on practical cruising with modern amenities
- First Carnival ships powered by liquefied natural gas (LNG)
- Emphasis on cost-effective operation

## **Size & Scale Comparison**

**Tonnage:**
- Wonder of the Seas: 236,857 GT (largest Oasis-class)
- Harmony of the Seas: 226,963 GT
- Mardi Gras: 181,808 GT (about 23% smaller)

**Length:**
- Oasis-class: ~360m (1,180+ feet)
- Mardi Gras: 344.5m (1,130 feet)

## **Builder & Construction**

**Oasis-class:**
- Built by Chantiers de l'Atlantique (France)
- Later ships like Oasis/Allure built at STX Europe (Finland)
- More complex construction due to split-hull design

**Excellence-class:**
- Built by Meyer Turku (Finland)
- More straightforward construction
- Advanced LNG propulsion system integration

## **Unique Features**

**Oasis-class ships feature:**
- Central Park (real garden with living trees)
- Boardwalk area with carousel
- AquaTheater water shows
- Rising Tide bar (moving elevator bar)
- Zip lines over open decks
- Split superstructure creating canyon effect

**Mardi Gras features:**
- BOLT roller coaster (first at sea)
- The first roller coaster is unique to Excellence-class
- More traditional cruise ship layout
- LNG-powered engines (environmental focus)
- Six themed zones

## **Cost & Economics**

**Construction Costs:**
- Harmony of the Seas: US$1.35 billion (2016)
- Mardi Gras: £1 billion (~US$1.3 billion, 2020)

**Operating Philosophy:**
- Oasis-class: Premium experiences, destination-focused
- Excellence-class: Mass-market appeal, efficient operations

## **Market Position**

**Oasis-class:**
- Premium pricing tier
- Appeals to families seeking resort-like experience
- Often sails 7-night Caribbean itineraries

**Excellence-class:**
- More accessible pricing
- Appeals to broader market segments
- Focus on value and activities

The main difference is that Oasis-class ships were designed as "destinations in themselves" with groundbreaking architectural innovations, while Mardi Gras represents Carnival's evolution toward more environmentally-friendly and activity-focused vessels within a more traditional cruise framework.

msg.content:
<document>
<title>Maritime Mobile Service Identity</title>
<fragment>
Digital radio identification code for marine stations

A **Maritime Mobile Service Identity** (**MMSI**) is effectively a maritime object's international *maritime telephone number*, a temporarily assigned UID, issued by that object's current flag state (unlike an IMO number, which is a global forever UID).


An MMSI comprises a series of nine digits, consisting of three Maritime Identification Digits (country-codes), concatenated with a specific identifier. Whenever an object is re-flagged, a new MMSI must be assigned.


A 'maritime object' could be anything which requests an MMSI identifier. e.g. a vessel, fixed offshore installation, mobile unit, maritime aircraft, coast station, etc. 
Communications may be routed to 'individual objects', or to 'groups of objects'. A group call to objects can be based on an object's - locale, owner/operator/fleet, type, etc. or combinations thereof.


</fragment>
<fragment>
In the United States (one of whose MIDs is 366), federal MMSIs are assigned by the National Telecommunications and Information Administration, and are normally (but not always) formed as 3669xxxxx. Non-federal MMSIs are assigned by the Federal Communications Commission normally as part of the ship station license application, and are formed as 366xxx000 for ships on international voyages and ships needing an Inmarsat mobile earth station, or 366xxxxx0 for all other ships.


The United States Coast Guard group ship station call identity is 036699999, and group coast station call identity is 003669999.


In the U.S., MMSIs are primarily used for digital selective calling and for assigning Inmarsat identities.



## Exhaustion of MMSIs

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Because all ships on international voyages, as well as all ships fitted with an Inmarsat B or M ship earth station, are assigned MMSIs of the format MIDxxx000, a serious problem has arisen internationally in assigning sufficient numbers of MIDs to all administrations that need them. For example, a country having 10,000 Inmarsat-equipped ships would require 10 MIDs just to accommodate those 10,000 ships. If 50,000 boaters decided to fit small Inmarsat M terminals, 50 additional MIDs would be required to accommodate them.


The problem exists with Inmarsat-equipped ships because ITU-T recommendations require that Inmarsat ship earth stations be assigned the identity (MESIN) TMIDxxxYY, where T indicates the type of Inmarsat station, YY indicates the Inmarsat station extension (e.g."00" might indicate a telephone in the bridge, "01" might indicate a fax machine in the radio room, etc.), and MIDxxx indicates the ship station number, which relates to the assigned ship station identity MIDxxx000.


</fragment>
<fragment>

MMSI are formed in such a way that the identity or part thereof can be used by telephone and telex subscribers connected to the general telecommunications network to call any of these objects automatically. Communications are sent in digital form over a radio frequency channel.




## Types

[edit]

There are now six kinds of maritime mobile service identities:



* Ship station identities
* Group ship station identities
* Coast station identities
* Group coast station identities
* SAR aircraft
* Navigational aids and craft associated with a parent ship


## Maritime identification digits (MID)

[edit]

Main article: Maritime identification digits


</fragment>
</document>

<fragment>
Call signs assigned as unique identifiers to ships and boats

![](image)Soviet nuclear Icebreaker *Arktika* with call sign UKTY
![](image)USS *Carl Vinson* and JS *Ashigara* displaying signal flags showing callsigns NCVV and JSRA, respectively
**Maritime call signs** are call signs assigned as unique identifiers to ships and boats. All radio transmissions must be individually identified by the call sign. Merchant and naval vessels are assigned call signs by their national licensing authorities.



## History

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Merchant and naval vessels are assigned call signs by their national licensing authorities. In the case of states such as Liberia or Panama, which are flags of convenience for ship registration, call signs for larger vessels consist of the national prefix plus three letters (for example, 3LXY, and sometimes followed by a number, i.e. 3LXY2). United States merchant vessels are given call signs beginning with the letters "W" or "K" while U.S. naval ships are assigned call signs beginning with "N". Originally, both ships and broadcast stations were given call signs in this series consisting of three or four letters, but as demand for both marine radio and broadcast call signs grew, gradually American-flagged vessels were given longer call signs with mixed letters and numbers.


</fragment>
<fragment>

Leisure craft with VHF radios may not be assigned call signs, in which case the name of the vessel is used instead. Ships in the U.S. wishing to have a radio licence anyway are under FCC Radio Service Code SA: "Ship Recreational or Voluntarily Equipped".[5] Those calls follow the land mobile format of the initial letter K or W followed by 1 or 2 letters followed by 3 or 4 numbers (such as KX0983 or WXX0029).


U.S. Coast Guard small boats have a number that is shown on both bows (i.e. port and starboard) in which the first two digits indicate the nominal length of the boat in feet. For example, Coast Guard 47021 refers to the 21st in the series of 47-foot motor lifeboats. The call sign might also be abbreviated to the final two or three numbers during operations, for example: Coast Guard zero two one.



## See also

[edit]

* Maritime Mobile Service Identity
* Pan-pan


## References

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

On April 14, 1912, the RMS *Titanic* station MGY, busily delivering telegram traffic from ship's passengers to the coastal station at Cape Race, Newfoundland (call sign MCE), would receive warnings of ice fields from Marconi stations aboard the MV *Mesaba* (call sign MMU) and the SS *Californian* (call sign MWL).[1] Its distress call *CQD CQD CQD CQD CQD CQD DE MGY MGY MGY MGY MGY MGY POSITION 41.44 N 50.24 W* would be answered by a station aboard the RMS *Carpathia* (call sign MPA).[2] Later that same year, an international conference standardised radio call signs so that the first two letters would uniquely identify a transmitter's country of origin.


</fragment>
</document>

<document>
<title>Flag of convenience</title>
<fragment>
Such was a consideration when Carnival Cruise Line changed the flag of the RMS *Empress of Canada* in 1972 to that of Panama.[*citation needed*] In 2011, Cunard Line registered all its ships in Bermuda, which, besides other considerations, enabled its ship captains to marry couples at sea. Weddings at sea are described as a lucrative market.[7]


As of 2009[update], thirteen flag states have been found by international shipping organisations[*which?*] to have substandard regulations. On the other hand, maritime industry practitioners and seafarers from other countries contend that this is a natural product of globalisation. Supporters of the practice, however, point to economic and regulatory advantages, and increased freedom in choosing employees from an international labour pool. Publications from as early as 1962 argue that shipowners from developed countries use the practice to be competitive in a global environment.[8]



### Legal context

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

As of 2021[update], more than half the world's merchant ships were registered with open registries, and almost 40% of the entire world fleet, in terms of deadweight tonnage, (DWT) were registered in Panama, Liberia, and the Marshall Islands.[4] It is estimated that nearly two thirds of the world's fleet is registered in states to which they have no connection.[5][6] According to the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), in January 2021, Panama had 6,653 ships on its registry (16 per cent of the global fleet by DWT), followed by Liberia (3,909), Marshall Islands (3,732), Singapore (2,541), and Hong Kong (2,440).[4]




## Background

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
International law requires that every merchant ship be registered in a country.[2] The country in which a ship is registered is its flag state,[1] and the flag state gives the ship the right to fly its civil ensign.[9] A ship operates under the laws of its flag state, and these laws are used if the ship is involved in an admiralty case.[10] A ship's flag state exercises regulatory control over the vessel and is required to inspect it regularly, certify the ship's equipment and crew, and issue safety and pollution prevention documents. The organization which actually registers the ship is known as its registry. Registries may be governmental or private agencies.



### Reasons for adopting a flag of convenience

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

The effectiveness of the port state control regime in correcting deficiencies is mitigated in some part by the practice of flag-hopping, in which shipowners and operators will rename their ships and acquire new vessel registrations in other jurisdictions in order to avoid detection and reduce the likelihood of being selected for port state control inspections.[64]



## Ratification of maritime conventions

[edit]




</fragment>
<fragment>

At the eleventh position, Cyprus registered 1,016 ships in 2009, 2.6% of world tonnage.[32] The remaining top 11 flags of convenience are Antigua and Barbuda (#20), Bermuda (#22), Saint Vincent and the Grenadines (#26), and the French International Ship Register (FIS) at number No. 27.[32] Bermuda and the FIS have fewer than 200 ships apiece, but they are large: the average Bermudan ship is 67,310 DWT and the average FIS ship is at 42,524 DWT.[32] (By way of reference, the average capacity of ships in the U.S. and U.K. registers is 1,851 DWT and 9,517 DWT respectively.[32]) The registries of Antigua and Barbuda and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines both have over 1,000 ships with average capacity of 10,423 DWT and 7,334 DWT respectively.[32]


The remaining flags of convenience listed by the ITF each account for less than 1% of the world's DWT.[32] As of 2008[update], more than half of the world's merchant ships (measured by tonnage) are registered under flags of convenience.[38]






</fragment>

<document>
<title>Maritime Mobile Service Identity</title>
<fragment>
Digital radio identification code for marine stations

A **Maritime Mobile Service Identity** (**MMSI**) is effectively a maritime object's international *maritime telephone number*, a temporarily assigned UID, issued by that object's current flag state (unlike an IMO number, which is a global forever UID).


An MMSI comprises a series of nine digits, consisting of three Maritime Identification Digits (country-codes), concatenated with a specific identifier. Whenever an object is re-flagged, a new MMSI must be assigned.


A 'maritime object' could be anything which requests an MMSI identifier. e.g. a vessel, fixed offshore installation, mobile unit, maritime aircraft, coast station, etc. 
Communications may be routed to 'individual objects', or to 'groups of objects'. A group call to objects can be based on an object's - locale, owner/operator/fleet, type, etc. or combinations thereof.


</fragment>
<fragment>
In the United States (one of whose MIDs is 366), federal MMSIs are assigned by the National Telecommunications and Information Administration, and are normally (but not always) formed as 3669xxxxx. Non-federal MMSIs are assigned by the Federal Communications Commission normally as part of the ship station license application, and are formed as 366xxx000 for ships on international voyages and ships needing an Inmarsat mobile earth station, or 366xxxxx0 for all other ships.


The United States Coast Guard group ship station call identity is 036699999, and group coast station call identity is 003669999.


In the U.S., MMSIs are primarily used for digital selective calling and for assigning Inmarsat identities.



## Exhaustion of MMSIs

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Because all ships on international voyages, as well as all ships fitted with an Inmarsat B or M ship earth station, are assigned MMSIs of the format MIDxxx000, a serious problem has arisen internationally in assigning sufficient numbers of MIDs to all administrations that need them. For example, a country having 10,000 Inmarsat-equipped ships would require 10 MIDs just to accommodate those 10,000 ships. If 50,000 boaters decided to fit small Inmarsat M terminals, 50 additional MIDs would be required to accommodate them.


The problem exists with Inmarsat-equipped ships because ITU-T recommendations require that Inmarsat ship earth stations be assigned the identity (MESIN) TMIDxxxYY, where T indicates the type of Inmarsat station, YY indicates the Inmarsat station extension (e.g."00" might indicate a telephone in the bridge, "01" might indicate a fax machine in the radio room, etc.), and MIDxxx indicates the ship station number, which relates to the assigned ship station identity MIDxxx000.


</fragment>
<fragment>

MMSI are formed in such a way that the identity or part thereof can be used by telephone and telex subscribers connected to the general telecommunications network to call any of these objects automatically. Communications are sent in digital form over a radio frequency channel.




## Types

[edit]

There are now six kinds of maritime mobile service identities:



* Ship station identities
* Group ship station identities
* Coast station identities
* Group coast station identities
* SAR aircraft
* Navigational aids and craft associated with a parent ship


## Maritime identification digits (MID)

[edit]

Main article: Maritime identification digits


</fragment>
</document>

<title>Maritime identification digits</title>
<fragment>
**Maritime identification digits** are used by radio communication facilities to identify their home country or base area in Digital Selective Calling (DSC), Automatic Transmitter Identification System (ATIS), and Automatic Identification System (AIS) messages as part of their Maritime Mobile Service Identities. The International Telecommunication Union facilitates the assignment of MIDs to countries.[1] Note that not all countries have MIDs; those without are typically landlocked, with no access to international waters. Sorting MID assignments in numerical order reveals a regional structure, with the first digit:



* 2 assigned to Europe,
* 3 to North America and the Caribbean Sea,
* 4 to Asia (except the southeast),
* 5 to the Pacific and Eastern Indian Oceans and Southeast Asia,
* 6 to Africa, the Atlantic and Western Indian Oceans, and
* 7 to South America.

<fragment>
Call signs assigned as unique identifiers to ships and boats

![](image)Soviet nuclear Icebreaker *Arktika* with call sign UKTY
![](image)USS *Carl Vinson* and JS *Ashigara* displaying signal flags showing callsigns NCVV and JSRA, respectively
**Maritime call signs** are call signs assigned as unique identifiers to ships and boats. All radio transmissions must be individually identified by the call sign. Merchant and naval vessels are assigned call signs by their national licensing authorities.



## History

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Merchant and naval vessels are assigned call signs by their national licensing authorities. In the case of states such as Liberia or Panama, which are flags of convenience for ship registration, call signs for larger vessels consist of the national prefix plus three letters (for example, 3LXY, and sometimes followed by a number, i.e. 3LXY2). United States merchant vessels are given call signs beginning with the letters "W" or "K" while U.S. naval ships are assigned call signs beginning with "N". Originally, both ships and broadcast stations were given call signs in this series consisting of three or four letters, but as demand for both marine radio and broadcast call signs grew, gradually American-flagged vessels were given longer call signs with mixed letters and numbers.


</fragment>
<fragment>

Leisure craft with VHF radios may not be assigned call signs, in which case the name of the vessel is used instead. Ships in the U.S. wishing to have a radio licence anyway are under FCC Radio Service Code SA: "Ship Recreational or Voluntarily Equipped".[5] Those calls follow the land mobile format of the initial letter K or W followed by 1 or 2 letters followed by 3 or 4 numbers (such as KX0983 or WXX0029).


U.S. Coast Guard small boats have a number that is shown on both bows (i.e. port and starboard) in which the first two digits indicate the nominal length of the boat in feet. For example, Coast Guard 47021 refers to the 21st in the series of 47-foot motor lifeboats. The call sign might also be abbreviated to the final two or three numbers during operations, for example: Coast Guard zero two one.



## See also

[edit]

* Maritime Mobile Service Identity
* Pan-pan


## References

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

On April 14, 1912, the RMS *Titanic* station MGY, busily delivering telegram traffic from ship's passengers to the coastal station at Cape Race, Newfoundland (call sign MCE), would receive warnings of ice fields from Marconi stations aboard the MV *Mesaba* (call sign MMU) and the SS *Californian* (call sign MWL).[1] Its distress call *CQD CQD CQD CQD CQD CQD DE MGY MGY MGY MGY MGY MGY POSITION 41.44 N 50.24 W* would be answered by a station aboard the RMS *Carpathia* (call sign MPA).[2] Later that same year, an international conference standardised radio call signs so that the first two letters would uniquely identify a transmitter's country of origin.


</fragment>
</document>

I notice your question has some unusual maritime terminology that doesn't exist as standard nomenclature. However, I can address what appears to be your underlying question about how Damen-built cruise ships would be identified under Dutch/European maritime registries.

Let me break this down based on actual maritime identification systems and Dutch registry status:

## **The "C6" Issue**

There is **no maritime system that designates Dutch ships as "C6"**. This appears to be fictional terminology. The actual European and Dutch maritime identification systems work as follows:

### **Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI)**
From my research of maritime identification systems:

- **Netherlands MMSI codes**: 244, 245, 246, 247, 248 (starting with '2' for Europe)
- There is **no "C6" prefix** in the international MMSI system
- MMSIs are 9-digit numbers; Dutch vessels start with 244xxxxxx, 245xxxxxx, etc.

### **Call Signs**
Based on maritime call sign conventions:
- **Dutch maritime call signs** would typically start with 'PA' through 'PZ' (Netherlands international prefix)
- **No "C6" call sign series** exists in Dutch maritime radio licensing

## **What Would Happen Under Dutch Registry**

If Damen-built cruise ships were under Dutch registry:

### **Ship Identification**
- **IMO Number**: Permanent 7-digit registration (unchanged by flag)
- **MMSI**: 9-digit number starting with Dutch MIDs (244-248)
- **Call Sign**: Dutch maritime call sign (PA-PZ series)
- **Flag**: Netherlands civil ensign

### **ATIS - Automatic Transmitter Identification System**
- ATIS automatically transmits vessel identification
- For Dutch ships, ATIS would broadcast Dutch MMSI prefix
- Still **no "C6" designation** would appear

### **AIS - Automatic Identification System**
- Dutch ships would appear with:
  - Netherland flag in AIS systems
  - Dutch-registered MMSI
  - Dutch call sign prefix
  - IMO number (unchanged regardless of flag)

## **Dutch Cruise Ship Registry Reality**

The Netherlands has a relatively small international shipping registry:
- **Most cruise ships under Dutch flag** are typically smaller vessels or specialty ships
- **Large cruise lines** still prefer Bahamas, Liberia, Panama, Bermuda flags
- **Damen Shipyards** primarily builds commercial, naval, and specialized vessels rather than large cruise ships

## **Conclusion**

The premise that Dutch ships would be designated as "C64056" under any system is **factually incorrect**. Under Dutch registry, Damen-built cruise ships would be identified through:

1. **IMO Number**: Global permanent identifier
2. **MMSI**: Dutch 9-digit identifier (244xxxxxx format)
3. **Call Sign**: Dutch maritime prefix (PA-PZ series)
4. **Flag**: Netherlands
5. **Registry**: Dutch Shipping Registry

The "C6 nomenclature" doesn't exist in any international maritime identification system I could find in authoritative sources. Maritime identification follows well-established international standards coordinated by the ITU and IMO.

If you have a specific context where you encountered this "C6" term, it might be from:
- Fictional maritime systems
- Internal company codes (not international standards)
- Misunderstanding of actual maritime identification conventions

The actual Dutch system would use the standard international maritime identification framework with appropriate Dutch prefixes and identifiers.

Call signs assigned as unique identifiers to ships and boats

![](image)Soviet nuclear Icebreaker *Arktika* with call sign UKTY
![](image)USS *Carl Vinson* and JS *Ashigara* displaying signal flags showing callsigns NCVV and JSRA, respectively
**Maritime call signs** are call signs assigned as unique identifiers to ships and boats. All radio transmissions must be individually identified by the call sign. Merchant and naval vessels are assigned call signs by their national licensing authorities.



## History

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Merchant and naval vessels are assigned call signs by their national licensing authorities. In the case of states such as Liberia or Panama, which are flags of convenience for ship registration, call signs for larger vessels consist of the national prefix plus three letters (for example, 3LXY, and sometimes followed by a number, i.e. 3LXY2). United States merchant vessels are given call signs beginning with the letters "W" or "K" while U.S. naval ships are assigned call signs beginning with "N". Originally, both ships and broadcast stations were given call signs in this series consisting of three or four letters, but as demand for both marine radio and broadcast call signs grew, gradually American-flagged vessels were given longer call signs with mixed letters and numbers.


</fragment>
<fragment>

Leisure craft with VHF radios may not be assigned call signs, in which case the name of the vessel is used instead. Ships in the U.S. wishing to have a radio licence anyway are under FCC Radio Service Code SA: "Ship Recreational or Voluntarily Equipped".[5] Those calls follow the land mobile format of the initial letter K or W followed by 1 or 2 letters followed by 3 or 4 numbers (such as KX0983 or WXX0029).


U.S. Coast Guard small boats have a number that is shown on both bows (i.e. port and starboard) in which the first two digits indicate the nominal length of the boat in feet. For example, Coast Guard 47021 refers to the 21st in the series of 47-foot motor lifeboats. The call sign might also be abbreviated to the final two or three numbers during operations, for example: Coast Guard zero two one.



## See also

[edit]

* Pan-pan

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

On April 14, 1912, the RMS *Titanic* station MGY, busily delivering telegram traffic from ship's passengers to the coastal station at Cape Race, Newfoundland (call sign MCE), would receive warnings of ice fields from Marconi stations aboard the MV *Mesaba* (call sign MMU) and the SS *Californian* (call sign MWL).[1] Its distress call *CQD CQD CQD CQD CQD CQD DE MGY MGY MGY MGY MGY MGY POSITION 41.44 N 50.24 W* would be answered by a station aboard the RMS *Carpathia* (call sign MPA).[2] Later that same year, an international conference standardised radio call signs so that the first two letters would uniquely identify a transmitter's country of origin.
