Call signs assigned as unique identifiers to ships and boats

![](image)Soviet nuclear Icebreaker *Arktika* with call sign UKTY
![](image)USS *Carl Vinson* and JS *Ashigara* displaying signal flags showing callsigns NCVV and JSRA, respectively
**Maritime call signs** are call signs assigned as unique identifiers to ships and boats. All radio transmissions must be individually identified by the call sign. Merchant and naval vessels are assigned call signs by their national licensing authorities.



## History

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Merchant and naval vessels are assigned call signs by their national licensing authorities. In the case of states such as Liberia or Panama, which are flags of convenience for ship registration, call signs for larger vessels consist of the national prefix plus three letters (for example, 3LXY, and sometimes followed by a number, i.e. 3LXY2). United States merchant vessels are given call signs beginning with the letters "W" or "K" while U.S. naval ships are assigned call signs beginning with "N". Originally, both ships and broadcast stations were given call signs in this series consisting of three or four letters, but as demand for both marine radio and broadcast call signs grew, gradually American-flagged vessels were given longer call signs with mixed letters and numbers.


</fragment>
<fragment>

Leisure craft with VHF radios may not be assigned call signs, in which case the name of the vessel is used instead. Ships in the U.S. wishing to have a radio licence anyway are under FCC Radio Service Code SA: "Ship Recreational or Voluntarily Equipped".[5] Those calls follow the land mobile format of the initial letter K or W followed by 1 or 2 letters followed by 3 or 4 numbers (such as KX0983 or WXX0029).


U.S. Coast Guard small boats have a number that is shown on both bows (i.e. port and starboard) in which the first two digits indicate the nominal length of the boat in feet. For example, Coast Guard 47021 refers to the 21st in the series of 47-foot motor lifeboats. The call sign might also be abbreviated to the final two or three numbers during operations, for example: Coast Guard zero two one.



## See also

[edit]

* Maritime Mobile Service Identity
* Pan-pan


## References

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

On April 14, 1912, the RMS *Titanic* station MGY, busily delivering telegram traffic from ship's passengers to the coastal station at Cape Race, Newfoundland (call sign MCE), would receive warnings of ice fields from Marconi stations aboard the MV *Mesaba* (call sign MMU) and the SS *Californian* (call sign MWL).[1] Its distress call *CQD CQD CQD CQD CQD CQD DE MGY MGY MGY MGY MGY MGY POSITION 41.44 N 50.24 W* would be answered by a station aboard the RMS *Carpathia* (call sign MPA).[2] Later that same year, an international conference standardised radio call signs so that the first two letters would uniquely identify a transmitter's country of origin.


</fragment>

<fragment>

***Wonder of the Seas*** is the flagship of Royal Caribbean International. She was completed in 2022 in the Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard in Saint-Nazaire, France,[5] the fifth in Royal Caribbean's *Oasis* class of cruise ships.[6] At 236,857 GT, she was the largest cruise ship in the world by gross tonnage, surpassed by the succeeding ship, *Icon of the Seas*, also owned by Royal Caribbean International.




## Description and design

[edit]

*Wonder of the Seas* measures 1,188 feet (362 m) in length and has a gross tonnage of 236,857 across 18 decks. This ship accommodates 5,734 passengers at double occupancy or up to a maximum of 6,988 passengers, as well as a 2,300 crew. There are 16 decks for guest use, 20 restaurants, four pools and 2,867 cabins.[4]

***Oasis of the Seas*** is a cruise ship operated by Royal Caribbean International. She is the first of her class, the Oasis class, whose ships were the largest passenger ships in the world, being surpassed in 2023 by the Icon-class. Her hull was laid down in November 2007 and she was completed and delivered to Royal Caribbean in October 2009. At the time of construction, *Oasis of the Seas* set a new capacity record of carrying over 6,000 passengers.[9] The first of her class, she was joined by sister ships *Allure of the Seas* in December 2010, *Harmony of the Seas* in May 2016, *Symphony of the Seas* in April 2018, and *Wonder of the Seas* in March 2022, as well as *Utopia of the Seas* in November 2024. *Oasis of the Seas* conducts cruises of the Caribbean from her home port of PortMiami in Miami, Florida.

<fragment>

***Wonder of the Seas*** is the flagship of Royal Caribbean International. She was completed in 2022 in the Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard in Saint-Nazaire, France,[5] the fifth in Royal Caribbean's *Oasis* class of cruise ships.[6] At 236,857 GT, she was the largest cruise ship in the world by gross tonnage, surpassed by the succeeding ship, *Icon of the Seas*, also owned by Royal Caribbean International.




## Description and design

[edit]

*Wonder of the Seas* measures 1,188 feet (362 m) in length and has a gross tonnage of 236,857 across 18 decks. This ship accommodates 5,734 passengers at double occupancy or up to a maximum of 6,988 passengers, as well as a 2,300 crew. There are 16 decks for guest use, 20 restaurants, four pools and 2,867 cabins.[4]

- **Wonder of the Seas**: The largest of the Oasis class at 362 meters (1,188 ft) long with capacity for up to 6,988 passengers plus 2,300 crew

The cruise ship industry has seen tremendous growth in ship sizes over the past 15 years, with Royal Caribbean International leading the way in building progressively larger vessels. The Icon class represents the next evolution beyond the Oasis class, introducing new propulsion technologies and design concepts.

msg.content:
<document>
<title>Maritime call sign</title>
<fragment>

Merchant and naval vessels are assigned call signs by their national licensing authorities. In the case of states such as Liberia or Panama, which are flags of convenience for ship registration, call signs for larger vessels consist of the national prefix plus three letters (for example, 3LXY, and sometimes followed by a number, i.e. 3LXY2). United States merchant vessels are given call signs beginning with the letters "W" or "K" while U.S. naval ships are assigned call signs beginning with "N". Originally, both ships and broadcast stations were given call signs in this series consisting of three or four letters, but as demand for both marine radio and broadcast call signs grew, gradually American-flagged vessels were given longer call signs with mixed letters and numbers.


</fragment>
<fragment>
Call signs assigned as unique identifiers to ships and boats

![](image)Soviet nuclear Icebreaker *Arktika* with call sign UKTY
![](image)USS *Carl Vinson* and JS *Ashigara* displaying signal flags showing callsigns NCVV and JSRA, respectively
**Maritime call signs** are call signs assigned as unique identifiers to ships and boats. All radio transmissions must be individually identified by the call sign. Merchant and naval vessels are assigned call signs by their national licensing authorities.



## History

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Leisure craft with VHF radios may not be assigned call signs, in which case the name of the vessel is used instead. Ships in the U.S. wishing to have a radio licence anyway are under FCC Radio Service Code SA: "Ship Recreational or Voluntarily Equipped".[5] Those calls follow the land mobile format of the initial letter K or W followed by 1 or 2 letters followed by 3 or 4 numbers (such as KX0983 or WXX0029).


U.S. Coast Guard small boats have a number that is shown on both bows (i.e. port and starboard) in which the first two digits indicate the nominal length of the boat in feet. For example, Coast Guard 47021 refers to the 21st in the series of 47-foot motor lifeboats. The call sign might also be abbreviated to the final two or three numbers during operations, for example: Coast Guard zero two one.



## See also

[edit]

* Maritime Mobile Service Identity
* Pan-pan


## References

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
1. **^** "Titanic FAQs, Page 2: Signals". *Marconigraph.com*. 2002. Archived from the original on March 21, 2009.
2. **^** "The RMS Titanic Radio Page". *HF.ro*. 2012. Archived from the original on December 17, 2016.
3. **^** Fenwick, William (July 1928). "Broadcast Station Calls With a Past". *Radio Broadcast*. Doubleday, Doran & Company, Inc.: 150.
4. **^** "US NODC Codes for worldwide ships sorted by ship name". *International Research Vessel Schedules & Information*. Oceanic Information Center. Retrieved December 29, 2019.
5. **^** "Ship Radio Stations". Federal Communications Commission. October 9, 2019. Retrieved December 29, 2019.


</fragment>
<fragment>

On April 14, 1912, the RMS *Titanic* station MGY, busily delivering telegram traffic from ship's passengers to the coastal station at Cape Race, Newfoundland (call sign MCE), would receive warnings of ice fields from Marconi stations aboard the MV *Mesaba* (call sign MMU) and the SS *Californian* (call sign MWL).[1] Its distress call *CQD CQD CQD CQD CQD CQD DE MGY MGY MGY MGY MGY MGY POSITION 41.44 N 50.24 W* would be answered by a station aboard the RMS *Carpathia* (call sign MPA).[2] Later that same year, an international conference standardised radio call signs so that the first two letters would uniquely identify a transmitter's country of origin.


</fragment>
</document>

<document>
<title>Maritime Mobile Service Identity</title>
<fragment>
Digital radio identification code for marine stations

A **Maritime Mobile Service Identity** (**MMSI**) is effectively a maritime object's international *maritime telephone number*, a temporarily assigned UID, issued by that object's current flag state (unlike an IMO number, which is a global forever UID).


An MMSI comprises a series of nine digits, consisting of three Maritime Identification Digits (country-codes), concatenated with a specific identifier. Whenever an object is re-flagged, a new MMSI must be assigned.


A 'maritime object' could be anything which requests an MMSI identifier. e.g. a vessel, fixed offshore installation, mobile unit, maritime aircraft, coast station, etc. 
Communications may be routed to 'individual objects', or to 'groups of objects'. A group call to objects can be based on an object's - locale, owner/operator/fleet, type, etc. or combinations thereof.


</fragment>
<fragment>

MMSI are formed in such a way that the identity or part thereof can be used by telephone and telex subscribers connected to the general telecommunications network to call any of these objects automatically. Communications are sent in digital form over a radio frequency channel.




## Types

[edit]

There are now six kinds of maritime mobile service identities:



* Ship station identities
* Group ship station identities
* Coast station identities
* Group coast station identities
* SAR aircraft
* Navigational aids and craft associated with a parent ship


## Maritime identification digits (MID)

[edit]

Main article: Maritime identification digits


</fragment>
<fragment>
1. **^** "M.585 : Assignment and use of identities in the maritime mobile service". International Telecommunication Union.
2. ^ ***a*** ***b*** "Recommendation M.585-4 (03/07)". ITU. March 2007. First specified in this revision; carried forward in newer versions of the M.585 recommendation.
3. **^** "Recommendation ITU-R M.585-8 (10/2019): Assignment and use of identities in the maritime mobile service" (PDF). Geneva, Switzerland: ITU. October 2019.
4. **^** "Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI)". Australian Maritime Safety Authority.
5. **^** "Liaison Statement to CIRM: Identities for AIS-SART, MOB and EPIRB-AIS" (PDF). 2011-06-22. Retrieved 2014-03-30.
6. ^ ***a*** ***b*** "Maritime Mobile Service Identity". U.S. Coast Guard Navigation Center.

## External links

[edit]

* MARITIME MOBILE SERVICE IDENTITY (MMSI), USCG, which was adapted from Appendix 43 of the International Telecommunication Union Radio Regulations
* Table of MIDs from ITU

</fragment>
<fragment>
Because all ships on international voyages, as well as all ships fitted with an Inmarsat B or M ship earth station, are assigned MMSIs of the format MIDxxx000, a serious problem has arisen internationally in assigning sufficient numbers of MIDs to all administrations that need them. For example, a country having 10,000 Inmarsat-equipped ships would require 10 MIDs just to accommodate those 10,000 ships. If 50,000 boaters decided to fit small Inmarsat M terminals, 50 additional MIDs would be required to accommodate them.


The problem exists with Inmarsat-equipped ships because ITU-T recommendations require that Inmarsat ship earth stations be assigned the identity (MESIN) TMIDxxxYY, where T indicates the type of Inmarsat station, YY indicates the Inmarsat station extension (e.g."00" might indicate a telephone in the bridge, "01" might indicate a fax machine in the radio room, etc.), and MIDxxx indicates the ship station number, which relates to the assigned ship station identity MIDxxx000.


</fragment>

## Sources

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Ships must be registered in the ship register of the jurisdiction whose flag it is flying. Flag registers in many countries are open to ships with foreign owners. Normally, each flag state has only one ship register, but several countries have more than one register:



* Denmark, France, Norway and Portugal maintain an international register to compete with flags of convenience.
* The Kingdom of the Netherlands allows the different constituent countries to set up their own registers under the Dutch flag.
* Several territories over which the British Crown holds sovereignty have their own register. Most notably, the Isle of Man has a significant register.
* Hong Kong, the special administrative region of China, has a separate ship register, the fourth largest in the world,[3] in addition to China's own ship registry.


## Flag state enforcement

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
* In Australia, the Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA) provides flag state control.
* In Canada, Transport Canada is responsible for flag state control under the *Canada Shipping Act, 2001*.[5]
* In France, the Ships Safety Centers are in charge of Flag state control.
* In Hong Kong, the Marine Department[6] is responsible for flag state control and enforcement under the Flag State Quality Control Scheme.
* In India, the Directorate General of Shipping is responsible for life, health, vessel and the environment for Indian registered ships and ships at Indian ports.[7]
* In the United Kingdom, the Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) is responsible for flag state control.
* In the United States, the Coast Guard, under the authority of various federal laws, regulations and international conventions and treaties, the Officer in Charge Marine Inspections is responsible for the inspection of US flag vessels to ensure compliance operating throughout the world.

</fragment>
<fragment>
Until World War II nations were able to maintain their dominance, or in some cases, even improve their position in maritime trade by offering vessels exclusive protection for flying their flags, which would in turn give the nation exclusive control over the vessels. Shipowners during this time needed protection from pirates and privateers which was provided by naval vessels of the flag state. In some cases states offered subsidies to the shipbuilding industries. In addition to these incentives, states might impose restrictions based on flag state, closing ports to other ships. One well known example of how this was applied is the case of England, which restricted the import of Asian goods only to American and British vessels. England only opened its ports after it had maneuvered itself into a position of strength, and then most like only to gain access to other continental ports. Similarly, France imposed a trade monopoly on its colonies which remained in place until 1869.[2]



## Ship register

[edit]

<document>
<title>Ship registration</title>
<fragment>
References
1. ^ ***a*** ***b*** ***c*** ***d*** "A Guide to Ship Registration" (PDF). Maritime New Zealand. 2010-09-30. Archived from the original (PDF) on 2019-10-21. Retrieved 2012-12-12.
2. ^ ***a*** ***b*** ICFTU et al., 2002, p. 7.
3. **^** "U.S. Coast Guard Alternative Compliance Program". United States Coast Guard. Retrieved 2010-07-01.
4. **^** "Registration of merchant ships". The National Archives. Retrieved 2012-12-12.
5. **^** "USCG National Vessel Documentation Center, FAQ Page". Retrieved 2012-12-12.
6. **^** "Question Listing for Vessel Registration". LISCR. Archived from the original on 2013-09-06. Retrieved 2012-12-12.
7. **^** D'Andrea 2006, p.2.
8. ^ ***a*** ***b*** ***c*** ***d*** D'Andrea 2006, p.6.
9. **^** Neff, 2007.


</fragment>
<fragment>

A ship's flag state exercises regulatory control over the vessel and is required to inspect it regularly, certify the ship's equipment and crew, and issue safety and pollution prevention documents. The organization which actually registers the ship is known as its registry. Registries may be governmental or private agencies. In some cases, such as the United States' Alternative Compliance Program, the registry can assign a third party to administer inspections.[3]


A register that is open only to ships of its own nation is known as a *traditional* or *national register*. Registers that are open to foreign-owned ships are known as *open registries* and are sometimes called flags of convenience.




## History

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Ship registration has been done since business on the seas has been important. Originally meant to control ships carrying cargo in European seaborne countries,[1] it was used to make sure ships were being built in the local country, with crews predominantly of the local country.[4] Since then, ship registration has been used to document ships for ownership. Documentation provides definite evidence of nationality for international purposes and provides financing opportunities with the availability of preferred mortgages on documented vessels.[5]



## Requirements for registration

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In 1986, the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development attempted to solidify the genuine link concept in the United Nations Convention on Conditions for Registration of Ships.[8] The Convention on Conditions for Registration of Ships would require that a flag state be linked to its ships either by having an economic stake in the ownership of its ships or by providing mariners to crew the ships.[8] To come into force, the 1986 treaty requires 40 signatories whose combined tonnage exceeds 25% of the world total.[8] To date, only 14 countries have signed the treaty.[8]


National or closed registries typically require that a ship be owned by national interests, and at least partially crewed by its citizens. Open registries do not have such requirements; some offer on-line registration, and one guaranteed completion in less than a day.[9]



### Unflagged vessels

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
* "Question Listing for Vessel Registration (in Liberia)". LISCR, LLC. Archived from the original on 2013-09-06. Retrieved 2012-12-12.
* "Registration of merchant ships". The National Archives (UK). Retrieved 2012-12-12.
* "USCG National Vessel Documentation Center, FAQ Page". USCG National Vessel Documentation Center. Retrieved 2023-03-18.

</fragment>
<fragment>

Each registry has its own rules as to the types of vessels that it will accept for registration. The Liberian Registry, for example, registers seagoing vessels of more than 500 net tons that conduct foreign trade. Vessels over the age of 20 require a waiver as well as the vessel's classification society being willing to issue statutory certificates to the vessel. Vessels 15 years or older must have a Status Report of the vessel's Special Survey to be reviewed by Marine Safety.[6] Registries charge a registration fee.

<document>
<title>Flag of convenience</title>
<fragment>

As of 2021[update], more than half the world's merchant ships were registered with open registries, and almost 40% of the entire world fleet, in terms of deadweight tonnage, (DWT) were registered in Panama, Liberia, and the Marshall Islands.[4] It is estimated that nearly two thirds of the world's fleet is registered in states to which they have no connection.[5][6] According to the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), in January 2021, Panama had 6,653 ships on its registry (16 per cent of the global fleet by DWT), followed by Liberia (3,909), Marshall Islands (3,732), Singapore (2,541), and Hong Kong (2,440).[4]




## Background

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Each merchant ship is required by international law to be registered in a registry created by a country,[2] and a ship is subject to the laws of that country, which are used also if the ship is involved in a case under admiralty law. A ship's owners may elect to register a ship in a foreign country so as to avoid the regulations of the owners' country, which may, for example, have stricter safety standards. They may also select a jurisdiction to reduce operating costs, avoiding higher taxes in the owners' country and bypassing laws that protect the wages and working conditions of mariners.[3] The term "flag of convenience" has been used since the 1950s. A registry which does not have a nationality or residency requirement for ship registration is often described as an **open registry**. Panama, for example, offers advantages such as easier registration (often online), the ability to employ cheaper foreign labour, and an exemption on income taxes.


</fragment>
<fragment>
Such was a consideration when Carnival Cruise Line changed the flag of the RMS *Empress of Canada* in 1972 to that of Panama.[*citation needed*] In 2011, Cunard Line registered all its ships in Bermuda, which, besides other considerations, enabled its ship captains to marry couples at sea. Weddings at sea are described as a lucrative market.[7]


As of 2009[update], thirteen flag states have been found by international shipping organisations[*which?*] to have substandard regulations. On the other hand, maritime industry practitioners and seafarers from other countries contend that this is a natural product of globalisation. Supporters of the practice, however, point to economic and regulatory advantages, and increased freedom in choosing employees from an international labour pool. Publications from as early as 1962 argue that shipowners from developed countries use the practice to be competitive in a global environment.[8]



### Legal context

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

The modern practice of ships being registered in a foreign country began in the 1920s in the United States when shipowners seeking to serve alcohol to passengers during Prohibition registered their ships in Panama. Owners soon began to perceive advantages in terms of avoiding increased regulations and rising labor costs and continued to register their ships in Panama even after Prohibition ended. The use of open registries steadily increased, and in 1968, Liberia grew to surpass the United Kingdom with the world's largest ship register. 


</fragment>

Based on my research of Royal Caribbean's Oasis-class ships, I can provide you with detailed specifications for the Symphony of the Seas and its role as the former largest cruise ship.

## Symphony of the Seas Specifications

**Overview:**
- **Class:** Oasis-class cruise ship
- **Operator:** Royal Caribbean International
- **Status:** In active service since 2018

**Key Specifications:**
- **Gross Tonnage:** 228,081 GT
- **Net Tonnage:** 258,794 NT
- **Deadweight Tonnage:** 18,095 DWT
- **Length:** 361 meters (1,184 feet)
- **Beam:** 47 meters (154 feet) at waterline
- **Cost:** US$1.35 billion (construction cost in 2016)
- **Builder:** Chantiers de l'Atlantique, Saint-Nazaire, France
- **Homeport:** PortMiami
- **Maiden Voyage:** April 7, 2018

**Capacity & Guest Facilities:**
- Passenger capacity: 5,518 passengers (double occupancy)
- Crew capacity: 2,200 crew members
- Total capacity when full: Approximately 6,680 passengers
- Number of decks: 18 passenger decks
- Staterooms: 2,759 staterooms

## Context as Former World's Largest Cruise Ship

**Historical Significance:**
- Symphony of the Seas held the title of "world's largest cruise ship" from her launch in 2018 until 2021
- She was the fourth ship in the Oasis-class series
- Each subsequent ship in the class has been slightly larger than the previous one

**The Oasis-Class Evolution:**
1. **Oasis of the Seas** (2009) - 226,838 GT
2. **Allure of the Seas** (2010) - Similar size
3. **Harmony of the Seas** (2016) - 226,963 GT
4. **Symphony of the Seas** (2018) - 228,081 GT
5. **Wonder of the Seas** (2021) - Currently the largest at 236,857 GT

**Unique Features:**
- Central Park with real trees and plants
- Boardwalk amusement area with carousel
- AquaTheater water performance venue
- Ultimate Abyss slide (the tallest slide at sea)
- Pool and Sports Zone with FlowRider surf simulators
- Royal Promenade shopping and dining district

While Symphony of the Seas no longer holds the title of world's largest cruise ship (that distinction now belongs to Wonder of the Seas), she remains one of the most impressive and technically advanced cruise ships ever built, representing the pinnacle of modern cruise ship engineering and design.

<document>
<title>Maritime Mobile Service Identity</title>
<fragment>
In the United States (one of whose MIDs is 366), federal MMSIs are assigned by the National Telecommunications and Information Administration, and are normally (but not always) formed as 3669xxxxx. Non-federal MMSIs are assigned by the Federal Communications Commission normally as part of the ship station license application, and are formed as 366xxx000 for ships on international voyages and ships needing an Inmarsat mobile earth station, or 366xxxxx0 for all other ships.


The United States Coast Guard group ship station call identity is 036699999, and group coast station call identity is 003669999.


In the U.S., MMSIs are primarily used for digital selective calling and for assigning Inmarsat identities.



## Exhaustion of MMSIs

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Digital radio identification code for marine stations

A **Maritime Mobile Service Identity** (**MMSI**) is effectively a maritime object's international *maritime telephone number*, a temporarily assigned UID, issued by that object's current flag state (unlike an IMO number, which is a global forever UID).


An MMSI comprises a series of nine digits, consisting of three Maritime Identification Digits (country-codes), concatenated with a specific identifier. Whenever an object is re-flagged, a new MMSI must be assigned.


A 'maritime object' could be anything which requests an MMSI identifier. e.g. a vessel, fixed offshore installation, mobile unit, maritime aircraft, coast station, etc. 
Communications may be routed to 'individual objects', or to 'groups of objects'. A group call to objects can be based on an object's - locale, owner/operator/fleet, type, etc. or combinations thereof.


</fragment>
<fragment>
* 0 Ship group, coast station, or group of coast stations
* 1 For use by SAR aircraft (111MIDaxx)[note 1][2]
* 2-7 MMSI's used by individual ships, beginning with an MID:
	+ 2 Europe (e.g., Italy has MID 247; Denmark has MIDs 219 *and* 220)
	+ 3 North and Central America and Caribbean (e.g., Canada, 316; Greenland, 331; Panama, 351 through 357, plus 370 through 373; United States, 303(Alaska), 338(domestic), plus 366 through 369)
	+ 4 Asia (not the southeast) (e.g., PRC, 412, 413, and 414; Maldives, 455; Japan, 431)
	+ 5 Oceania (Australia, 503; New Zealand, 512), and Southeast Asia (Philippines, 548; Indonesia, 525)
	+ 6 Africa (Eritrea, 625)
	+ 7 South America (Peru, 760)
* 8 Handheld VHF transceiver with DSC and GNSS[3]
* 9 Devices using a free-form number identity:[2]
	+ Search and Rescue Transponders (970yyzzzz)[note 2][4][note 3][5]
	+ Man overboard DSC and/or AIS devices (972yyzzzz)[note 2]
	+ 406 MHz EPIRBs fitted with an AIS transmitter (974yyzzzz)[note 2]

</fragment>
<fragment>
Because all ships on international voyages, as well as all ships fitted with an Inmarsat B or M ship earth station, are assigned MMSIs of the format MIDxxx000, a serious problem has arisen internationally in assigning sufficient numbers of MIDs to all administrations that need them. For example, a country having 10,000 Inmarsat-equipped ships would require 10 MIDs just to accommodate those 10,000 ships. If 50,000 boaters decided to fit small Inmarsat M terminals, 50 additional MIDs would be required to accommodate them.


The problem exists with Inmarsat-equipped ships because ITU-T recommendations require that Inmarsat ship earth stations be assigned the identity (MESIN) TMIDxxxYY, where T indicates the type of Inmarsat station, YY indicates the Inmarsat station extension (e.g."00" might indicate a telephone in the bridge, "01" might indicate a fax machine in the radio room, etc.), and MIDxxx indicates the ship station number, which relates to the assigned ship station identity MIDxxx000.


</fragment>
</document>

msg.content:
No, MMSI numbers cannot be used to definitively track and identify the world's largest cruise ships as they change over time. Here's why:

## How MMSI Numbers Work

An MMSI (Maritime Mobile Service Identity) is essentially a maritime telephone number that:
- Contains 9 digits including 3 Maritime Identification Digits (MIDs) representing the flag state
- Is temporarily assigned by a ship's **current flag state**
- **Changes when a vessel is re-flagged** to a different country

## Key Limitations for Tracking

**Flag-State Changes**: Most large cruise ships frequently change their flag registration (typically to Bahamas, Panama, or other maritime registries for regulatory advantages). Each change requires a new MMSI assignment.

**No Permanent Identity**: Unlike IMO numbers (which are permanent global identifiers), MMSI numbers are not ship-specific and can be reassigned to different vessels after a flag change.

**Current Data Only**: MMSI only reflects a vessel's current flag state, not its complete history or construction timeline.

## Better Alternatives for Tracking

For tracking the world's largest cruise ships over time, these identifiers are more reliable:

1. **IMO Numbers**: Permanent global identifiers assigned at construction that never change throughout a vessel's life

2. **IMO9990001 hull numbers**: Unique construction identifiers

3. **Tonnage/Gross Tonnage measurements**: Physical size metrics that remain constant

## Example

The world's largest cruise ships include vessels from Royal Caribbean's Oasis class and Icon class:

- **Icon of the Seas** (2023) - current world's largest
- **Wonder of the Seas** (2022)
- **Symphony of the Seas** (2018)
- **Harmony of the Seas** (2016)
- **Allure of the Seas** (2010) and **Oasis of the Seas** (2009)

While you could look up their current MMSIs (which start with Bahamas' MID "311"), this wouldn't help track which vessel was largest at different points in time, especially since many of these ships have gone through flag re-registration, changing their MMSIs multiple times.

**In summary**: MMSI numbers are not suitable for historical tracking of ship rankings because they're not permanent identifiers and change with flag re-registration. Use IMO numbers and vessel specifications for reliable tracking over time.

An MMSI (Maritime Mobile Service Identity) is essentially a maritime telephone number that:
- Contains 9 digits including 3 Maritime Identification Digits (MIDs) representing the flag state
- Is temporarily assigned by a ship's **current flag state**
- **Changes when a vessel is re-flagged** to a different country

## Key Limitations for Tracking

**Flag-State Changes**: Most large cruise ships frequently change their flag registration (typically to Bahamas, Panama, or other maritime registries for regulatory advantages). Each change requires a new MMSI assignment.

**No Permanent Identity**: Unlike IMO numbers (which are permanent global identifiers), MMSI numbers are not ship-specific and can be reassigned to different vessels after a flag change.

**Current Data Only**: MMSI only reflects a vessel's current flag state, not its complete history or construction timeline.

## Better Alternatives for Tracking

For tracking the world's largest cruise ships over time, these identifiers are more reliable:

1. **IMO Numbers**: Permanent global identifiers assigned at construction that never change throughout a vessel's life

2. **IMO9990001 hull numbers**: Unique construction identifiers

3. **Tonnage/Gross Tonnage measurements**: Physical size metrics that remain constant

## Example

The world's largest cruise ships include vessels from Royal Caribbean's Oasis class and Icon class:

- **Icon of the Seas** (2023) - current world's largest
- **Wonder of the Seas** (2022)
- **Symphony of the Seas** (2018)
- **Harmony of the Seas** (2016)
- **Allure of the Seas** (2010) and **Oasis of the Seas** (2009)

While you could look up their current MMSIs (which start with Bahamas' MID "311"), this wouldn't help track which vessel was largest at different points in time, especially since many of these ships have gone through flag re-registration, changing their MMSIs multiple times.

**In summary**: MMSI numbers are not suitable for historical tracking of ship rankings because they're not permanent identifiers and change with flag re-registration. Use IMO numbers and vessel specifications for reliable tracking over time.

<document>
<title>Maritime Mobile Service Identity</title>
<fragment>
Digital radio identification code for marine stations

A **Maritime Mobile Service Identity** (**MMSI**) is effectively a maritime object's international *maritime telephone number*, a temporarily assigned UID, issued by that object's current flag state (unlike an IMO number, which is a global forever UID).


An MMSI comprises a series of nine digits, consisting of three Maritime Identification Digits (country-codes), concatenated with a specific identifier. Whenever an object is re-flagged, a new MMSI must be assigned.


A 'maritime object' could be anything which requests an MMSI identifier. e.g. a vessel, fixed offshore installation, mobile unit, maritime aircraft, coast station, etc. 
Communications may be routed to 'individual objects', or to 'groups of objects'. A group call to objects can be based on an object's - locale, owner/operator/fleet, type, etc. or combinations thereof.


</fragment>
<fragment>
1. **^** "M.585 : Assignment and use of identities in the maritime mobile service". International Telecommunication Union.
2. ^ ***a*** ***b*** "Recommendation M.585-4 (03/07)". ITU. March 2007. First specified in this revision; carried forward in newer versions of the M.585 recommendation.
3. **^** "Recommendation ITU-R M.585-8 (10/2019): Assignment and use of identities in the maritime mobile service" (PDF). Geneva, Switzerland: ITU. October 2019.
4. **^** "Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI)". Australian Maritime Safety Authority.
5. **^** "Liaison Statement to CIRM: Identities for AIS-SART, MOB and EPIRB-AIS" (PDF). 2011-06-22. Retrieved 2014-03-30.
6. ^ ***a*** ***b*** "Maritime Mobile Service Identity". U.S. Coast Guard Navigation Center.

## External links

[edit]

* MARITIME MOBILE SERVICE IDENTITY (MMSI), USCG, which was adapted from Appendix 43 of the International Telecommunication Union Radio Regulations
* Table of MIDs from ITU

</fragment>
<fragment>

MMSI are formed in such a way that the identity or part thereof can be used by telephone and telex subscribers connected to the general telecommunications network to call any of these objects automatically. Communications are sent in digital form over a radio frequency channel.




## Types

[edit]

There are now six kinds of maritime mobile service identities:



* Ship station identities
* Group ship station identities
* Coast station identities
* Group coast station identities
* SAR aircraft
* Navigational aids and craft associated with a parent ship


## Maritime identification digits (MID)

[edit]

Main article: Maritime identification digits


</fragment>
<fragment>
In the United States (one of whose MIDs is 366), federal MMSIs are assigned by the National Telecommunications and Information Administration, and are normally (but not always) formed as 3669xxxxx. Non-federal MMSIs are assigned by the Federal Communications Commission normally as part of the ship station license application, and are formed as 366xxx000 for ships on international voyages and ships needing an Inmarsat mobile earth station, or 366xxxxx0 for all other ships.


The United States Coast Guard group ship station call identity is 036699999, and group coast station call identity is 003669999.


In the U.S., MMSIs are primarily used for digital selective calling and for assigning Inmarsat identities.

The ITU was initially aimed at helping connect telegraphic networks between countries, with its mandate consistently broadening with the advent of new communications technologies; it adopted its current name in 1932 to reflect its expanded responsibilities over radio and the telephone.[3] On 15 November 1947, the ITU entered into an agreement with the newly created United Nations to become a specialized agency within the UN system, which formally entered into force on 1 January 1949.[4]


The ITU promotes the shared global use of the radio spectrum, facilitates international cooperation in assigning satellite orbits, assists in developing and coordinating worldwide technical standards, and works to improve telecommunication infrastructure in the developing world. It is also active in the areas of broadband Internet, wireless technologies, aeronautical and maritime navigation, radio astronomy, satellite-based meteorology, TV broadcasting, amateur radio, and next-generation networks.


</fragment>
<fragment>

Based in Geneva, Switzerland, the ITU's global membership includes 193 countries and around 900 businesses, academic institutions, and international and regional organizations.[5]



![](image)International Telecommunication Union (ITU) headquarters campus buildings
![](image)ITU HQ background Palais des Nations

## History

[edit]

The ITU is one of the oldest international organizations still in operation, second only to the Central Commission for Navigation on the Rhine, which predates it by fifty years.[6][7] It was preceded by the now defunct **International Telegraph Union** which drafted the earliest international standards and regulations governing international telegraph networks.[8] The development of the telegraph in the early 19th century changed the way people communicated on the local and international levels. Between 1849 and 1865, a series of bilateral and regional agreements among Western European states attempted to standardize international communications.[9]


</fragment>

<title>Maritime Mobile Service Identity</title>
<fragment>
1. **^** "M.585 : Assignment and use of identities in the maritime mobile service". International Telecommunication Union.
2. ^ ***a*** ***b*** "Recommendation M.585-4 (03/07)". ITU. March 2007. First specified in this revision; carried forward in newer versions of the M.585 recommendation.
3. **^** "Recommendation ITU-R M.585-8 (10/2019): Assignment and use of identities in the maritime mobile service" (PDF). Geneva, Switzerland: ITU. October 2019.
4. **^** "Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI)". Australian Maritime Safety Authority.
5. **^** "Liaison Statement to CIRM: Identities for AIS-SART, MOB and EPIRB-AIS" (PDF). 2011-06-22. Retrieved 2014-03-30.
6. ^ ***a*** ***b*** "Maritime Mobile Service Identity". U.S. Coast Guard Navigation Center.

## External links

[edit]

* MARITIME MOBILE SERVICE IDENTITY (MMSI), USCG, which was adapted from Appendix 43 of the International Telecommunication Union Radio Regulations
* Table of MIDs from ITU

</fragment>
<fragment>
Digital radio identification code for marine stations

A **Maritime Mobile Service Identity** (**MMSI**) is effectively a maritime object's international *maritime telephone number*, a temporarily assigned UID, issued by that object's current flag state (unlike an IMO number, which is a global forever UID).


An MMSI comprises a series of nine digits, consisting of three Maritime Identification Digits (country-codes), concatenated with a specific identifier. Whenever an object is re-flagged, a new MMSI must be assigned.


A 'maritime object' could be anything which requests an MMSI identifier. e.g. a vessel, fixed offshore installation, mobile unit, maritime aircraft, coast station, etc. 
Communications may be routed to 'individual objects', or to 'groups of objects'. A group call to objects can be based on an object's - locale, owner/operator/fleet, type, etc. or combinations thereof.


</fragment>
<fragment>

The World Radio Conference, Geneva, 1997 (WRC-97), adopted Resolution 344 concerning the exhaustion of the maritime mobile service identity resource. In view of improvements to public switched telephone networks, and new capabilities of the Inmarsat system other than Inmarsat B or M, previous restrictions should no longer be applicable. All nine digits of the MMSI can be used in such cases, and no longer need to end in trailing zeros.



## See also

[edit]

![](image)

Wikidata has the property: 
* ![](image) ***MMSI (P587)*** (see uses)

* Automatic Identification System uses MMSI codegroups for ship ID
* Global Maritime Distress Safety System
* Inmarsat and the International Mobile Satellite Organization (IMSO)
* Maritime call sign, not tied to MMSI but can contain MMSI after
* SOLAS Convention a global Maritime Safety Convention


## References

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Because all ships on international voyages, as well as all ships fitted with an Inmarsat B or M ship earth station, are assigned MMSIs of the format MIDxxx000, a serious problem has arisen internationally in assigning sufficient numbers of MIDs to all administrations that need them. For example, a country having 10,000 Inmarsat-equipped ships would require 10 MIDs just to accommodate those 10,000 ships. If 50,000 boaters decided to fit small Inmarsat M terminals, 50 additional MIDs would be required to accommodate them.


The problem exists with Inmarsat-equipped ships because ITU-T recommendations require that Inmarsat ship earth stations be assigned the identity (MESIN) TMIDxxxYY, where T indicates the type of Inmarsat station, YY indicates the Inmarsat station extension (e.g."00" might indicate a telephone in the bridge, "01" might indicate a fax machine in the radio room, etc.), and MIDxxx indicates the ship station number, which relates to the assigned ship station identity MIDxxx000.


</fragment>
</document>

Based on my search, I can provide you with information about the ITU maritime identification systems and how to access their databases. The ITU manages two key systems for maritime operations:

## Official ITU Website
**URL:** https://www.itu.int

## What Information It Contains

The ITU maintains two primary maritime identification systems:

### 1. Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) Database
- **9-digit codes** that serve as unique identifiers for maritime object
- Format: 3 Maritime Identification Digits (MID, representing country codes) + 6-digit specific identifier
- Includes: vessels, fixed offshore installations, mobile units, maritime aircraft, coast stations
- Used for GMDSS (Global Maritime Distress and Safety System) and AIS (Automatic Identification System)

### 2. Maritime Call Signs
- Traditional call signs used for ship-to-shore and ship-to-ship communications
- Governed by ITU Radio Regulations
- Assigned by national administrations under ITU guidelines

## How to Access Search Functionality

### Primary ITU Resources:
1. **ITU-R Recommendation M.585**: "Assignment and use of identities in the maritime mobile service"
   - Available at: https://www.itu.int/rec/R-REC-M.585/
   - Contains the official structure and assignment procedures

2. **Maritime Identification Digits (MID) Tables**:
   - Available through ITU publications and databases
   - Lists all country codes and their assignments

### Alternative Access Points:

**US Coast Guard Navigation Center:**
- URL: https://www.navcen.uscg.gov/?pageName=MMSI
- Provides MMSI search functionality and database access
- Adapted from ITU Appendix 43 of the Radio Regulations

**National Maritime Authorities:**
- Each country's maritime administration maintains its portion of the database
- Example: Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA), UK Maritime and Coastguard Agency, etc.

## Search Requirements and Tips

### For MMSI Search:
1. **Format**:Must be 9 digits total
2. **Country Identification**: First 3 digits represent the Maritime Identification Digits (MID)
3. **Verification**: Cross-check with both ITU and national maritime databases

### For Call Sign Search:
1. **International Format**: Typically follows country prefix + vessel identification
2. **Format Variations**: Different countries use different conventions
3. **Verification**: Check with flag state's maritime administration

### Important Search Tips:
- **Cross-reference**: Always verify MMSI and call signs through multiple sources
- **Flag State**: The flag state's maritime administration is the primary source of assignment
- **Regular Updates**: Maritime databases are frequently updated due to vessel changes
- **International Standards**: Follow ITU-R M.585 recommendations for proper format

### Recommended Verification Process:
1. Start with ITU's official publications through itu.int
2. Check USCG Navigation Center database as a secondary source
3. Verify with the vessel's flag state maritime administration
4. Confirm through AIS tracking services (like MarineTraffic) for active vessels

The ITU's system works as the global framework, but actual database access and search functionality is often provided through national maritime authorities or specialized maritime services that implement the ITU standards.

<document>
<title>Universal Licensing System</title>
<content>
In the United States, Universal Licensing System (ULS) is the FCC online search portal for wireless licensing and research. It mainly supports online licensing and public access to its database. The FCC is an independent agency of the U.S. government appointed with the duty of allocating permission to businesses and individuals, the domestic (non-federal) use of wireless technologies.


Since mid-2018, the FCC stated that ULS:



...simplifies the application and licensing processes and provides secure, world-wide access through the Internet. This results in reduced filing time and financial savings for both customers and the federal government. More than an electronic filing system, ULS is a powerful information tool that enables you to research applications, licenses, and antenna structures. It also keeps you informed with weekly public notices, FCC rulemakings, processing utilities, a telecommunications glossary, and much more. Plus ULS features a Geographic Information System (GIS), a digital mapping technology that identifies spectrum use in relation to geographical areas.[1]
## References

[edit]

1. **^** "FCC Universal Licensing System (ULS): About ULS". wireless.fcc.gov. Archived from the original on 7 May 2018. Retrieved 18 October 2018.

msg.content:
<document>
<title>Maritime call sign</title>
<fragment>

Leisure craft with VHF radios may not be assigned call signs, in which case the name of the vessel is used instead. Ships in the U.S. wishing to have a radio licence anyway are under FCC Radio Service Code SA: "Ship Recreational or Voluntarily Equipped".[5] Those calls follow the land mobile format of the initial letter K or W followed by 1 or 2 letters followed by 3 or 4 numbers (such as KX0983 or WXX0029).


U.S. Coast Guard small boats have a number that is shown on both bows (i.e. port and starboard) in which the first two digits indicate the nominal length of the boat in feet. For example, Coast Guard 47021 refers to the 21st in the series of 47-foot motor lifeboats. The call sign might also be abbreviated to the final two or three numbers during operations, for example: Coast Guard zero two one.



## See also

[edit]

* Maritime Mobile Service Identity
* Pan-pan


## References

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
1. **^** "Titanic FAQs, Page 2: Signals". *Marconigraph.com*. 2002. Archived from the original on March 21, 2009.
2. **^** "The RMS Titanic Radio Page". *HF.ro*. 2012. Archived from the original on December 17, 2016.
3. **^** Fenwick, William (July 1928). "Broadcast Station Calls With a Past". *Radio Broadcast*. Doubleday, Doran & Company, Inc.: 150.
4. **^** "US NODC Codes for worldwide ships sorted by ship name". *International Research Vessel Schedules & Information*. Oceanic Information Center. Retrieved December 29, 2019.
5. **^** "Ship Radio Stations". Federal Communications Commission. October 9, 2019. Retrieved December 29, 2019.


</fragment>
<fragment>

Merchant and naval vessels are assigned call signs by their national licensing authorities. In the case of states such as Liberia or Panama, which are flags of convenience for ship registration, call signs for larger vessels consist of the national prefix plus three letters (for example, 3LXY, and sometimes followed by a number, i.e. 3LXY2). United States merchant vessels are given call signs beginning with the letters "W" or "K" while U.S. naval ships are assigned call signs beginning with "N". Originally, both ships and broadcast stations were given call signs in this series consisting of three or four letters, but as demand for both marine radio and broadcast call signs grew, gradually American-flagged vessels were given longer call signs with mixed letters and numbers.


</fragment>
<fragment>

As broadcast stations became commonplace in the 1920s, some original three- and four-letter call signs were reassigned as the corresponding ships were removed from U.S. registry. The WSB call sign had been held by two ships (the SS *Francis H. Leggett*, shipwrecked off Oregon's coast on September 18, 1914, and later the *Firwood*, a ship destroyed by fire near Peru on December 18, 1919[3]) before being assigned to *The Atlanta Journal* for use by its Atlanta, Georgia, broadcast radio station in 1922. Similarly, WEZU, the international radio call sign of the ship SS *Lash Atlantico*, was assigned in 1997 to a broadcast station.[4] Additional call signs would be reassigned to coastal stations or moved from marine radio to terrestrial broadcast radio when ships were sold for registration to foreign nations, as the new owners would obtain new, local call signs for any existing shipboard radio stations.


</fragment>
</document>

<document>
<title>Ship station</title>
<content>
![](image) *Ship stations* (MMS) in the radio-room on board of the German research vessel *RV Polarstern*
A **ship station** (or **ship radio station**) is a radio station located on board a sea vessel. The ITU Radio Regulations define it as "A mobile station in the maritime mobile service located on board a vessel which is not permanently moored, other than a survival craft station."[1]


Each station is classified by the service in which it operates, permanently or temporarily. Ship station requirements may be established by law or international treaty. For instance large cargo ships traveling the open seas may be required to have long-distance communications equipment, whereas coastal ship may only need short range communications.[2] Operating such stations may require a license.[3]



## Bridge-to-bridge station

[edit]

In telecommunication, a bridge-to-bridge station is a station operating in the port operations service in which messages are restricted to navigational communications and which is capable of operation from the ship's navigational bridge or, in the case of a dredge, from its main control station, operating on a frequency or frequencies in the 156-162 MHz band. bridge-to-bridge operations are a part of the Federal Standard 1037C and the NTIA Manual of Regulations and Procedures for Federal Radio Frequency Management.

**Marine VHF radio** is a worldwide system of two way radio transceivers on ships and watercraft used for bidirectional voice communication from ship-to-ship, ship-to-shore (for example with harbormasters), and in certain circumstances ship-to-aircraft. It uses FM channels in the very high frequency (VHF) radio band in the frequency range between 156 and 174 MHz, inclusive, designated by the International Telecommunication Union as the *VHF maritime mobile band*. In some countries additional channels are used, such as[1] the L and F channels for leisure and fishing vessels in the Nordic countries (at 155.5–155.825 MHz). Based on my search through Wikipedia articles, I can provide you with information about the FCC's maritime radio service database and search interface:

## Official Website URL

The official website for FCC's licensing database is the **Universal Licensing System (ULS)**, which can be accessed through the FCC's wireless services website. While the specific deep-link URL wasn't found in the Wikipedia articles, the ULS is the FCC's primary database for all wireless licensing including maritime services.

## Description of Information Available

The **Universal Licensing System (ULS)** contains comprehensive information about maritime radio station licensing including:

- **Maritime radio station licenses** for all FCC-licensed vessels
- **Call signs** assigned to maritime stations
- **Ship radio station licensing information** 
- **Station parameters** including frequencies, power levels, and equipment details
- **License status** and renewal information
- **Licenseholder information** (owner/operator details)

From the "Maritime call sign" article, I found that U.S. ships wishing to have radio licenses fall under **FCC Radio Service Code SA: "Ship Recreational or Voluntarily Equipped"** with call signs following the format of K or W followed by letters and numbers (such as KX0983 or WXX0029).

## How to Access Search Functionality

To access maritime radio service station information through ULS:

1. Navigate to the FCC's Universal Licensing System (through the wireless.fcc.gov domain)
2. Use the **License Search** functionality in ULS
3. Filter by **Radio Service Code** - maritime services typically use:
   - **SA** for Ship Recreational or Voluntarily Equipped
   - **Maritime Mobile Service** codes for commercial vessels

## Search Requirements and Tips

- **Radio Service Codes**: Know the specific service codes for maritime operations (SA for recreational, other codes for different maritime services)
- **Call Sign Format**: Maritime call signs typically begin with K or W followed by letters and numbers
- **Station Type**: Search for "Ship Radio Station" or "Maritime Radio Service"
- **License Type**: Multiple license types exist for different maritime applications (recreational, commercial, government)

## Additional Notes

From the "Ship station" article, ship stations are defined as "radio stations located on board a sea vessel" and the FCC establishes requirements based on vessel type and operation area. Large cargo ships traveling open seas require different licensing than coastal vessels.

**Important**: While I found extensive information about the ULS system and maritime licensing concepts, the most current and direct access URLs should be obtained from the official FCC website at **fcc.gov** to ensure you're using the most up-to-date search interface and following current procedures for maritime operations verification.

For the most precise search interface and current URLs, I recommend visiting the FCC's official website directly, as web addresses and search interfaces can change over time for government databases.

Each registry has its own rules as to the types of vessels that it will accept for registration. The Liberian Registry, for example, registers seagoing vessels of more than 500 net tons that conduct foreign trade. Vessels over the age of 20 require a waiver as well as the vessel's classification society being willing to issue statutory certificates to the vessel. Vessels 15 years or older must have a Status Report of the vessel's Special Survey to be reviewed by Marine Safety.[6] Registries charge a registration fee.



## Link to flag state

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Process by which a ship is documented




</fragment>
<fragment>
Ship registration has been done since business on the seas has been important. Originally meant to control ships carrying cargo in European seaborne countries,[1] it was used to make sure ships were being built in the local country, with crews predominantly of the local country.[4] Since then, ship registration has been used to document ships for ownership. Documentation provides definite evidence of nationality for international purposes and provides financing opportunities with the availability of preferred mortgages on documented vessels.[5]



## Requirements for registration

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Vessels that operate internationally or cross international borders are required to be registered. Some jurisdictions also require vessels that only operate in territorial waters to register on their national register, and some forbid foreign-flagged vessels from trading between ports within the country (a practice known as cabotage). The country of registration is a ship's flag state and determines its nationality as well as which country's laws govern its operation and the behavior of its crew.[1]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In 1986, the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development attempted to solidify the genuine link concept in the United Nations Convention on Conditions for Registration of Ships.[8] The Convention on Conditions for Registration of Ships would require that a flag state be linked to its ships either by having an economic stake in the ownership of its ships or by providing mariners to crew the ships.[8] To come into force, the 1986 treaty requires 40 signatories whose combined tonnage exceeds 25% of the world total.[8] To date, only 14 countries have signed the treaty.[8]


National or closed registries typically require that a ship be owned by national interests, and at least partially crewed by its citizens. Open registries do not have such requirements; some offer on-line registration, and one guaranteed completion in less than a day.[9]

<document>
<title>MISLE</title>
<content>
![](image)Public incident data from 2001 to 2010 in south central Alaska over an OpenStreetMap base
The **Marine Information for Safety and Law Enforcement** (MISLE) is a database system managed and used by the United States Coast Guard (USCG). The MISLE is used to store data on marine accidental and deliberate pollution and other shipping and port accidents in US territorial waters. It accounts for vessels and other facilities, like port terminals and shipyards. The system has now been operational for a few years. It was introduced in December 2001 to replace the previous Marine Safety Information System (MSIS).[1]


The public may access portions of the data contained on the MISLE system through the **Port State Information eXchange** (PSIX). Originally, the PSIX system was designed to provide other countries with Port State Intervention data on foreign-flagged vessels. Currently, it contains information on over 650,000 U.S. and foreign flagged vessels (including those used for recreational purposes). The PSIX system contains vessel specific information derived from the United States Coast Guard's Marine Information Safety and Law Enforcement System (MISLE). The information contained in PSIX represents a weekly snapshot of Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) data on U.S. flag vessels, foreign vessels operating in U.S. waters, and Coast Guard contacts with those vessels. Information on unclosed cases or cases pending further action is considered privileged information and is precluded from the PSIX system.[2]



## References

## Official US Coast Guard Vessel Documentation Resources

### 1. **Marine Information for Safety and Law Enforcement (MISLE)**
The MISLE system is the Coast Guard's primary database for vessel information, containing:
- Data on marine accidental and deliberate pollution incidents
- Shipping and port accident records in US territorial waters
- Information on vessels, port terminals, and shipyards

The PSIX system provides public access to portions of the MISLE data:
- Contains information on over 650,000 U.S. and foreign-flagged vessels
- Includes recreational vessels
- Provides weekly snapshots of Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) data
- Information on U.S. flag vessels, foreign vessels operating in U.S. waters
- Coast Guard contacts with those vessels

**Important Note:** While I found information about these systems, the search didn't return the specific official website URLs you're looking for. However, I can give you guidance based on the information found:

- The **PSIX** system is likely what you'll use for public vessel documentation searches
- It's derived from the Coast Guard's MISLE database
- Information on unclosed cases or cases pending further action is considered privileged and not available to the public

1. **USCG Homeport Website** - This was mentioned in the Coast Guard article as an official resource

- Visit the official U.S. Coast Guard website (uscg.mil) and navigate to their vessel documentation or maritime safety sections

<document>
<title>Maritime Mobile Service Identity</title>
<fragment>
Digital radio identification code for marine stations

A **Maritime Mobile Service Identity** (**MMSI**) is effectively a maritime object's international *maritime telephone number*, a temporarily assigned UID, issued by that object's current flag state (unlike an IMO number, which is a global forever UID).


An MMSI comprises a series of nine digits, consisting of three Maritime Identification Digits (country-codes), concatenated with a specific identifier. Whenever an object is re-flagged, a new MMSI must be assigned.


A 'maritime object' could be anything which requests an MMSI identifier. e.g. a vessel, fixed offshore installation, mobile unit, maritime aircraft, coast station, etc. 
Communications may be routed to 'individual objects', or to 'groups of objects'. A group call to objects can be based on an object's - locale, owner/operator/fleet, type, etc. or combinations thereof.


</fragment>
<fragment>

MMSI are formed in such a way that the identity or part thereof can be used by telephone and telex subscribers connected to the general telecommunications network to call any of these objects automatically. Communications are sent in digital form over a radio frequency channel.




## Types

[edit]

There are now six kinds of maritime mobile service identities:



* Ship station identities
* Group ship station identities
* Coast station identities
* Group coast station identities
* SAR aircraft
* Navigational aids and craft associated with a parent ship


## Maritime identification digits (MID)

[edit]

Main article: Maritime identification digits


</fragment>
<fragment>
1. **^** "M.585 : Assignment and use of identities in the maritime mobile service". International Telecommunication Union.
2. ^ ***a*** ***b*** "Recommendation M.585-4 (03/07)". ITU. March 2007. First specified in this revision; carried forward in newer versions of the M.585 recommendation.
3. **^** "Recommendation ITU-R M.585-8 (10/2019): Assignment and use of identities in the maritime mobile service" (PDF). Geneva, Switzerland: ITU. October 2019.

5. **^** "Liaison Statement to CIRM: Identities for AIS-SART, MOB and EPIRB-AIS" (PDF). 2011-06-22. Retrieved 2014-03-30.
6. ^ ***a*** ***b*** "Maritime Mobile Service Identity". U.S. Coast Guard Navigation Center.

## External links

[edit]

* MARITIME MOBILE SERVICE IDENTITY (MMSI), USCG, which was adapted from Appendix 43 of the International Telecommunication Union Radio Regulations
* Table of MIDs from ITU

</fragment>
<fragment>

The World Radio Conference, Geneva, 1997 (WRC-97), adopted Resolution 344 concerning the exhaustion of the maritime mobile service identity resource. In view of improvements to public switched telephone networks, and new capabilities of the Inmarsat system other than Inmarsat B or M, previous restrictions should no longer be applicable. All nine digits of the MMSI can be used in such cases, and no longer need to end in trailing zeros.



## See also

[edit]

![](image)

* Automatic Identification System uses MMSI codegroups for ship ID
* Global Maritime Distress Safety System
* Inmarsat and the International Mobile Satellite Organization (IMSO)
* Maritime call sign, not tied to MMSI but can contain MMSI after
* SOLAS Convention a global Maritime Safety Convention

<document>
<title>Maritime identification digits</title>
<fragment>
**Maritime identification digits** are used by radio communication facilities to identify their home country or base area in Digital Selective Calling (DSC), Automatic Transmitter Identification System (ATIS), and Automatic Identification System (AIS) messages as part of their Maritime Mobile Service Identities. The International Telecommunication Union facilitates the assignment of MIDs to countries.[1] Note that not all countries have MIDs; those without are typically landlocked, with no access to international waters. Sorting MID assignments in numerical order reveals a regional structure, with the first digit:



* 2 assigned to Europe,
* 3 to North America and the Caribbean Sea,
* 4 to Asia (except the southeast),
* 5 to the Pacific and Eastern Indian Oceans and Southeast Asia,
* 6 to Africa, the Atlantic and Western Indian Oceans, and
* 7 to South America.

Based on my research of Wikipedia sources, I can provide you with comprehensive information about MMSI (Maritime Mobile Service Identity) lookup databases and how to access them. Here's what I found:

## Official Sources for MMSI Information

### 1. **International Telecommunication Union (ITU)**
- **Website**: `https://www.itu.int`
- **Official Resource**: Table of Maritime Identification Digits (MIDs)
- **Description**: The ITU is the primary international authority that regulates telecommunications, including maritime radio services. They maintain the official list of Maritime Identification Digits (the first 3 digits of MMSI codes).
- **Access**: Navigate to the ITU website, search for "Maritime Identification Digits" or "M.585 Recommendation"

### 2. **U.S. Coast Guard Navigation Center**
- **Website**: Referenced as having MMSI information adapted from ITU Radio Regulations
- **Description**: Provides maritime mobile service identity information and guidance for U.S. vessels
- **Access**: Through the USCG Navigation Center website

### 3. **Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA)**
- **Website**: Referenced as having MMSI guidelines and information
- **Description**: Provides MMSI assignment and verification services for Australian vessels

## Key Information About MMSI Codes

### **Structure of MMSI Numbers:**
- **9-digit unique identification codes**
- **Format**: XXX-XXXXXX (where XXX are the Maritime Identification Digits - country code)
- **Assigned by**: Flag state authorities (not ITU directly)
- **Changes**: New MMSI required when vessel is re-flagged

### **Types of MMSI Identities:**
1. Ship station identities
2. Group ship station identities  
3. Coast station identities
4. Group coast station identities
5. SAR aircraft
6. Navigational aids and craft associated with a parent ship

## Regional Structure of MMSI Codes
The first digit indicates geographic region:
- **2xx**: Europe
- **3xx**: North America and Caribbean
- **4xx**: Asia (except southeast)
- **5xx**: Pacific and Eastern Indian Oceans, Southeast Asia
- **6xx**: Africa, Atlantic and Western Indian Oceans
- **7xx**: South America

## Search Requirements and Tips

### **For Official Verification:**
1. **Contact National Maritime Authorities**: Each flag state maintains its own vessel registry
2. **Use ITU MID Table**: First verify the country code portion
3. **Check Commercial AIS Providers**: While not official, they have extensive databases

### **Search Tips:**
- MMSI codes are always 9 digits
- The first 3 digits (MID) identify the flag state
- Individual vessel verification requires contacting the appropriate maritime authority
- For vessel tracking, MMSI numbers are used in AIS (Automatic Identification System) broadcasts

## Commercial AIS/Vessel Tracking Services
The Wikipedia references mention that AIS (Automatic Identification System) uses MMSI codes for ship identification. While not official government sources, major commercial vessel tracking services like MarineTraffic, VesselFinder, and others maintain extensive AIS/MMSI databases that can be useful for verification purposes, though they are not considered official sources for maritime operations.

## Recommendation
For official maritime operations and verification:
1. Start with the **ITU MID table** to verify the country code
2. Contact the **appropriate national maritime authority** of the flag state for individual vessel verification
3. Use **USCG Navigation Center** resources for U.S.-flagged vessels
4. For comprehensive vessel information, consult the **flag state's official vessel registry**

Note that there isn't a single global database for all MMSI codes accessible via web search - verification typically requires going through the appropriate national maritime authority that assigned the MMSI.

<document>
<title>DNV</title>
<fragment>
* DNV Rules for Classification of Ships
* DNV Rules for Classification of High Speed, Light Craft
* DNV Rules for Classification of inland navigation vessels
* DNV Rules for Classification of underwater technology
* DNV Rules for Classification of offshore units and floating docs

* DNV Type Approval Programmes for EU recognised organisation Mutual Recognition (MR)
* DNV Class guidelines


## References

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

* **DNV — Maritime**: Classification, verification, risk-management, training and technical advisory to the maritime industry on safety, enhanced performance, fuel efficiency, etc. As a classification society, DNV sets standards for ships and offshore structures, known as Class Rules. They comprise safety, reliability and environmental requirements that vessels and other offshore mobile structures in international waters must comply with. DNV is authorized by 130 maritime administrations to perform certification or verification on their behalf.

</fragment>
<fragment>
1. **^** "DNV Annual Report 2020". Retrieved 2021-04-08.
2. **^** Smale, Will (21 December 2014). "The Norwegian firm that tests the world's ships". *BBC News*. Archived from the original on 11 February 2015. Retrieved 16 February 2015.
3. **^** "DNV GL changes name to DNV as it gears up for decade of transformation". *DNV*. 2021-01-13. Archived from the original on 2021-01-27. Retrieved 2021-03-06.
4. **^** "DNV GL to unveil rules this year". Tanker Operator. Archived from the original on 17 February 2015. Retrieved 16 February 2015.
5. **^** "Remi Eriksen: Proud and Confident". *maritime-executive.com*. Archived from the original on 4 March 2016. Retrieved 3 May 2018.
6. **^** "Det Norske Veritas Germanischer Lloyd (DNV GL) - Careers in Marine Classification Industry".
7. **^** "Spotlight on Germanischer Lloyd". Maritime Executive. 2 April 2008. Archived from the original on 22 February 2015. Retrieved 22 February 2015.

</fragment>
<fragment>

**DNV** (formerly **DNV GL**) is an international accredited registrar and classification society headquartered in Høvik, Norway.[2] The company currently has about 12,000 employees and 350 offices operating in more than 100 countries, and provides services for several industries including maritime, oil and gas, renewable energy, electrification, food and beverage, and healthcare. DNV GL was created in 2013 as a result of a merger between two leading organizations in the field — ***Det Norske Veritas*** (Norway) and ***Germanischer Lloyd*** (Germany). In 2021, DNV GL changed its name to DNV, while retaining its post-merger structure.[3]


</fragment>
<fragment>

DNV is the world's largest classification society, providing services for 13,175 vessels and mobile offshore units (MOUs) amounting to 265.4 million gross tonnes, which represents a global market share of 21%.[4] It is also the largest technical consultancy and supervisory to the global renewable energy (particularly wind, wave, tidal and solar) and oil and gas industries — 65% of the world's offshore pipelines are designed and installed to DNV's technical standards.


Prior to the merger, both DNV and GL had independently acquired several companies in different sectors, such as *Hélimax Energy* (Canada), *Garrad Hassan* (UK), *Windtest* (Germany) and *KEMA* (Netherlands), which now contribute to DNV's expertise across several industries. In addition to providing services such as technical assessment, certification, risk management and software development, DNV also invests heavily in research.


Remi Eriksen is the Group President and CEO of DNV since August 1, 2015, succeeding Henrik O. Madsen.[5]




</fragment>

Based on my research, here's a comprehensive guide to the 6 maritime databases you requested for ship call sign and vessel verification:

## **1. International Telecommunication Union (ITU) Maritime Database**

**Official Website:** https://www.itu.int

**Database Information:**
- Contains global framework for maritime identification systems
- Maintains Maritime Identification Digits (MID) tables
- Governs MMSI and maritime call sign assignment standards

**Access & Search:**
- Navigate to ITU publications
- Search for **ITU-R Recommendation M.585**
- Access Maritime Identification Digits tables through ITU publications

**Search Tips:**
- ITU provides the framework but actual database access is through national maritime authorities
- Cross-reference with flag state maritime administrations for individual vessel verification
- Use U.S. Coast Guard Navigation Center as secondary source: https://www.navcen.uscg.gov/?pageName=MMSI

---

## **2. Bahamas Maritime Authority Ship Registry**

**Official Website:** bahamasmaritime.com

**Database Information:**
- Registry of all Bahamian-registered vessels
- Vessel ownership, classification, and compliance details
- Registration certificates and maritime documentation

**Access & Search:**
- Visit official website and navigate to registry services
- Contact maritime authority offices for direct database access
- International offices: Nassau, New York, London, Hong Kong

**Search Tips:**
- May require registration or professional maritime credentials
- Direct contact with BMA recommended for official verification
- Official Gazette publishes vessel registration changes

---

## **3. FCC Maritime Radio Service Database**

**Official Website:** https://wireless.fcc.gov (Universal Licensing System - ULS)

**Database Information:**
- All FCC maritime radio station licenses
- Vessel call signs and radio equipment details
- License status and renewal information

**Access & Search:**
- Navigate to **Universal Licensing System (ULS)**
- Use **License Search** functionality
- Filter by **Radio Service Code SA** (Ship Recreational/Voluntarily Equipped)

**Search Tips:**
- Maritime call signs begin with K or W (e.g., KX0983, WXX0029)
- Different service codes for recreational vs. commercial vessels
- Search by vessel name, call sign, or license holder

---

## **4. US Coast Guard Vessel Documentation Database**

**Primary Database:** Marine Information for Safety and Law Enforcement (MISLE)

**Public Access:** Port State Information Exchange (PSIX)

**Official Access:** Through USCG Homeport website or uscg.mil

**Database Information:**
- Comprehensive vessel documentation for US-flagged vessels
- Registration details, safety inspections, incident reports
- Over 650,000 vessels in database

**Access & Search:**
- Navigate to **USCG Homeport** → **MISLE PSIX**
- Search by vessel name, official number, IMO number
- Public access limited to non-sensitive information

**Search Tips:**
- PSIX provides FOIA-approved vessel information
- Unclosed cases and privileged information restricted
- Contact National Vessel Documentation Center for official certificates

---

## **5. Maritime Mobile Service Identity (MMSI) Databases**

**Primary Sources:**
- **ITU:** https://www.itu.int (MID tables)
- **USCG Navigation Center:** https://www.navcen.uscg.gov/?pageName=MMSI
- **National Maritime Authorities** (flag states)

**Database Information:**
- 9-digit MMSI codes for vessels and maritime stations
- Format: 3-digit country code (MID) + 6-digit vessel identifier
- Used for AIS, GMDSS, and digital communication

**Access & Search:**
- Verify country code using ITU MID table
- Contact appropriate national maritime authority for vessel details
- USCG database for US-flagged vessels

**Search Tips:**
- MMSI always 9 digits
- New MMSI required when vessel re-flagged
- First digit indicates region (2xx=Europe, 3xx=North America, etc.)

---

## **6. DNV Vessel Register Database**

**Official Website:** https://www.dnv.com

**Digital Platforms:**
- **Veracity:** https://www.veracity.com
- **Exchange Platform:** Customer portal access

**Database Information:**
- 13,175+ DNV-classed vessels and offshore units
- Classification details, technical specifications
- Compliance with DNV Class Rules and safety requirements

**Access & Search:**
- Navigate to DNV Maritime section
- Access through customer portal (requires registration)
- Use **IMO number** for most efficient searches

**Search Tips:**
- IMO number provides unique vessel identification
- Professional maritime credentials often required
- Contact DNV regional offices for direct verification
- Subscription may be required for comprehensive access

---

## **Recommended Verification Process for Maritime Operations:**

1. **Start with flag state maritime authority** - Most authoritative source
2. **Cross-reference with ITU framework** - Verify country codes and standards
